item.title: [Mercatus Center] Shreyas Narla and Kadambari Shah on the 'The 1991 Project'
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、口述史作为"反熵工程"：一个隐藏的悖论

表面上看，1991 Project 是在做一件"档案学"的工作——抢救即将消失的记忆。但真正惊人的是它揭示的一个反常识事实：印度作为世界上最古老的官僚体系之一，居然不知道自己历任首席经济顾问的确切上任日期。Shankar Acharya 是第 10 任 CEA，可前 9 任的入职月份都要靠事后拼凑。

这暴露了一个更深的系统性真相：印度政府是一个"高吞吐、零沉淀"的系统。它每天处理海量决策，但几乎不留下"决策的元数据"——谁在什么时候、基于什么想法、受谁影响做了什么。这与印度作为"世界最大民主制"的宏大叙事形成了刺眼的反差。1991 Project 本质上不是在写历史，而是在为一个失忆的国家做记忆器官移植手术。

跨领域联系：这非常像神经科学里的"陈述性记忆 vs 程序性记忆"——印度政府拥有极强的"程序性记忆"（继续运作的能力），却几乎没有"陈述性记忆"（能被检索、被反思的知识）。而一个没有陈述性记忆的组织，注定会重复自己的失败。

二、一个让人意外的观察：改革不是"想法的胜利"，而是"社交网络的胜利"

访谈里最反直觉的一个片段是：Shreyas 在德里 T3 航站楼"劫持"了 Chidambaram，仅仅因为提到 "Rangarajan 已经录过"，对方态度立刻转变。这不是关于内容的说服，而是关于信任链的传递。

这揭示了一个被主流经济学严重低估的真相：1991 改革的技术方案早在 1960 年代就存在（Bhagwati-Desai 1968 那本书基本预言了一切），改革之所以能落地，不是因为想法赢了，而是因为 Manmohan Singh 花了 30 年时间做了一件事——"人才侦察"（talent scout）。他把 Rakesh Mohan、Montek、Y.V. Reddy、Urjit Patel 这些人一个个从世界银行、地方任所、研究所拽进政策核心圈，直到有一天危机来临，整个网络已经就位。

跨领域连接：这与 Silicon Valley 的运作机制惊人相似。 PayPal Mafia 之所以能改变世界，不是因为 PayPal 的技术多革命，而是因为它孵化了一个高信任度的人才网络。1991 改革的"Manmohan Mafia"是同一种现象的政府版本。这暗示了一个大胆推论：印度过去 20 年改革停滞的真正原因，不是缺少想法，而是这个"信任网络"没有被复制。 Shruti 启动 1991 Fellowship 的行为，本质上是在做"网络的再生产工程"——这比任何政策论文都更接近改革的真正杠杆点。

三、一个隐藏的系统性真相：为什么"记忆缺失"和"改革停滞"是同一个问题

访谈里有一个极容易被忽略的连接：Kadambari 提到，联合政府改革在 15-20 年后停滞，原因是"这些人升上去了，但没人培养下一代"。而 Shreyas 提到，为什么信息如此难找？因为"没有交接、没有离任访谈"。

这两件事其实是同一个病灶的两个症状：印度政府缺乏"知识的世代传递机制"。

用生物学的类比：这就像一个物种拥有强大的个体生存能力（现任官员非常能干），但繁殖机制（培养下一代技术官僚）严重退化。结果就是——每一代改革者都必须从零开始重新发明轮子，每一次危机都要靠"运气"派上合适的人。

更深一层的意外观察：1991 Project 无意中做了一件比它自己意识到的更重要的事——它不仅在记录改革，它在示范"改革所需要的那种基础设施"应该长什么样。"triangulation"（三角验证）、跨代的 mixer、Chatham House 规则的会议、fellowship 项目——这些看似是"研究工具"，实际上是印度政府自己应该内建、但从未内建的制度性记忆器官。

一个刺耳的推论：如果一个私人智库（Mercatus + 一个五人小团队）能建成比印度财政部更完整的印度经济改革档案，那这不是他们做得好，而是印度国家能力在某个维度上的彻底失败。 而这个失败，恰恰是下一轮改革最应该攻克的对象——比劳动法、土地法都更根本。

啊哈时刻：1991 Project 表面上是"回望过去"，本质上是在为一个还没到来的国家能力革命做原型设计。它示范的不是"我们该学历史"，而是"我们该建什么样的记忆基础设施才能持续改革"。

📝 转录文本

开场与介绍

Welcome to Ideas of India, where we examine academic ideas that can propel India forward. My name is Shruti Rajagopalan and I'm a senior research fellow at the Mercatus Centre at George Mason University. Today my guests are my colleagues Shreyas Narla and Kadambari Shah. Shreyas is a research scholar and Kadambari is a research associate at the Mercatus Centre with the India Programme.

We talked about completing five years of the 1991 project, how it started, its scope, the oral histories of the reformers in 1991, papers, essays, fellowships, and much more. For a full transcript of this conversation, including helpful links of all the references mentioned, click the link in the show notes or visit mercatus.org slash podcasts.

Hi, welcome to Ideas of India, though it feels like I'm in one of our team meetings because today my guests are my wonderful colleagues Kadamri Shah and Shreyas Nalla, who've been on the podcast before and whom all of you know as my listeners. And today we're going to talk about the 1991 reforms and the 1991 project. This week and month is the 35th anniversary of the 1991 reforms. It's almost hard for me to believe. And also the fifth anniversary of the project. We kicked it off in the 30th year of the reforms. So it is such a pleasure to have both of you here and thank you for joining me.

Glad to be back. Though we've pretty much been here the whole time.

Thank you for having us, Shruti. Yeah, this is so much fun.

So like I said, you know, this is the 35th anniversary. It just feels like I must be getting really old because I remember the reforms actually happening and reading about it in the papers and things like that. And second, I also can't believe it's been five years of the project. It still feels like, you know, every day we're doing something new. Every week we're discovering something new. But I guess we've been at this for a while.

项目的起源

Yeah, I don't think I've ever asked you guys, you know, I joined the project a year into it, but how did it start?

Oh, that's a good story. So the way it started is we were talking about the reforms and that time one of our colleagues and, you know, all of our good friend Prakhar Mishra was on the team before he was off to his, to do his doctoral studies. So Shreyas, Prakhar and I used to work with each other. It was COVID and we were talking about the reforms. And I realized that they didn't know too much about it, which is really weird now that you know, both of them is like, they are very like they're about as nerdy as it gets when it comes to the policy wonk space. And I was like, if they don't know exactly why the 1991 reforms happened or how they happened, then no one will know.

Right. Because, you know, as I always say, 70% plus of India was born after me, which means like a very large number of Indians, almost two thirds were born after the reforms. And they really don't have any lived experience of socialism and licensed permit Raj command and control times. So they've really just lived in this forced liberalization world without licensed permit Raj in the draconian way it used to be. There is still a lot of licensed permit Raj at local and state levels.

So that was really what got me started. And I said, if they don't know the story, then hardly anyone knows the story. And the only people who know the story are those older than me. So we started talking about it and Shreyas you were there right at the start. What did we decide to do in the beginning? Now my memory is failing me a bit.

So Kadambari actually, I mean to answer your question and then to get to your question Shruti, I'm a lawyer by training which means that I'm going to only look at the law and never really ask the question where did this come from and how did this come about and what's the context in which these laws are being legislated upon. It's a given for me. So when I look at a labor law, when I look at an industrial disputes act, or when I looked at the MRTP for his, you know, that was the extent of my exposure to history of policy, so to speak, or the law. Or if I look at a competition act, I'm looking at them as just their laws, but not necessarily why they're happening and in what context they're taking place.

And this is exactly what the conversation was five years ago, or a little over five years ago, when Shruti, Prakhar and I were chatting about the '91 reforms. And I realized I had a sort of a headline understanding of what the reforms were, because if you either went to law school or you had some exposure to studying economics at school level, you hear the abbreviation LPG. And that's about it. I kind of get a sense of who Narasimha Rao was or who Manmohan Singh was. Vinay had written the Half-Line book, Sanjaya Bhargava, though he wrote Accidental Prime Minister. In a way, these conversations were happening. These books were out there. One was reading. You had some understanding of it. But again, I'm a post-91 child, so I basically grew up with having consumer goods at home. So I don't have lived experience. I didn't have a sense of how different life was before that. And even through the educational journey, you're really taking a lot of things as a given.

And which is what actually motivated us to start the 91 Project with the idea that this will be a pedagogical project. We will write materials for my generation, my peers, and who have come afterwards as a way to, one, get exposed to what this literature is, but in a way that it's well understood by people from across the spectrum of disciplines, where the economic jargon or the technical concepts will not go over our head. We will understand what really happened, understand the weight of the situation as well. Because when you're talking about the crisis, when you're talking about balance of payments crisis, and you're talking about the war that was happening, these are terms, but what do they really mean, right? To somebody who's not studied economics.

So that was the intent behind what we set up the 9to1 project to be, which meant that we were going to have, you know, these simple timelines to explain how the crisis unfolded and then what did the reforms do. We wrote these few early pieces, Shruti's essay and mine and Prakhar's essay, which was really a narrative style of portraying the importance of the episode, what the reforms did and what it really unleashed for the Indian economy. That was really what the project was supposed to be about. But of course, you know, when we touch something, it's not going to be just a simple thing. So, but that's really the origin story.

And now I realize, you know, hearing Shreya's talk that he was working on a paper on MRTP actually. So that's the big part of how the conversation started. But the other part of it was also, I just realized no one even knew what had happened. So our initial efforts were actually just to tell people what had happened.

危机的实质

Like right now we have a West Asian crisis, right? We had a similar West Asian crisis and war, oil prices went up. Like all these things happened then, except India had such few reserves. And the Indian economy was generally in such a terrible situation that very soon it came to a point where India did not have enough money to pay for more than two weeks worth of exports. And that's the crisis part.

And in a country as large as India and an economy as large as India, there are many silent crises which we don't talk about. I mean, people not getting jobs, just very... The fact that there are still so many people who are so poor and without opportunity or it is so hard for people to start a business. There are lots of little and large crises going on in India. But the crisis which birth the reforms was actually just about not being able to pay your bills, which was an enormous embarrassment, right? To actually have to ship the gold out of the country because you have, you know, no one trusts that your economic ability to pay something back. It was a very big moment.

So the initial part of the project, to answer your question, was all about, let's tell people what happened. In what order it happened, what was the political instability, you know, three prime ministers in quick succession, what was the economic instability with the Gulf War and rising oil prices and enormous deficits and a currency which was actually had nothing to do with its real value and had a huge black market and so on. And then you know how the reforms actually tackled it.

So that was... It was supposed to be a really simple project, Kadamdi. We started ideating it around like March and it was supposed to end end of July and we were done and that's it. And then of course, as Shreya says, nothing is ever done when we touch it. It just kind of becomes a thing.

No, I'm so glad that this project was started not only because it helped me learn as well as a post-91 child myself, but also because it's been so exciting to work on since I joined the team.

When did you join the team? This was about a year into the, or maybe like six months since the release of the project, right? And about nine months of us ideating.

Exactly. Exactly.

Yeah. And that's a good origin story too, because I wanted Kadambari to be on our team well before that. And you know, when she had finished her master's degree, like we've known each other a while. So I had actually spoken to her about what her plans are. And she was doing some very exciting research for one of her professors. And I was like, okay, if you're doing exciting research with someone else and it's, you know, putting you on the right track, then you stay at that and maybe we'll work together another time. And then six months later, two things happened. One, the 1991 project happened, which she was very interested in joining. And two, Prakhar started his PhD. So we really needed someone on the project. And it was like, we both called each other and we were like, okay, now is the time to do this. So that was also like a very nice, you know, part of, so she was really there when the project started, just not directly working on it.

口述史项目的启动

Yeah, I think one of the very first meetings I joined was actually an oral history with Mr. Montek Singhaluvalia.

Oh, that's right. Yeah. Was he your first oral history? No, he wasn't our first oral history. He was our third one. The first one was Dr. Rangarajan, that's right.

Before you jump in on the oral history with, you know, Montic and Rangarajan, how did we get started on the oral histories exactly?

So this actually goes to the starting point of the 91 Project. I was called on to work on writing the biographies of the reformers, because of my general interest in policy history, you said, hey, why don't you at least document who these reformers were and exactly what their points of intervention was in the 91 story.

I wanted him to do a lot more, by the way, but Shreyas was like, I'm not an economist and I have no idea what I'm talking about. And I'm like, trust me, you know enough economics to be able to do this. But I don't know, Shreyas was very nervous because I think he got scared by the MRTP Act. I think one was one that for sure, but I think...

I mean, everyone was scared of the MRTP Act, as we know from history, including our reformers, because they had the tough task of actually displaying it.

I started out sort of documenting these profiles and fascinating to see how what their backgrounds were but also to understand how these players interacted with each other, what their points of intervention was, whether it was Dr Rangarajan as a deputy governor and then he comes back as governor, Montixing Aluvalia who worked at the World Bank and then sort of enters into the finance ministry as an economic advisor and then sort of you know we know his journey right up to his role as commerce secretary in 91 and there and you know later on as the secretary department of economic affairs as finance secretary.

Some of them had written their memoirs, some of them had just written some essays or book chapters, we had some general sense of the story and there were obviously you know some papers that were written, you know these survey chapters and survey papers, we had all the big names, the usual you know you have Manmohan Singh, Narsimha, Montek and everybody. That's how you know, that's what's the documented material, whether it's the wiki entry or any of the other papers or survey chapters written.

There were some journal papers that documented some names, but, you know, these are long forgotten. We're talking 30 years ago, 25 years ago. These were written. If you're actually in it, you're trying to read and look at, maybe you'll find it on a JSTOR. And that's the level of engagement with the episode. That means that it's one, this information is clear. I would say gate kept, but it was definitely an information that's not easily accessible to a larger group of people.

And so when we were setting up the 91 Project, we set up those timelines, we wrote these biographies, we made, you know, and people appreciated it. You know, people wrote to us from our fraternity. There was KP Krishnan and, you know, so who sort of spoke to us about it. And in fact, I remember going to meet him at Prakhar. And he started dropping these names of different secretaries, joint secretaries who were in the ministry at that point in time. I had not heard of Jayantar Roy in any story, but he was the Commerce Ministry's economic advisor. And that's how I discovered—and NK Singh had just written his memoirs. I had not read it yet, but he came up in conversation that he was at the fund division in the finance ministry as joint secretary. And the fact that Rakesh Mohan had been around for a long time, and of course it was his book chapter that he wrote in the 25th anniversary volume that he had produced, so it was in a way it was him talking about his journey.

But obviously when you know we are piecing these stories together and then we had folks like KP talking to us and telling us all these little anecdotes... And it felt interesting and exciting. And I said, but where do we get them from? And then they said, well, you know, this is when you speak to these actual reformers. You'll have to talk to them. And when you talk to them, you'll get to know about it. But they're also old, which means that we don't have the luxury of time. And also the fact that we have to respect their, you know, I mean, I'm not going to mention these details, but there were several of our reformers who were not medically in a position to talk to us. And that was already like five years ago. And so there was a sense of urgency there.

And that was the origin point where we were encouraged from members in the policy communities. They may have written memoirs, but not everything makes it to the memoir. They may have been survey chapters, not everything makes it to the final edit, which means that through the cracks, you will miss out the nuances of their relationships, the influences.

Also, you know, this intergenerational thing, right, Reyes? Like, you know, so for instance, Ajay Shah and Niranjan Rajat Hyakshu, we all know really well. They've heard these stories firsthand from, let's say, Vijay Kilkar or Rangarajan or someone like that. Now we are hearing a second version of it.

That's true. And it's like, first of all, now memory is failing. You know, you don't want this to be a Chinese whispers kind of thing, right? Where they hear it from a source and then we hear it from them. And so that was one thing that they warned us about that we can tell you some information, but you should go straight to the source.

制度记忆的缺失

Uh, but the second part of it also is I realized we don't have good institutional history and memory. So, you know, so much of this was done by technocrats, right Kadamri? So you know this, you worked with government. We don't have a system where when a particular bureaucrat or technocrat leaves an office, they don't do an exit interview. They don't do any kind of handoff. We can't even find in India starting and ending dates. And when I say dates, I don't mean the exact date. I mean years. Okay. We can't even find the year when someone started and someone ended in a particular department or office.

So unless we actually talk to the people and then triangulate the same information from two, three different sets of people, you don't have a good handle on what actually happened. You know, so it's a little bit like Roshamon, right? You know, there's some material out there and there's something you can pick and then you actually have to go to people and they all are slightly different versions of this. And then, you know, if like four out of five people give you a very similar version, you're like, okay, I think that's the right one. Right. Or we, we'll take that as the, as the dominant account.

So that was a very big part of it, but that we, we realized that really during the oral history, but we realized that even before starting the oral history project that we just don't know enough. And you guys know this and you've heard me say this many times.

I think this is India's second freedom. I think the reforms are as important as getting universal adult franchise or something, because I think participating in the marketplace is as important as participating in the political space. And not everyone was allowed to participate in the marketplace, whether as a consumer or as a producer, it doesn't matter. You just don't have market access. So for me, it was like, this is, I think, one of the most important things that's happened in my lifetime. And one of the most important things that has happened in post-independent India. And we just don't have a good sense of it.

This reminds me of a little anecdote that Dr. Acharya mentioned to us in his oral history. where when he became chief economic advisor, this is I'm talking just after the 91 reforms, you know, the 92 period. And then he has one of the longest tenures, actually the longest tenure.

Sorry to interrupt, but that itself was hard to piece together because of the chief economic advisor, there was an economic consultant and another economic advisor, all in quick succession. And we were like, what is going on? So even that took us a second to get a handle on, you know, the move from Deepak Nair to Ashok Desai to Shankar Acharya.

Exactly. And the fact that there is this whole concept of a UPSC entry and a non-UPSC entry, I mean, where are these rule books? Who gets to understand that? Unless someone tells you and explains this to you.

But Shankaracharya told us that how when he became chief economic advisor, there was no board. And when I say board, like a wooden board, a plaque in the office of the chief economic advisor, which oftentimes an industry secretary or a finance secretary office would have, where you get to have the entire list of all the previous chief economic advisors with their date of appointment to the date of retirement. One didn't exist for the chief economic advisor's office, and he was the 10th chief economic advisor. So nine people had already held that post. And there wasn't a clear, and even for those nine, he said, because he set it up, finally documented. And he said that even for those nine, for the early, some of the ones, some of the advisors, they didn't have the exact date. They had maybe the month rough, like a rough estimate of the month they joined in the month, but not even the date.

So, I'm talking about like maybe roughly about 45-50 years of independence and within that period we didn't have one of the senior most technocratic positions in the Union Government of India didn't have a clean... In the finance ministry. The finance ministry of all ministries didn't have a clean record of who held that office for how long or how specifically how long they held that office.

方法论的建立

And that's the sense you get from these oral histories as well. And so, but this is the thing. Oral histories, if you just generally look at how they are done is, like you said, it's a free-flowing conversation. You can go talk to them and you must make them feel comfortable. They'll start speaking. They'll remember. They'll recollect. They'll share. That's how often they go. You press the record button and you just go run with it.

A lot of the, at that point in time, the 1947 partition project was doing a lot of the rounds in India. Delhi was rife with these sessions or events that the 1947 partition project was doing. And that was the moment you kind of had a sense of how oral histories were being done. And they were all, like I said, very, I wouldn't say casual, but they were definitely a lot more personable. It's like a you know having a family type of conversation and then you're just capturing the essence of it.

But we couldn't do that for something like this. Maybe one part of it is also like, it made sense to do it that way for that particular project. Because partition is also like, you know, personal memories, people are talking about very traumatic events. And we also knew that that just wouldn't work for us because we are not trying to get the texture of something. We're actually trying to get the technical details of something, right? So, which is why we never went the oral history way. We were going the documentation way. And you know, all credit to Shreyas. He's the one who figured out how to marry the two together. How do we marry really good documentation and excellent methodological discipline with also getting people to share their memories of what happened. And, you know, so you need a lot of room for technical detail, but you also need a lot of room for personal and institutional memory. And I think Shreyas is the one who cracked that puzzle because none of us knew what we were doing.

Well, I mean, I can't take the entire credit there because, you know, you have to look for inspiration, you have to look for guidance. And one of the places we had looked for was obviously World Bank had done an institutional memory oral history project, but it felt like a bit of an in-group speak kind of a thing where there were a lot of, perhaps also because I was coming up from the outside, so I necessarily didn't understand the references, but those transcripts kind of read like an ongoing conversation. And I was eavesdropping without much context. And I realized that if 91 Project with the intention we had set it up, our oral histories couldn't do that.

And so, you know, and at that time, you know, Prakhar leading the way and given how enterprising he is with his networks, he was able to tap into different people to set up some meetings for us. I remember you had made the connection with Nona Storr, who was at GMU. And Nona had done oral histories internally at the Mercatus Center a while ago, I believe. So when we first spoke to Nona, she understood this dilemma, you know, it can't be these personal conversations. It's also institutional memory. So how do we do it? So she said, it's fine to send them questions in advance. Now, she said, let's figure out how you do that, because you can't be too, you know, too specific to the point that you sort of curb and then alter their memory because you're prompting them but at the same time you can't be loosey-goosey in the ref in the way you're drafted you know you're asking those questions because then how will they recollect and have the specific details you're looking for so you'll have to find that right balance now i mean you know that was going to be a trial and error for us.

We spoke to Ryan Perkins who was at Stanford University at that uh you know still at Stanford University but um he was a wonderful reference point for us because he had set up, I think he was the curator for the South Asian and Islamic studies. So he was one of the top archivists for that particular department. So he gave us some insight. Stanford has a very rich, detailed work on oral history projects. They have these lovely 10 tips to remember kind of stuff. They also had templates for contracts of how do you handle oral history and post-production and releases and things like that. So Prakhar and I really sat down, we had these conversations with these individuals. We had all these leads from KP Krishnan and Ajay Shah who had done these sessions with us, giving us some frameworks to fall back on in understanding who to speak to and what context we must speak to them with.

And then came up with this rubric, complete our proposed to Prakhar on this one, where he said we're going to ask them questions about the reforms, about the individuals and the ideas and influences, which is really our Mercatus framework, we are now the three eyes and how we're going to craft these questions. So a lot of workshopping those questions where one, when we first started out and you wrote that fantastic cold email to Dr. Rangarajan and he really, really just so generously wrote back and responded.

And then in a way, we worked out that template where the first thing that we do is we spoke to the reformers. We talked to them and generally had to get a sense of how comfortable they were participating, what they wanted to speak about, what were the limits. So really, as I call it, setting the boundaries. And that made it to our note as we developed the project that the first thing we do is we set boundaries for the reformers of what they want to talk about. You know, we've been writing papers on a variety of topics. We did the whole policy paper series, you know, and you kind of are the hem of running that project. Do tell us more about that.

It was just picking up from the same idea that led to the writing section on the website, the video series and so on that what is the next set of reforms that we need to look at going forward? And the policy paper series stemmed from that idea itself, where we wrote papers among the team, but also commissioned papers from outside because we wanted to get an idea about what reforms are yet to be done. The world looks very different today than it did in '91, which means that the reforms needed today are different from what was needed then.

And we were very lucky to get great scholars in their fields to tell us what we should be doing. So we had Shreyas of course on India's competition law and the risks of being anti-big or anti-scale in ways that hurt growth and consumers. Dr. Arvind Panagaria wrote on India's trade policy and the case for returning to a more liberal trade regime. We had Amartya Lahiri and Devashy Smith writing on India's central development challenge, creating productive jobs through labor intensive manufacturing and exports. Sarthak Pradhan and Pranay Kottasthane wrote on India's climb up the innovation ladder and the policy barriers that still hold back Indian firms. Praveen Krishna wrote on India's trade agreements and whether they've actually worked a serious trade strategy. Shruti and I wrote on how India's labor laws prevent firms from scaling and discourage them from hiring more workers. And Ankita Dinkar and Samrut Surana wrote on electricity challenges faced by Indian manufacturers like unreliable power, high tariffs and barriers to open access.

And we started this two years ago and look at how relevant everything became right from the trade war to semiconductor and growing our R&D like somehow we were poised like we could see this coming and we put out papers.

Exactly. And the effort continues, right? I mean, you know, these were, of course, all looking at issues at the union level, so to speak, and you're talking about trade and this thing, but electricity has much more resonance over the state policy level. This is a common chapter. We experienced this at the India, Ideas of India conference in, you know, in Bangalore last year, and the conversations thereafter, especially in light of the deregulation agenda, is we've all looked at the union level, we've all looked at what could be done, but the interest now is at the state list of the constitution and how do we go about thinking about reforms at the state level.

We've been working on our land series and we wrote one and published on land use conversion laws and just the multiplicity of regulatory overload there. and how that gets in the way of making land accessible easily for different uses without having to go through different loops just to do something and make the most of your land and continuing on that trajectory of building work on that. But this requires extreme effort because you're trying to study 20, 21 states whose laws are accessible, going through those documents, notifications, circulars. I mean, it's the three of us and Ankita and our team and a few of our collaborators And Ankit Bhatia who's written a couple of the papers with us.

But you know that I somehow find still to be easier shares. Like the thing that Katamdi is talking about which is getting outside people to write and then get it peer reviewed and shepherd that project start to finish is like a big one to do any paper series actually. Very right. So you're coordinating across so many different people. Yeah, internally we all work very... The internal team works in a fairly frictionless way. Yeah, yeah, that is true. That is true. Not so much the state we are trying to study. Unlike the states.

1991 Fellowship：培养下一代

Kadavari, what is on the docket for the papers?

So actually, the next big step for us is that we've launched the 1991 fellowship. And we've got—speaking of how hard it is to get people to write, and especially from the outside, but also to find people who are working on these ideas. So that, I mean, the 1991 fellowship is your brainchild, Shruti. Do you want to talk a little bit about that?

Yeah, so I mean, yeah, this is also directly related to what we're doing with the paper series. But, you know, it became crystal clear to us while doing the 1991 project that a lot of the macro stability, currency related, you know, monetary and fiscal side of the reforms were all done at the union level. And we've kind of done a lot of work there and also the worst has been crossed. Like we've already seen that this year, right? I mean, we had another kind of balance of payment stress, but it didn't turn into a crisis, right? So a lot of the reforms that were done 30, 35 years ago, they've actually held us in very good stead.

Now, what remains to be done is almost all state level subjects, right? So Shreyas and I come from a legal background. We have the state list, the union list and the concurrent list. Labor, of course, is a big area on the concurrent list, but a lot of the land, agriculture, energy policy, all of this needs to be done at the state level.

And there were two things happening. One is most people don't think of state level reforms as the cool thing to work on. So that's one kind of problem. But I think that number is, you know, increasing slowly but steadily. There are more and more people working at state level policy. But the second problem is any time we talk to people, whether it's the think tank community or someone else, and we see the next stage is really state level policy and what are you doing about it? They say, "Oh, we'd love to do something on it, but where's the talent?" And, you know, I've heard this lament for 20 years. I've been in this business and in these circles for a really long time. 20 years ago, I didn't know anyone who could tell me anything about Odisha's energy policy. 20 years have passed and there's still not too many people.

So Mercatus has a very, very clear vision and mission, which is classical liberal ideas, but ideas don't live in the air, right? They're incubated in individuals and networks. So really the Mercatus approach to all of this is can we find and incubate the talent? Mercatus has hundreds of fellows. This is from, you know, sort of high school level, undergrad, masters, PhDs, postdocs, professors. You know, also the Emerging Ventures Fellows, Policy Fellows. So we really have them at each level. We have, I think, just on the academic side of things, about six to eight hundred fellows every year at Mercatus through various programs. So the idea that I landed on in a very sort of obvious way, just because of where we are and where I come from, is we need to figure out the state level policy talent and we need to incubate it.

So what we started was the 1991 fellowship, and this is basically for young people working on any one or say two policy areas at the state level. So they can pick the policy areas they're working on, they can pick the states they're working on, and we incubate them for a period of three years. And you do need a couple of years to build a lot of specialization, context, and domain knowledge. And then, you know, I have no doubt that these guys will do great in the world. So we put out a call for all this started and got wrapped up pretty quickly. We hatched this idea last year in October. We launched the fellowship in Jan. We announced the fellows last month and they are off, right? Like we've already done their orientation. They just this, you know, in the last couple of weeks, they've gone back to their respective states and and they're off on their own working on their cool projects so we also tend to do things pretty quickly at Mercatus like once we decide something is important we do it.

Uh i think of the 1991 fellowship very much as proof of concept that the talent exists out there and if we can back them with institutional support and financial support and incubation and network them across a broader policy community we will get great results at the state level i have no doubt. So I don't want another 20 years to pass for the same lament that, you know, there aren't enough young people working at the state level that we can just hire. So I will, I have taken it upon myself that we will solve this problem.

And of course, you guys are very involved in designing the fellowship, picking the fellows, interviewing them, the orientation, all of it. And Ankita Dinkar, our colleague who's not with us on this podcast is the program manager because she's literally running this program in New Delhi right now with them. That's basically the idea of the fellowship. And we have 12 fantastic young fellows. They come from different domains. They come from 10 different states. We've covered a huge number of areas as well as states. About half of India lives in these states is the way I like to put it. I have no doubt that they'll all go on to have very, very good policy careers because you know, everything depends on the talent. Now, how much of the reforms happen is a matter of timing and chance and political viability and all of those things, right? Like the Overton window needs to be there and shifted already in place. And there needs to be a moment when it can happen. But to keep the powder ready, as we've learned from the 1991 reformers, is to do this hard work of finding the people, incubating them and making sure that they have all the resources, connections and networks to really do what needs to be done so that India can become, and India and Indians can become very rich, which is pretty much the only goal I have.

Yeah, and also makes Kadamri's life so much simpler, right? Like now, Kadamri, there are 12 people who are working exactly on reform ideas, And hopefully that's a steady stream of very cool papers that you can midwife onto the 1991 project as the next part of the project, right?

Most definitely. And I mean, the project, we, I mean, my hope is that it grows with with, you know, more papers, more videos, more oral histories. And at the end of the day, this project has always been and will continue to be a community-led project. And if anyone listening has an idea that they'd like to write about or, you know, something they'd like to share on the oral histories or something that they'd like us to add to the public repository, I would highly encourage them to reach out to us and, you know, we'll see what we can do to take it forward.

Yeah. Yeah, and even if there are corrections to be made, actually, I would encourage all of it. If you've gotten something wrong, I mean, this is a huge project spanning lots of years and lots of people. So all of that is welcome. New ideas are welcome. And you don't need to have any credentials to start writing on state level reforms. I think don't worry about editorial support. I mean, these are all the things the project will provide. What we really need are ideas coming from the local context, because we hate the idea of exporting best practices from the first world to India or from Tamil Nadu to Bengal, right? Like we need ideas to be highly contextual, highly local and trying to solve the problem that's actually constraining that particular economy. So I think that's our bigger effort. But yeah, I mean, I hope this goes in amazing places.

致谢：一整个村庄

I mean, I can start off thanking everyone who was a big support and part of the oral history project itself, because that has taken a good five years of putting it together and really thinking through from everyone from KP Krishna, Najesh Shah, Dr. Kelkar, Niranjan for just helping us with the ideas and framework and getting started on it. I mentioned about Nona Store and Ryan Perkins and everyone we interacted to get the feedback on. It's strange to thank Prakhar because I feel like he's still part of us in our group, even though he's not with the team officially. But for just really setting up the ground and getting us started with the whole oral histories project as well.

And of course— And then abandoning us. So it's hard to do research. Yeah, but still being a sounding board for us. I'm just—yeah, I'm teasing. I am so thrilled he was there at the beginning to help us get started.

Absolutely. And of course, you know, every person who was instrumental in just doing the back end effort and making each recording possible. We had Dallas in-house when we recorded some of the oral histories at the Mercatus office. On the ground, you know, everybody from, you know, Gaurav Chintamani, who sent his students like Anshul Jain and Prakhar Yadav, very helpful in doing their oral histories in India. There was Saurabh Mishra along the way. Just everybody coming together and helping us with these oral histories. There was Varun in Chennai, who was wonderful, when we recorded with Dr. Gangaraj. And of course, you know, one part is the audience. Anant Krishnamoorthy, like the other people who helped us set all of that up.

Was each of them really coming forth and sending their teams and their, and sort of helping us really one step at a time building on, you know, regarding, and then we had help with the transcripts, you know, because once we had the, oh my God, that is a mountain to climb to clean up 50 plus hours of oral history, transcripts and sort of really keeping it clean and making sure every word is heard and sort of clear. We had a lot of help from Mary Horan, who I think did the larger chunk of those transcripts. And then our, well now former intern, but soon to be research fellow at Mercatus, Akrit Hari Kumar, who took the pains to just go over those transcripts and giving it another scrub. Really helpful.

But you know, giving this institutional legitimacy was obviously of course, folks at Mercatus, but also our legal team, Rakshanda, Deka and Pradyuman Kaista, who really created the legal framework of how we are recording these materials, the copyright and how it will be shared with the interviewees that we got on board. And just creating that sort of institutional apparatus to sort of do the oral history work.

And how can we not thank the people who participated? Oh my God, yeah. Yeah, the people were amazing.

Exactly. Dr. Rangarajan, Dr. Vijay Kelkar, Montik Singh Aluvalia, Dr. Shankar Acharya, Dr. Rakesh Mohan, P. Chidambaram, Dr. Ashok Desai, Jairam Ramesh, you know, Martin Wolf, who you recorded with, Narayan Murthy, Tarun Das, all of them just so generously speaking to us. And obviously the ones who made the connections, particularly Karti Shandilya, for just, you know, sending out those emails for us and putting us in touch and making all of this come together.

Yeah. And we have a few more scheduled. Hopefully they'll happen when they happen. When they happen. And, you know, we'll take it from there. But, you know, now we have a tribe, we have people backing us up and I think what more can we ask for? So, yeah.

And it's not just the oral history, we have so many people to thank for the entire project as well. In terms of the website, you know, in the early days, Margit really helped us get version one up. For version two, Somesh and Arvind, who are both EV winners, they also helped us get this version up. And then, of course, all the teams at Mercatus that help us keep it going, the IT team, Jeff Holmes and Ashley Webb, and the strategic engagement team as well, just in terms of whether it's the fellowship, whether it's something for the project, they're always so ready to help us. The publications team that gets our writing into shape and makes sure that there are no typos and that we are following all the guidelines that we're supposed to for our conferences, the events team and Ashley Schiller and of course our partners in the conference, Nilekani Philanthropies and Dr. Janvi Nilekani. We would not be able to do any of the things that we do without these people. And of course, everyone who attended our conferences as well over the years.

The writing section of the website also would not have come about if people had not been so ready to share their ideas. And we've had essays from of course Shreyas and Prakhar and Shruti from the team but also from Dinyar Patel, Anupam Manur, Anirudh Berman, Udai Bhatia, Renuka Sane, Ovi Karva, Sahil Diyo, Shampifi Joshi, Aditi Bhavmik, Samruti, Bharkavi Zaveri, Jayad Joshi, Shahid Mohammad Loan, Harini Subramanian Dastur and everyone who contributed to our paper series as well, which was the team, of course, but also Tarvin Panagaria, Amartya Lahiri, Devashree Shmitra, Sarthak Pradhan, Pranay Kottasthane, Praveen Krishna.

And in addition to our writing the video series over the years, which has grown into multiple series, So with India's reform journey revisited, we had Montek Singhaluwalia, Narayan Ramchandran, Janvi Nilaygini, Amit Verma, Pratika Hingorani, Manish Sabharwal, Mohit Satyanand, Bhargavi Zaveri, Shubho Roy, Vidya Mahambray, Ajay Shah, Anupam Manur, Shaon Ray, MR Madhavan, Mahima Vasisht, KP Krishnan, Movna Anand, Neelanjan Sircar, Suyash Rai, and of course, Shruti in the series as well. And in Bangalore last year, we shot three new series which included India's Reforms in Practice, which featured Sumita Dhaura, Soumya Dhanraj, Bhuvana Anand, Prabhat Kumar, Chakshu Roy, Siddharth Raman, Shekhar Iyer, Rahul Aluwalia, Rahul Tongia, Lavish Mandari, Alok Kumar, Karan Nag, and Shreyas and myself. We had series on conversations on deregulation featuring Manish Sabarwal, Aimar Madhavan, Rakesh Mohan, Suman Berry, Amit Verma, and Montek Singhaluwalia. And an exciting series on Book Spotlight where we featured people who have written books to talk about why they wrote the book, what they want readers to take away, and the ideas that they explored. So we had Akshay Jaitley, Rahul Bajoria, Rukmini S, Ajit Ranade, Pranay Kottasthane, Vinay Sitapati, Arvind Subramanian, Kartik Muralidharan, Rajiv Mantri, Shaon Ray, MR Sharan, and Nitin Pai in that series. We also had a couple of webinars that we did and Doug Owen, Arvind Panagaria, Shruti, and Larry White spoke on Dr. Panagaria's recent book, The Nehru Development model history and its lasting impact.

We have everybody to thank for this and Dr. Panagaria for his time and generosity in shooting the Talking Trade series with us as well.

Yeah, and you know, we've also met like new people along the way, right? Nomsita and Vaishnav, who are recording this video for us too, have recently joined this tribe. And the other part of it is, like when you were reading out that list of names, I've known many of them for a long time, but there are so many new people. And that's what makes me happiest about this community that our interns have now become doctoral students or joined policy places or are working on this full time. And that makes me really, really happy. Like it takes a village, but a big part of it taking a village is also making the village. And I think that's what the 1991 project is all about. How do we create that community to keep this going?

Very nice. And when you have sounding boards like Niranjan Rajadakshan, Amit Verma and Prem Panikkar, I mean, how can you go wrong? Right. So that's just the whole. We've had very, very good mentors yeah we've been so fortunate but yeah and and the the biggest cheerleaders within mercatus of course you know Daniel Rothschild when we first started he was just like let's get this up and running now Ben Klutzy like you know Tyler and Pete Betke of course have always been great advisors to us on everything that we touch so it's it's been remarkable to do this truly and all the professors thank you both of you.

No, I mean, I'm also grateful to the professors who are listing our materials in their classrooms for reading. Exactly. Yeah. Yeah, you know, and that came from Kinshu Dang. I don't know if he mentioned Kinshu yet, but she was the first one to say that there's a demand for this from students in colleges and econ clubs because we were getting all these messages and we didn't know what to do. And Kinshu was like, hey, I think we need to address this. And she was the one who started the newsletter going to all these econ clubs who reached out to us. And that's how it got into reading groups and curricula and so on.

Yeah, and of course, in terms of supporting the project also, Keelan, who helps us with everything in troubleshooting, everything that we need. We really wouldn't be able to do this without him.

Yeah, Keelan runs our life. So yeah, he keeps everything going, not just the 1991 project. But yeah, no big shout out to all of you. The core team is pretty small, as everyone has heard many times. It's Shreyas Kadambari and Ankita Dinkar who are really the full-time people on the team. And then everyone else at Mercatus or outside who kind of comes in and helps us with special projects. But all of this became worthwhile as people started reading and researching and really reaffirmed our faith that if you put things out there, you know, there are enough people who are interested and involved and enough people who care about good research that they will come. And that's been validated now many times over in the past five years.

结语

So I'm very grateful to both of you, not just for working on this project, but for also taking time to do this podcast in the middle of crazy, very delayed, but now suddenly very heavy monsoons in India and with all our internet and tech troubles and so on. So thank you so much for doing this and thank you for coming back on Ideas of India.

Thank you so much, Shruti. Thank you for leading the way. Truly. Thank you. Yeah, this project wouldn't exist without you. So thank you for, you know, giving us all the support that we need to make it happen and work on it and all the ideas that you give us uh for it and you you really lead this project and we thank you for that and thank you for having us on the podcast as well and the mentorship at the mentorship as always that you know what i say right the ideas versus the work i'm like gyan is more.

Now I'm happy to give the Gyan and the idea. Someone has to do the work, which is always the hard part. So what is scarce is people who are willing to do the work. So yeah. Thank you guys. What a privilege. Thank you. Yeah. Thanks so much. See you guys soon in the office.

Also, check out our initiative commemorating 30 years of India's market reforms at the1991project.com.

item.description:
## 一、口述史作为"反熵工程"：一个隐藏的悖论
表面上看，1991 Project 是在做一件"档案学"的工作——抢救即将消失的记忆。但真正惊人的是它揭示的一个反常识事实：**印度作为世界上最古老的官僚体系之一，居然不知道自己历任首席经济顾问的确切上任日期**。Shankar Acharya 是第 10 任 CEA，可前 9 任的入职月份都要靠事后拼凑。
这暴露了一个更深的系统性真相：**印度政府是一个"高吞吐、零沉淀"的系统**。它每天处理海量决策，但几乎不留下"决策的元数据"——谁在什么时候、基于什么想法、受谁影响做了什么。这与印度作为"世界最大民主制"的宏大叙事形成了刺眼的反差。1991 Project 本质上不是在写历史，而是在**为一个失忆的国家做记忆器官移植手术**。
跨领域联系：这非常像神经科学里的"陈述性记忆 vs 程序性记忆"——印度政府拥有极强的"程序性记忆"（继续运作的能力），却几乎没有"陈述性记忆"（能被检索、被反思的知识）。而一个没有陈述性记忆的组织，注定会重复自己的失败。
## 二、一个让人意外的观察：改革不是"想法的胜利"，而是"社交网络的胜利"

item.title: [Lex Clips] The controversial reason slavery was abolished | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一份没有诗意的自由宣言

有一个反直觉的事实值得咀嚼：林肯故意让《解放宣言》读起来像一份提货单（bill of lading）——没有崇高辞藻、没有道德宣言、没有关于人性的雄辩。这个被后世视为美国道德转折点的文件，在诞生那一刻是刻意反诗意的。

这里藏着一个深刻的系统性洞察：当一个道德变革必须借助非道德的通道才能实现时，它的语言必须先"降格"，才能在制度中"升格"。林肯不能以"人权"名义解放奴隶——他没有那个宪法权力；但他可以以"战时总司令的军事必要"名义这么做。于是，人类历史上最重大的解放行动之一，被伪装成一份军需调度令。

自由的地理学悖论

这里有一个几乎黑色幽默的悖论：《解放宣言》只在林肯管不到的地方生效。

美军已经控制的南方地区——奴隶们"够得着"的地方——不适用；仍在反叛、林肯政令根本无法执行的地方——才被"宣布"自由。这相当于说：我只解放我救不到的人。

但如果你把它放在系统论里看，这不是荒谬，而是一个精妙的边界机制：自由随着军队推进而"物质化"。宣言不是一次性事件，而是一个移动的相变面——军队走到哪里，法律状态就在哪里从"奴役"翻转为"自由"。这与物理学里的波前传播结构惊人相似：势能已经写在方程里，但实际发生要等波前扫过。宣言写的是方程，军队是波前。

跨领域连接：联盟数学与道德妥协

再看一个容易被忽略的层面——这份文件的形态是被"联盟数学"逼出来的。

林肯的军队里，共和党人不够打赢战争，他必须留住民主党人。而民主党人愿意为"恢复联邦"流血，却不愿为"解放黑人"流血。于是解放必须被重新包装为一种战争工具——不是为了黑人，而是为了惩罚叛乱者、削弱敌方战力。

这和现代产品设计、政治联盟构建、甚至开源项目治理里的核心问题是同构的：当你需要一个异质联盟支持某个变革，你就必须找到一个"最小公约动机"作为官方叙事，而把真正的动机藏在执行结构里。乔布斯卖 iPod 不卖"数字版权革命"，Linus 卖 Git 不卖"去中心化哲学"，林肯卖"战争必胜工具"不卖"人是生而平等的"。

最深的变革，往往披着最平庸的外衣入场——因为只有平庸才能穿过联盟里所有人的心理海关。这也是为什么一个世纪后马丁·路德·金必须用完全相反的策略——极致的道德语言——来完成林肯没法用道德语言完成的事情。两人是同一条道路上、由制度位置决定的两种镜像战术。

📝 转录文本

一、《解放宣言》作为一种军事策略

Lex： So, uh the Emancipation Proclamation was in part a military strategy.

Gary Gallagher： Abraham Lincoln based it entirely on his war-making power as commander-in-chief in a time of open rebellion.

His inclination — there's no… He's often been criticized for not including so the soaring language he was capable of in the Emancipation Proclamation. One historian likened it to a bill of lading. It had all the soaring language of a bill of lading.

He did that on purpose. He did it because he he he doesn't have the power to strike at slavery in the absence of a war, the president doesn't, and he did it because he knows that he can't win the war with only Republicans in the army. He needs to keep Democrats on board with the war as well. They're not in favor of emancipation. The one way that they might accept it is as a tool to help achieve union, and to do that we've got to strike at the rebels — way, strike at slavery. That will hurt their war effort, and it will also punish the people who brought on the war, and that would make…

So, Lincoln hoped that by basing it strictly on his war power, it might be more widely accepted across all parts of the loyal states, uh and not as controversial as it was.

二、争议与民主党人的反应

It was still intensely controversial. It alienated many Democrats when he issued it, who said:

"You're changing what this war is about. We're willing to to shed our blood and maybe risk our lives to restore the union of the founders. I'm not going to risk my life to free a black person."

That's a very very common attitude among Democrats.

三、《解放宣言》到底做了什么？

Lex： So, what did the the Emancipation Proclamation actually do? It emphasized the freeing of slaves in the South.

Gary Gallagher： It's even more complicated than that.

The only place that Lincoln said he had the power as the war leader to strike at slavery is where the rebels were actually still in rebellion and in control. So, any place where the US Army was in control, any place — he said that is is in essence United States territory. Now, I can't free them there because I don't have the power. I can only free them where we don't have the power.

So, he exempted parts of states and areas in the South that it didn't apply to as of the moment he signed it. Going forward, any place that the United States Army went where it hadn't been on January 1st 1863 — the Emancipation Proclamation applied and enslaved people would be freed by it.

At the literally at the time he signed it, it didn't free anybody because he's only saying I can free them where we're not in control. We have to be in control for this to have effect, for this to have power.

四、军队作为自由的边界

Lex： So, in part this is why the army was the boundary which the freeing was happening.

Gary Gallagher： It's absolutely the boundary.

And Congress had already passed what was called the Second Confiscation Act. It passed this in in July of 1862. It announced that all enslaved people belonging to rebels were free. It it didn't apply to people who could prove they were unionists living in the South and on states.

Lincoln didn't make that distinction in the Emancipation Proclamation. His proclamation is broader than the Second Confiscation Act was.

item.description:
## 一份没有诗意的自由宣言
有一个反直觉的事实值得咀嚼：林肯故意让《解放宣言》读起来像一份**提货单**（bill of lading）——没有崇高辞藻、没有道德宣言、没有关于人性的雄辩。这个被后世视为美国道德转折点的文件，在诞生那一刻是**刻意反诗意**的。
这里藏着一个深刻的系统性洞察：**当一个道德变革必须借助非道德的通道才能实现时，它的语言必须先"降格"，才能在制度中"升格"**。林肯不能以"人权"名义解放奴隶——他没有那个宪法权力；但他可以以"战时总司令的军事必要"名义这么做。于是，人类历史上最重大的解放行动之一，被伪装成一份军需调度令。
## 自由的地理学悖论
这里有一个几乎黑色幽默的悖论：**《解放宣言》只在林肯管不到的地方生效**。
美军已经控制的南方地区——奴隶们"够得着"的地方——不适用；仍在反叛、林肯政令根本无法执行的地方——才被"宣布"自由。这相当于说：**我只解放我救不到的人**。
但如果你把它放在系统论里看，这不是荒谬，而是一个精妙的**边界机制**：自由随着军队推进而"物质化"。宣言不是一次性事件，而是一个**移动的相变面**——军队走到哪里

item.title: [Mercatus Center] Shreyas Narla and Kadambari Shah on the 'The 1991 Project' | Ideas of India
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最令人震撼的观察：这个项目在无意识地"重演"1991改革本身

听完全部内容，最让我意外的不是印度改革的细节，而是这个"1991 Project"团队正在以一种近乎神秘的方式，复刻他们所研究的那场改革的每一个组织学特征：

  • 改革靠的是 少数互相信任的人 + 冷邮件式的横向连接（Rangarajan 从来不认识 Y.V. Reddy，凭一份公务员名单发掘他）——这个项目也是靠三个人 + 给部长发冷邮件、在机场"劫持"Chidambaram 起家的；
  • 改革之所以停摆是因为"没人培养下一代技术官僚"——项目团队因此把培育 stage-level 的年轻政策人才（1991 Fellowship）当成核心答案；
  • 改革在 M Document 里坚持 general equilibrium（六件事必须一起做）——项目也拒绝了"只做口述"或"只做档案"的单一路径，而是把口述史 + 专家委员会报告 + 传记 + 视频 + 会议 打包成一个整体才起作用。

换言之，他们不是在"研究"改革者的方法论——他们是在无意识地"是"那个方法论。 这是一个极罕见的"研究者—研究对象同构"现象。

二、跨领域连接：印度的"知识考古学"是一种不同于西方的认识论

Niranjan Rajadhyaksha 有一句轻描淡写却颠覆性的话被反复引用："印度经济思想史不在大学、不在期刊里——它埋在专家委员会报告里。"

这在跨领域上意味着什么？

  • 西方的知识传承走的是 university → journal → citation 的学术资本主义路径；
  • 而印度独立后 45 年里，连财政部首席经济顾问的姓名与任期都没有一块木牌记录——这不是"落后"，而是一种 完全不同的知识拓扑结构：印度的政策思想是通过 委员会 (committee) 这一临时性合议体 来沉淀、协商与传递的；
  • 类比：这更接近 中世纪伊斯兰世界的 majlis 传统，或 中国明清幕府/幕僚制度——知识不是被"发表"的，而是被"参与"的。

这就解释了一个诡异现象：为什么印度改革者的智识路径必须靠"triangulation"（三角验证），而不能靠单一权威文本——因为根本不存在那样的文本。这个项目本质上是在为印度发明一种它从未拥有过的知识基础设施。

三、被忽视的深层洞见：Manmohan Singh 的真正遗产不是改革，而是"人才管道"

这是整场对话中最反直觉的一个转折。所有讣告都在谈 Manmohan Singh 作为总理的核电协议、NREGA——只有这个团队看到了他真正的"元贡献"：

"改革之所以在 1991 之后能持续 15 年，然后戛然而止——是因为 Manmohan Singh 这一代人培养下一代的机制断裂了。"

这里有一个隐藏的系统性真相：制度变革的半衰期取决于制度设计者的 mentorship 半衰期。

  • 一个改革者如果只输出 policy，他的遗产会在 10-15 年内衰减；
  • 一个改革者如果输出 具备复制能力的年轻人（Rakesh Mohan、Montek、Shankar Acharya、Y.V. Reddy 都是他"扫描"出来的），遗产可以延续两三代；
  • 但当mentorship 的"复利"停止再投资时，整个改革共识会在一个隐蔽的临界点崩塌——外界看不到，因为它是渐进的。

这个洞见把政治经济学、组织行为学、复杂系统理论 (compound institutional capital) 串在了一起。而且它给现在的中国、越南、任何处于改革中段的国家提出了一个致命问题：你们的改革者今天在培养谁？

四、一个"啊哈时刻"：口述史的悖论——最专业的档案工作，反而必须从"业余的直觉"开始

Nona 告诉他们："别管方法论，先跟着直觉去做"——而最后产出的却是研究人员可以严谨引用的一级史料。这里的悖论是：方法论上的过度前置反而会杀死可用性，因为你会为了"正确"而错过所有那些愿意接你冷邮件、活着的、快 90 岁的当事人。这与创业中的 "ship first, iterate later" 是同一个认知结构——在窗口稍纵即逝的领域，'足够好的行动'胜过'完美的准备'。这或许是这个项目留给未来所有 institutional history 项目最重要的一课。

📝 转录文本

Ideas of India · The 1991 Project 五周年对谈

主持人： Shruti Rajagopalan
嘉宾： Kadambari Shah、Shreyas Narla
主题： 1991 改革 35 周年 & The 1991 Project 5 周年

一、开场：这不像访谈，更像团队例会

Hi, welcome to Ideas of India. दो इट फील्स लाइक आई एम इन वन ऑफ आवर टीम मीटिंग्स, बिकॉज़ टुडे माई गेस आर माय वंडरफुल कोलीग्स कादंबरी शाह एंड श्रेयस नारला — हु बीन ऑन द पॉडकास्ट बिफोर, एंड हूम ऑल ऑफ यू नो एस माय लिसनर्स।

टुडे वी आर गोना टॉक अबाउट द 1991 रिफॉर्म्स एंड द 1991 प्रोजेक्ट। दिस वीक एंड मंथ इज़ द 35th एनिवर्सरी ऑफ द 1991 रिफॉर्म्स — इट्स ऑलमोस्ट हार्ड फॉर मी टू बिलीव — एंड आल्सो द फिफ्थ एनिवर्सरी ऑफ़ द प्रोजेक्ट। वी किक्ड इट ऑफ इन द 30थ ईयर ऑफ़ द रिफॉर्म्स। सो इट इज़ सच अ प्लेज़र टू हैव बोथ ऑफ़ यू हियर।

"Glad to be back. नो, वी प्रीटी मच बीन हियर द होल टाइम। थैंक यू फॉर हैविंग अस, श्रुति।"

二、项目的缘起：一场 COVID 期间的意外发现

सो द वे इट स्टार्टेड — वी वर टॉकिंग अबाउट द रिफॉर्म्स। वान ऑफ़ आवर कॉलीग्स एंड गुड फ्रेंड प्रखर मिश्रा वाज़ ऑन द टीम बिफोर ही वेंट ऑफ़ टू डू हिज़ डॉक्टरल स्टडीज। सो श्रेयस, प्रखर एंड आय यूज़्ड टू वर्क विथ ईच अदर।

इट वाज़ कोविड, एंड वी वर टॉकिंग अबाउट द रिफॉर्म्स, एंड आय रियलाइज़ दैट दे डिडन्ट नो टू मच अबाउट इट — व्हिच इज़ रियली वियर्ड नाउ, बिकॉज़ दे आर अबाउट एस नर्डी एस इट गेट्स व्हेन इट कम्स टू द पॉलिसी वर्क स्पेस।

एंड आई वास लाइक: इफ दे डोंट नो एक्ज़ैक्टली व्हाई द 1991 रिफॉर्म्स हैपन ओर हाउ दे हैपन, देन नो वन विल नो। बिकॉज़, एस आई ऑलवेज से — 70% प्लस ऑफ़ इंडिया वाज़ बोर्न आफ्टर '91। व्हिच मीन्स ऑलमोस्ट टू-थर्ड्स ऑफ़ इंडियंस वर बोर्न आफ्टर द रिफॉर्म्स, एंड दे रियली डोंट हैव एनी लिव्ड एक्सपीरियंस ऑफ सोशलिज्म एंड लाइसेंस-परमिट राज।

Shreyas 的自我怀疑

"आय ऍम अ लॉयर बाय ट्रेनिंग, व्हिच मीन्स दैट आई एम गोइंग टू ओनली लुक एट द लॉ एंड नेवर रियली आस्क द क्वेश्चन — 'व्हेयर डिड दिस कम फ्रॉम, हाउ डिड दिस कम अबाउट, व्हाट्स द कॉन्टेक्स्ट?'
सो व्हेन आई लुक एट अ लेबर लॉ, व्हेन आई लुक एट इंडस्ट्रियल डिस्प्यूट्स एक्ट, व्हेन आई लुक एट द MRTP — फ़र्स्ट, यू नो, दैट वाज़ द एक्स्टेंट ऑफ़ माय एक्सपोज़र टू हिस्ट्री ऑफ़ पॉलिसी।"

एंड दिस इज़ एग्ज़ैक्टली व्हाट द कन्वर्सेशन वाज़ फाइव इयर्स एगो। आय हैड अ हेडलाइन अंडरस्टैंडिंग ऑफ व्हाट द रिफॉर्म्स वर — यू हियर द ऐब्रिविएशन "LPG" एंड दैट्स अबाउट इट। आय काइंड ऑफ़ गेट अ सेंस ऑफ़ हु नरसिम्हा राव वाज़ एंड हु मनमोहन सिंह वाज़। विनय हैड रिटन The Half-Lion; संजय बरू ने Accidental Prime Minister लिखी।

बट अगेन — आई एम अ पोस्ट-'91 चाइल्ड। आय बेसिकली ग्रू अप विथ हैविंग कंज़्यूमर गुड्स एट होम। सो आय डोंट हैव लिव्ड एक्सपीरियंस।

三、危机的本质：付不起两周的进口账单

टु आन्सर योर क्वेश्चन, श्रुति — आर इनिशियल एफ़र्ट्स वर एक्चुअली जस्ट टू टेल पीपल व्हाट हैड हैपन।

राइट नाउ वी हैव अ वेस्ट-एशियन क्राइसिस — वी हैड अ सिमिलर वेस्ट-एशियन क्राइसिस एंड वॉर, ऑइल प्राइसेस वेंट अप, ऑल दीज़ थिंग्स हैपन। एक्सेप्ट इंडिया हैड सच फ्यू रिज़र्व्स दैट इट केम टू अ पॉइंट वेयर इंडिया डिड नॉट हैव इनफ मनी टू पे फॉर मोर देन टू वीक्स वर्थ ऑफ इम्पोर्ट्स।

एंड इन अ कंट्री एस लार्ज एस इंडिया, देयर आर मेनी साइलेंट क्राइसिस — पीपल नॉट गेटिंग जॉब्स, पीपल स्टिल सो पुअर, हार्ड टू स्टार्ट अ बिज़नेस। बट द क्राइसिस व्हिच बर्थ द रिफॉर्म्स वाज़ जस्ट अबाउट नॉट बीइंग एबल टू पे योर बिल्स — व्हिच वाज़ एन इनॉर्मस एम्बरैसमेंट। टु एक्चुअली हैव टु शिप द गोल्ड आउट ऑफ़ द कंट्री, बिकॉज़ नो वन ट्रस्टेड योर इकोनॉमिक एबिलिटी टू पे समथिंग बैक।

सो द इनिशियल पार्ट ऑफ़ द प्रोजेक्ट वाज़: लेट्स टेल पीपल व्हाट हैप्पेंड। इन व्हॉट ऑर्डर इट हैप्पेंड, व्हाट वाज़ द पॉलिटिकल इनस्टेबिलिटी (थ्री प्राइम मिनिस्टर्स इन क्विक सक्सेशन), व्हाट वाज़ द इकोनॉमिक इनस्टेबिलिटी (गल्फ वॉर, राइज़िंग ऑइल प्राइसेस, इनॉर्मस डेफ़िसिट्स, अ करेंसी विद अ ह्यूज ब्लैक मार्केट)।

इट वाज़ सपोज़्ड टू बी अ रियली सिंपल प्रोजेक्ट, आदम। वी स्टार्टेड आइडिएटिंग अराउंड मार्च, एंड इट वाज़ सपोज़्ड टू एंड बाय एंड ऑफ़ जुलाई। एंड देन ऑफ़ कोर्स — एस श्रेयस सेज़ — नथिंग इज़ एवर डन व्हेन वी टच इट।

四、Shreyas 加入 & 传记撰写的起点

आय वाज़ कॉल्ड ऑन टू वर्क ऑन राइटिंग द बायोग्राफ़ीज़ ऑफ द रिफ़ॉर्मर्स। बिकॉज़ ऑफ़ माय जनरल इंटरेस्ट इन पॉलिसी हिस्ट्री, यू सेड: "हे, व्हाई डोंट यू डॉक्युमेंट हु दीज़ रिफ़ॉर्मर्स वर, एंड एग्ज़ैक्टली व्हाट देयर पॉइंट्स ऑफ इंटरवेंशन वर?"

बट श्रेयस वाज़ लाइक: "आय ऍम नॉट एन इकोनॉमिस्ट एंड आय हैव नो आइडिया व्हाट आय एम टॉकिंग ऑन।" आय थिंक ही गॉट स्केयर्ड बाय द MRTP एक्ट — एवरीवन वाज़ स्केयर्ड ऑफ़ द MRTP एक्ट।

आय स्टार्टेड सॉर्ट ऑफ़ डॉक्युमेंटिंग दीज़ प्रोफ़ाइल्स — फ़ैसिनेटिंग टु सी हाउ देयर बैकग्राउंड्स वर, हाउ दीज़ प्लेयर्स इंटरैक्टेड विद ईच अदर। डॉ. रंगराजन एस डिप्टी गवर्नर, देन कम्स बैक एस गवर्नर। मॉन्टेक सिंह अहलूवालिया, वर्ल्ड बैंक → इकोनॉमिक अडवाइज़र → कॉमर्स सेक्रेटरी '91 → फ़ाइनैंस सेक्रेटरी।

सम ऑफ़ देम हैड रिटन देयर मेमॉयर्स। सम हैड रिटन एस्सेज़ ऑर बुक चैप्टर्स। बट वी हैड ऑल द बिग नेम्स — मनमोहन सिंह, नरसिम्हा राव, मॉन्टेक। एंड देयर वर सम जर्नल पेपर्स दैट डॉक्युमेंटेड सम नेम्स — बट यू नो, दीज़ आर लॉन्ग-फ़ॉरगॉटन, 25–30 इयर्स ओल्ड।

五、口述历史的诞生：从 K.P. Krishnan 的一次会面开始

आय रिमेम्बर गोइंग टु मीट K.P. Krishnan विद प्रखर, एंड ही स्टार्टेड ड्रॉपिंग द नेम्स ऑफ़ डिफ़रेंट सेक्रेटरीज़ / जॉइंट सेक्रेटरीज़ हु वर इन द मिनिस्ट्री एट दैट पॉइंट। आय हैड नॉट हर्ड ऑफ़ जयंता रॉय — बट ही वाज़ द कॉमर्स मिनिस्ट्री इकोनॉमिक अडवाइज़र। एन.के. सिंह हैड जस्ट रिटन हिज़ मेमॉयर — ही केम अप इन कन्वर्सेशन।

एंड देन दे सेड: "यू विल हैव टु टॉक टु द एक्चुअल रिफ़ॉर्मर्स। बट दे आर आल्सो ओल्ड — व्हिच मीन्स दैट वी डोंट हैव द लक्ज़री ऑफ़ टाइम।"

देयर वर सेवरल ऑफ़ आर रिफ़ॉर्मर्स हु वर नॉट मेडिकली इन अ पोज़िशन टु टॉक टु अस — एंड दैट वाज़ ऑलरेडी फ़ाइव इयर्स एगो। सो देयर वाज़ अ सेंस ऑफ़ अर्जेंसी।

"Chinese Whispers" 问题

फॉर इन्स्टन्स, अजय शाह एंड निरंजन राजाध्यक्ष — दे हैव हर्ड द स्टोरीज़ फ़र्स्ट-हैंड फ़्रॉम विजय केलकर ओर रंगराजन। नाउ वी आर हिअरिंग अ सेकेंड वर्ज़न ऑफ़ इट। यू डोंट वांट दिस टु बी अ 'Chinese whispers' काइंड ऑफ़ थिंग — देयर दे हिअर इट फ़्रॉम अ सोर्स, एंड देन वी हिअर इट फ़्रॉम देम।

印度制度记忆的缺失

आय रियलाइज़्ड वी डोंट हैव गुड इंस्टिट्यूशनल हिस्ट्री एंड मेमोरी। सो मच ऑफ़ दिस वाज़ डन बाय टेक्नोक्रैट्स। वी डोंट हैव अ सिस्टम वेयर व्हेन अ ब्यूरोक्रैट लीव्स एन ऑफ़िस, दे डु एन एग्ज़िट इंटरव्यू ओर एनी काइंड ऑफ़ हैंडऑफ़।

वी कैन्ट ईवन फ़ाइंड इन इंडिया द स्टार्टिंग एंड एंडिंग डेट्स — एंड व्हेन आय से डेट्स, आय डोंट मीन the exact date, आय मीन the year — व्हेन समवन स्टार्टेड एंड एंडेड इन अ पर्टिकुलर डिपार्टमेंट।

Shankar Acharya 的木板轶事

दिस रिमाइंड्स मी ऑफ़ अन एनेकडोट डॉ. आचार्य मेंशंड। व्हेन ही बिकेम चीफ़ इकोनॉमिक अडवाइज़र, देयर वाज़ नो बोर्ड — लाइक अ वुडन प्लैक इन द ऑफ़िस ऑफ़ द CEA — दैट लिस्टेड ऑल प्रीवियस CEA'ज़ विद डेट ऑफ़ अपॉइंटमेंट टु डेट ऑफ़ रिटर्न। नाइन पीपल हैड ऑलरेडी हेल्ड दैट पोस्ट। ही फ़ाइनली गॉट इट डॉक्युमेंटेड — बट ईवन देन, फ़ॉर सम ऑफ़ द अर्ली वन्स, दे डिडन्ट हैव द एग्ज़ैक्ट डेट, ओनली अ रफ़ मन्थ।

45–50 इयर्स ऑफ़ इंडिपेंडेंस, एंड वन ऑफ़ द सीनियरमोस्ट टेक्नो पोज़िशन्स — इन द फ़ाइनैंस मिनिस्ट्री, ऑफ़ ऑल मिनिस्ट्रीज़ — डिडन्ट हैव अ क्लीन रेकॉर्ड।

"印度的第二次独立"

आय थिंक दिस इज़ इंडिया'ज़ सेकंड फ़्रीडम। द रिफ़ॉर्म्स आर एस इम्पॉर्टेंट एस गेटिंग यूनिवर्सल एडल्ट फ़्रैंचाइज़, बिकॉज़ पार्टिसिपेटिंग इन द मार्केटप्लेस इज़ एस इम्पॉर्टेंट एस पार्टिसिपेटिंग इन द पॉलिटिकल स्पेस। एंड नॉट एवरीवन वाज़ अलाउड टु पार्टिसिपेट इन द मार्केटप्लेस — विदर एस अ कंज़्यूमर ओर एस अ प्रोड्यूसर।

六、方法论：如何做一次严肃的口述史

बट ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़ — यू कैन गो टॉक टु देम, यू मस्ट मेक देम फ़ील कम्फ़र्टेबल, दे विल स्टार्ट स्पीकिंग, दे विल रिकलेक्ट, दे विल शेयर। ऑफ़्न दे गो: यू प्रेस द रेकॉर्ड बटन एंड यू जस्ट रन विद इट।

एट दैट पॉइंट, द 1947 Partition Project वाज़ डूइंग अ लॉट ऑफ़ द राउंड्स इन इंडिया। दिल्ली वाज़ राइफ़ विद दीज़ सेशन्स। सो यू काइंड ऑफ़ हैड अ सेंस ऑफ़ हाउ ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़ वर बीइंग डन।

बट वी कुड नॉट डु दैट फ़ॉर समथिंग लाइक दिस। पार्टिशन इज़ अबाउट पर्सनल मेमोरीज़ ऑफ़ ट्रॉमैटिक इवेंट्स — वी'र नॉट ट्राइंग टु गेट द टेक्स्चर ऑफ़ समथिंग, वी'र एक्चुअली ट्राइंग टु गेट द टेक्निकल डिटेल्स।

借鉴：世界银行 + Stanford + Nona Storr

वर्ल्ड बैंक हैड डन एन इंस्टिट्यूशनल मेमोरी प्रोजेक्ट, बट इट फ़ेल्ट लाइक अ बिट ऑफ़ "इन-ग्रुप स्पीक"। दे ट्रांसक्रिप्ट्स रेड लाइक एन ऑनगोइंग कन्वर्सेशन, आय वाज़ ईव्ज़ड्रॉपिंग विदआउट मच कॉन्टेक्स्ट।

देन प्रखर टैप्ड इनटु हिज़ नेटवर्क्स। यू'ड मेड द कनेक्शन विद Nona Storr एट GMU — शी हैड डन ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़ इंटर्नली एट Mercatus। शी सेड इट्स फ़ाइन टु सेंड देम क्वेश्चन्स इन अडवांस, बट यू कैन्ट बी टू स्पेसिफ़िक — यू'ल ऑल्टर देयर मेमोरी बिकॉज़ यू आर प्रॉम्प्टिंग देम। बट यू ऑल्सो कैन्ट बी लूज़ी-गूज़ी। यू'ल हैव टु फ़ाइंड दैट राइट बैलेंस।

वी स्पोक टु Ryan Perkins एट Stanford, हु वाज़ द क्यूरेटर फ़ॉर द साउथ एशियन एंड इस्लामिक स्टडीज़। Stanford हैज़ अ रिच डिटेल्ड वर्क ऑन ऑरल हिस्ट्री प्रोजेक्ट्स — लव्ली "10 tips to remember", टेम्पलेट्स फ़ॉर कॉन्ट्रैक्ट्स, हाउ यू हैंडल पोस्ट-प्रोडक्शन।

七、给 Rangarajan 发的第一封冷邮件

द फ़र्स्ट पर्सन हु रेकॉर्डेड विद अस वाज़ अ कोल्ड ईमेल टु डॉ. रंगराजन। एंड आय हैव लिव्ड इन अ टाइम व्हेन डॉ. रंगराजन'ज़ सिग्नेचर वाज़ ऑन द ₹100 नोट। ही वाज़ RBI गवर्नर — अ रियली बिग डील।

आय हैड नो अंडरस्टैंडिंग दैट इफ़ वी कोल्ड-ईमेल्ड हिम, ही विल राइट बैक। नॉट ओनली डिड ही राइट बैक — ही रोट बैक इन 24 आवर्स। ही डिडन्ट आस्क अस हु वी वर, ही डिडन्ट आस्क फ़ॉर एनी क्रेडेंशियल्स। ही जस्ट सेड: "दिस इज़ फ़ैंटास्टिक, यू गाइज़ आर डूइंग समथिंग अमेज़िंग। हाउ कैन आय हेल्प?"

एंड दैट वाज़ इट। वी वर ऑफ़ टु द रेसेज़। दिस वाज़ पीक कोविड, जस्ट बिफ़ोर द डेल्टा वेव। श्रेयस, प्रखर एंड आय मैनेज्ड टु गो टु मद्रास स्कूल ऑफ़ इकोनॉमिक्स एंड रेकॉर्ड द फ़र्स्ट टू सेशन्स इन-पर्सन।

ही आस्क्ड फ़ॉर 3–4 वीक्स बिफ़ोर, प्रेप्ड, लुक्ड ऐट द क्वेश्चन्स, मेड नोट्स। वी वर लाइक: "ओह! नाउ वी डु दिस विद एवरीवन एल्स।" ही टोल्ड अस ही नीड्स ब्रेक्स। सो वी वर लाइक: "ओह! वी शुड डु दिस विद ऑल ऑफ़ देम, बिकॉज़ पीपल गेट एग्ज़ॉस्टेड, देन दे स्टार्ट मिसरिमेम्बरिंग डिटेल्स।"

आय ऑलवेज जोक: व्हेन वी ग्रो अप, वी वांट टु बी लाइक रंगराजन।

八、机场"劫持" Chidambaram

आय वाज़ इन दिल्ली, वॉकिंग एट टर्मिनल थ्री। आय कुड सी — Mr. Chidambaram — ही इज़ सो डिस्टिंक्टिव, द व्हाइट वेष्टी। नो बिग गार्ड्स, नोबडी, जस्ट हिम।

आय हैड दिस 10-सेकंड डिलेमा: "शुड आय, ओर शुड आय नॉट?" आय सेड — वेल, यू नो, दिस इज़ नाउ ओर नेवर, आय डोंट नो व्हिच अदर वे टु रीच हिम। सो आय जस्ट सेड, "श्रुति सैद-कोस्ट हिम" — आय गॉट हिज़ अटेंशन।

आय सेड: "मि. चिदंबरम, फ़्रॉम... वी डु द 1991 Project।" आय गेव द क्विक 10-सेकंड स्पीएल। "वी आर डूइंग दीज़ ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़, टॉकिंग टु द रिफ़ॉर्मर्स।" अंटिल देन ही वाज़ जस्ट स्टेयरिंग एट मी।

देन आय सेड: "वी रेकॉर्डेड फ़र्स्ट विद डॉ. रंगराजन, एंड वी फ़िनिश्ड अबाउट फ़ोर आवर्स विद हिम।" — एंड हिज़ फ़ेस चेंज्ड कम्प्लीट्ली।

द क्रेडिबिलिटी एंड रेप्युटेशन दैट रंगराजन हैज़ — इट पास्ड ऑन टु अस, हेल्प्ड बिल्ड आर गुडविल सो मच दैट द मोमेंट आय ड्रॉप्ड हिज़ नेम, मि. चिदंबरम सेड: "जस्ट ईमेल मी, लेट्स सेट इट अप।"

九、Kadambari 加入 & 第一次录音的紧张

Kadambari जॉइन्ड लिटरली अ मन्थ आफ़्टर वी फ़िनिश्ड विद डॉ. रंगराजन इन डिसेंबर। स्टार्टेड विद अस इन जन। द फ़र्स्ट वन शी वाज़ ऑन वाज़ मॉन्टेक सिंह अहलूवालिया, फ़ॉलोड बाय डॉ. शंकर आचार्य।

"आय रिमेम्बर हाउ नर्वस आय वाज़ इन दैट वेरी फ़र्स्ट वन। आय थिंक आय बेयरली सेड थ्री वर्ड्स इन दैट एंटायर रेकॉर्डिंग। बट आय वाज़ जस्ट सो टेकन बाय सच अ सेंस ऑफ़ कॉलेजिएलिटी बिटवीन द डिफ़रेंट रिफ़ॉर्मर्स। ईवन व्हेन दे आर डिसअग्रीइंग विद ईच अदर, देयर इज़ अ सेंस ऑफ़ रेस्पेक्ट — व्हिच इज़ वेरी रेयर टु सी टुडे।"

आफ़्टर दैट फ़ॉलोड डॉ. अशोक देसाई, मि. नारायण मूर्ति। "आय फ़ील लाइक सो मच आय कुड लर्न, नॉट जस्ट फ़्रॉम देयर स्टोरीज़, बट द वे दैट दे कंडक्टेड देम्सेल्व्स।"

一个"啊哈"瞬间

व्हेन मॉन्टेक स्टार्टेड, अ फ़्यू मिनट्स इन, डॉ. राकेश मोहन कॉल्ड हिम — इट वाज़ अराउंड द टाइम ऑफ़ द बजट। दीज़ पीपल आर आउट ऑफ़ ऑफ़िस, यट स्टिल इंटरेस्टेड। द मोमेंट काड सेड "वुड यू प्लीज़ मेक एन इंट्रोडक्शन फ़ॉर अस टु राकेश मोहन?" — वेल, द होल थिंग इज़ हिस्ट्री। नाउ वी हैव डॉ. राकेश मोहन ऑन रेकॉर्ड।

"यू आर नॉट द ओनली हस्लर, श्रेयस। यू कोस्ट पीपल एट एयरपोर्ट्स — आय कोस्ट देम ऑन Zoom।"

十、专家委员会报告：印度经济思想的隐藏档案

"द हिस्ट्री ऑफ़ इंडियन इकोनॉमिक थॉट इज़ नॉट फ़ाउंड एट यूनिवर्सिटीज़ एंड जर्नल आर्टिकल्स — इट इज़ रियली बरीड इन एक्सपर्ट कमिटी रिपोर्ट्स।"
— निरंजन (राजाध्यक्ष)

दिस वन सेंटेंस निरंजन हैज़ ऑलवेज टोल्ड मी, बट इट रियली डिड नॉट लीव मी। वी डिडन्ट हैव अ डीप यूनिवर्सिटी कल्चर, वेरी फ़्यू जर्नल्स, अ लॉट ऑफ़ पीपल इन गवर्नमेंट वर नॉट राइटिंग फ़ॉर इकोनॉमिक जर्नल्स।

सो हाउ डु यू गेट ऑल दिस मैटेरियल? इट्स रियली थ्रू कमिटी रिपोर्ट्स।

挖掘过程：从图书馆到复印店

आय यूज्ड टु गो टु नेहरू लाइब्रेरी बैक इन द डे एंड गेट द फ़िज़िकल कॉपीज़ एंड स्कैन देम। ऑफ़्नटाइम्स दे ऑल वुड रेफ़र टु द P.C. Alexander Committee Report — ओह माय गॉड। पार्लियामेंट लाइब्रेरी हैड इट। वी वर एबल टु गेट एक्सेस, गेट अ कॉपी, स्कैन इट, कीप इट।

एज़ इट हैप्पेन्स — डॉ. पनगारिया वंस राँग टु आस्क: "डु यू, बाय चांस, हैप्पन टु हैव द Alexander Committee Report?" वेल, वी हैड इट! एंड ही टोल्ड अस, "यू आर द ओनली पीपल हु हैव इट।"

कैन यू इमैजिन? दिस इज़ समवन हुज़ बीन द वाइस चेयर ऑफ़ द नीति आयोग। ऑल दिस कमिटी रिपोर्ट्स यूज्ड टु लिव ऑन द प्लानिंग कमीशन वेबसाइट, बट व्हेन इट गॉट रीवैम्प्ड इनटु द नीति आयोग वेबसाइट, अ लॉट ऑफ़ दिस स्टफ़ गॉट मिस्ड।

Abid Hussain, P.C. Alexander, Sukhamoy Chakravarty, एंड Arjun Sengupta — दीज़ आर लाइक फ़ोर कमिटी रिपोर्ट्स दैट केम अप ओवर एंड ओवर एंड ओवर एगेन। दे वर द वेरी अर्ली वन्स। एंड नोबडी हैड कॉपीज़ ऑफ़ देम।

दिस इज़ अ लेबर ऑफ़ लव — स्टैंडिंग इन लाइन एट अ फ़ोटोकॉपी शॉप, गेटिंग इट डिजिटाइज्ड, मेकिंग श्योर द ऑरिजिनल कॉपी वाज़ सेंट बैक। अ लॉट ऑफ़ ब्लड, स्वेट एंड टियर्स हैज़ गॉन इनटु दिस।

十一、网站的演化：从一页滚动到"思想与影响"时间轴

द फ़र्स्ट पार्ट ऑफ़ व्हाट वी डिड — इट वाज़ जस्ट अ वेरी सिंपल वन-पेज स्क्रोल। एज़ द प्रोजेक्ट ग्रू, वी रियलाइज़्ड वी नीडेड टु शो अ लॉट मोर।

现在的四大板块

गोइंग टु द वेबसाइट, यू विल सी फ़ोर बकेट्स:

  1. Writing — essays, policy papers, op-eds
  2. Public Repository — expert committee reports, key 1991 documents (M-Document, Manmohan Singh's budget speech)
  3. Oral Histories — full recordings, transcripts, snippets
  4. Conversations & Video Series — India's Reform Journey Revisited, Conversations on Deregulation, Talking Trade, Book Spotlight

"Ideas and Influences" 板块

व्हाइल डूइंग द ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़, वी नोटिस्ड अनदर स्टोरी इमर्जिंग — द इंटलेक्चुअल रूट्स ऑफ़ रिफ़ॉर्म थिंकिंग।

फ़ॉर एग्ज़ैम्पल: Bhagwati & Desai (1968) India: Planning for Industrialization — क्रिटिक्ड प्रोटेक्शनिज़्म, अडवोकेटेड मार्केट रिफ़ॉर्म, फ़ोरशैडोइंग द इकोनॉमिक रिफ़ॉर्म्स। सम लेस-वेल-नोन वर्क्स लाइक Sudarshan on how post-1991 policies impacted poverty and progress।

नाउ ऑन द वेबसाइट देयर इज़ अ टाइमलाइन फ़्रॉम 1920 टु टुडे — ऑन द डिबेट्स, इवेंट्स, पीपल दैट कंट्रिब्युटेड टु दिस इंटलेक्चुअल स्टोरी बिहाइंड द रिफ़ॉर्म्स।

Rabbit-hole 方法论

वी आर प्रोज़ ऐट फ़ॉलिंग इनटु रैबिट होल्स। श्रेयस'ज़ रैबिट-होल टेंडेंसी रियली केम आउट इन द ऑरल हिस्ट्री प्रेप। कादंबरी'ज़ रियली केम आउट इन द वेबसाइट।

फ़ॉर इंस्टेंस — मोस्ट ऑफ़ द रिफ़ॉर्मर्स कॉल देम्सेल्व्स Fabian Socialists। सो देन यू'र लाइक: "OK, हु आर दीज़ Fabian Socialists?" — Sidney & Beatrice Webb, Harold Laski। यू हैव टु फ़ाइंड द बुक, फ़ाइंड अ क्लीन कॉपी, चेक इफ़ इट्स कॉपीराइट-एक्सपायर्ड।

द बिगेस्ट थिंग, कादंबरी, दैट यू मैनेज्ड टु डु — यू प्रोवाइडेड कॉन्टेक्स्ट। नॉट अ लॉन्ड्री लिस्ट ऑफ़ बुक्स — यू कॉन्टेक्स्चुअलाइज़्ड दीज़ वर्क्स।

十二、Doug Irwin 的邮件 & Manmohan Singh 的遗产

डग अर्विनne acknowledge किया अस in one of his major papers — एंड फिर एक ईमेल भेजी: "Shruti, this is such a fantastic repository. It made my life easy."

द डे वी गॉट दैट ईमेल, श्रेयस वाज़ एक्चुअली फ़्लोटिंग। ही वाज़ लेविटेटिंग इन हिज़ चेयर। हिज़ फ़ीट वर नॉट ऑन द ग्राउंड।

Vikrant Pandey - 概念验证

Vikrant Pandey — दैट डॉक्टरल स्टूडेंट एट यूनिवर्सिटी ऑफ़ मुंबई (नाउ प्रोफ़ेसर देयर) — अगेन, अ कोल्ड ईमेल। यूज्ड अ बिग चंक ऑफ़ द रिपॉज़िटरी फ़ॉर हिज़ डिज़र्टेशन। दैट रियली पुल्ड इट टुगेदर फ़ॉर मी। दैट कैरीड मी ऑन फ़ॉर टू इयर्स।

Manmohan Singh 的讣告

वी हैड आस्क्ड डॉ. मनमोहन सिंह फ़ॉर ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़, ही हैड अग्रीड। बट ड्यूरिंग कोविड ही वाज़ रियली इल। लेटर ही सेड: "आय वरी दैट माय मेमोरी विल बी फ़िक्शन। आय डोंट कम्प्लीट्ली ट्रस्ट दैट आय रिमेम्बर एवरी डिटेल। व्हाट यू'व डन इज़ अमेज़िंग — कैरी ऑन।" वी नेवर रेकॉर्डेड विद हिम।

व्हेन ही पास्ड अवे (24 डिसेंबर), एवरीबडी रोट अबाउट द रिफ़ॉर्म्स। मेजर न्यूज़पेपर्स कॉपी-पेस्टेड आर मैटेरियल एंड पुट इट ऑन देयर फ़्रंट पेज। वी बिकेम द प्राइमरी रिपॉज़िटरी फ़ॉर एवरीवन राइटिंग ऑन मनमोहन सिंह।

星探 Manmohan Singh

ओनली अस टॉक्स अबाउट हिम एज़ अ फ़ैंटास्टिक टैलेंट स्काउट। माय फ़ेवरेट स्टोरी इज़ Y.V. Reddy — मनमोहन सिंह अपेरेंटली यूज्ड टु लुक ऐट द लिस्ट ऑफ़ IAS ऑफ़िसर्स हु वर रियली गुड ऐट इकोनॉमिक्स, हु गॉट अ गुड रैंक। ही सेड: "या, ही शुडन्ट बी अ डिस्ट्रिक्ट कलेक्टर समवेयर फ़ार अवे — ही शुड बी ब्रॉट इनटु द इकोनॉमिक अडवाइज़री एंड टेक्नोक्रेसी।"

एंड सो मच ऑफ़ व्हाई द रिफ़ॉर्म्स कंटिन्यूड फ़ॉर सो लॉन्ग आफ़्टर 1991, एंड स्टॉप्ड आफ़्टर 15–20 इयर्स — इज़ बिकॉज़ ऑल दिस पीपल हैड मूव्ड अप, एंड नो वन हैड बॉदर्ड टु कल्टिवेट दैट नेक्स्ट जनरेशन।

十三、会议、视频、"Yes-And"文化

रिफ़ॉर्म्स आर वेरी पॉलिटिकली रिस्की एंड रेप्युटेशनली कॉस्टली। यू कैन्ट टेक अ रैंडम आइडिया ऑफ़ द स्ट्रीट — इट नीड्स टु बी एन आइडिया दैट हैज़ मेड इट्स इनरोड्स विद अ लॉट ऑफ़ क्रेडिबिलिटी एंड ट्रस्ट विदइन गवर्नमेंट।

हाउ डु यू डु दैट? थ्रू एक्सपर्ट कमिटीज़। एंड टु ईवन गेट कमिटीज़ सेट अप — यू नीड टु हैव दिस पीपल नो ईच अदर।

सो वी स्टार्टेड डूइंग: - रिसेप्शन्स एंड मिक्सर्स फ़ॉर ओल्डर एंड यंगर जनरेशन्स - इंडिया आइडियाज़ कॉन्फ़्रेंस (2022 Goa on Political Economy → 2023 Chennai on Digital Transformation → Deregulation in Indian States) - IMF मीटिंग्स के दौरान DC में मिक्सर — केम आउट ऑफ़ मनमोहन सिंह ऑब्च्युअरी सोर्स

Yes-And Culture

पीपल एट Mercatus जस्ट डोंट हैव बैगेज। इन इंडिया देयर वर सो मेनी नेसे-सेयर्स: "नो वन विल कोऑपरेट। इट विल बी सो एक्सपेंसिव। नो वन विल टॉक टु यंग पीपल।" Mercatus वाज़ जस्ट लाइक: "रन विद इट।" दे वर लाइक: "या, Stanford हैज़ द बेस्ट मेथडोलॉजी, यूज़ इट।"

Mercatus हैज़ दैट कल्चर ऑफ़ 'Yes-And' — दैट इम्प्रूव-ऑफ़-कॉमेडी कल्चर।

Mercatus 的思想史根基

आय ऍम सराउंडेड बाय हिस्टोरियन्स ऑफ़ थॉट। Peter Boettke, Tyler, Mario — ऑल फ़ैंटास्टिक हिस्टोरियन्स ऑफ़ इकोनॉमिक थॉट। स्टडीइंग द हिस्ट्री ऑफ़ इकोनॉमिक थॉट ऐट Mercatus — इट्स जस्ट समथिंग यू डु। GMU माइट बी द लास्ट प्लेस दैट स्टिल डज़ इट ऐट द PhD लेवल।

十四、政策论文系列

द नेक्स्ट सेट ऑफ़ रिफ़ॉर्म्स — व्हाट डज़ इंडिया नीड टुडे? वी हैव अल्रेडी पब्लिश्ड:

  • Shreyas — India's Competition Law and the risks of being anti-big or anti-scale
  • Arvind Panagariya — India's trade policy and the case for returning to a more liberal trade regime
  • Amartya Lahiri & Devashish Mitra — creating productive jobs through labor-intensive manufacturing
  • Sarthak Pradhan & Pranay Kotasthane — India's climb up the innovation ladder
  • Praveen Krishna — India's trade agreements
  • Shruti & Shreyas — how India's labor laws prevent firms from scaling
  • Ankita Dinkar & Samriddhi Surana — electricity challenges faced by Indian manufacturers

वी स्टार्टेड दिस टू इयर्स एगो, एंड लुक हाउ रेलिवेंट एवरीथिंग बिकेम — फ़्रॉम द ट्रेड वॉर टु सेमीकंडक्टर्स। वी कुड सी दिस कमिंग।

十五、1991 Fellowship — 州级人才管道

अ लॉट ऑफ़ द मैक्रो-स्टैबिलिटी, करेंसी, मॉनेटरी, फ़िस्कल साइड ऑफ़ द रिफ़ॉर्म्स वर ऑल डन ऐट द यूनियन लेवल। द वर्स्ट हैज़ बीन क्रॉस्ड — दिस ईयर वी हैड अनदर बैलेंस-ऑफ़-पेमेंट स्ट्रेस, बट इट डिडन्ट टर्न इनटु अ क्राइसिस।

नाउ व्हाट रिमेन्स इज़ ऑलमोस्ट ऑल स्टेट-लेवल सब्जेक्ट्स — लैंड, एग्रीकल्चर, एनर्जी।

टू प्रॉब्लम्स: 1. मोस्ट पीपल डोंट थिंक ऑफ़ स्टेट-लेवल रिफ़ॉर्म्स एज़ द "कूल थिंग"। 2. एनी टाइम यू टॉक टु थिंक टैंक्स — "व्हेयर इज़ द टैलेंट?" — आय हैव हर्ड दिस लैमेंट फ़ॉर 20 इयर्स।

解决方案

Mercatus हैज़ हंड्रेड्स ऑफ़ फ़ेलोज़ — हाइ-स्कूल, अंडरग्रैड, PhDs, पोस्ट-डॉक्स, प्रोफ़ेसर्स, इमरजेंट वेंचर फ़ेलोज़, पॉलिसी फ़ेलोज़। 6–800 फ़ेलोज़ एवरी ईयर।

सो: The 1991 Fellowship — यंग पीपल वर्किंग ऑन 1–2 पॉलिसी एरियाज़ ऐट द स्टेट लेवल। 3 years of incubation।

  • हैच्ड द आइडिया लास्ट अक्टूबर
  • लॉन्च्ड जनवरी
  • अनाउंस्ड फ़ेलोज़ लास्ट मंथ
  • 12 फ़ैंटास्टिक यंग फ़ेलोज़, 10 डिफ़रेंट स्टेट्स — कवरिंग अबाउट हाफ़ ऑफ़ इंडिया

Ankita Dinkar इज़ द प्रोग्राम मैनेजर, रनिंग द ऑरिएंटेशन इन न्यू दिल्ली राइट नाउ।

आय डोंट वांट अनदर 20 इयर्स टु पास फ़ॉर द सेम लैमेंट। आय हैव टेकन इट अपॉन माइसेल्फ़ दैट वी विल सॉल्व दिस प्रॉब्लम।

十六、致谢

Oral History Team:
K.P. Krishnan, Ajay Shah, Niranjan Rajadhyaksha, Nona Storr, Ryan Perkins, Prakhar Mishra, Gaurav Chintamani (और उनके students Anshul Jain, Prakhar Yadav), Saurabh Mishra, Varun (Chennai), Ashish Krishnamurthy (audio), Berri Han (transcripts), Akrit Harikumar (scrubbing)।

Legal Team: Raksha Deka, Pradyumn Kasta।

Reformers who spoke to us: Dr. Rangarajan, Dr. Vijay Kelkar, Montek Singh Ahluwalia, Dr. Shankar Acharya, Dr. Rakesh Mohan, P. Chidambaram, Dr. Ashok Desai, Jairam Ramesh, Martin Wolf (recorded by Shreyas), N. R. Narayana Murthy, Tarun Das।

Website: Sameshan and Arvind (EV winners); Mercatus IT team, Jeff Holmes।

Essayists: Dinyar Patel, Anupam Manur, Anirudh Burman, Uday Bhatia, Renuka Sane, Ovee Karwa, Sahil Deo, Shambhavi Joshi, Aditi Bhomick, Samriddhi, Bhargavi Zaveri, Jaidev Joshi, Shahid Mohammad Lone, Harini Subramanyam, Zerick Dastur।

Video Series Guests (partial): Naushad Forbes, Amit Varma, Manish Sabharwal, Karthik Muralidharan, Rajeev Mantri, Vinay Sitapati, Arvind Subramanian, R. Sharan, M. R. Sharan, Nitin Pai, Doug Irwin, Larry White।

Board of Advisors (informal): Montek Singh Ahluwalia, Dr. Rakesh Mohan — मेंटर्स जो हमें call the "Library of Congress of the 1991 Reforms"।

Institutional Support: Daniel Rothschild, Ben Klutsey, Tyler Cowen, Peter Boettke, Kinshuk Dang (newsletter to econ clubs), Kilan (ऑपरेशन्स), Harry David (publications, Boettke's former student), Ashleigh Sheller (events), Nilekani Philanthropies & Dr. Janhavi Nilekani (conference partners)।

十七、结语

"पीपल हु आर विलिंग टु डु द वर्क — दैट्स व्हाट इज़ स्केयर्स।"

"आय एम ग्यान इज़ मुफ़्त। नाउ आय हैव टु गिव द ग्यान एंड द आइडियाज़ — समवन हैज़ टु डु द वर्क, व्हिच इज़ ऑलवेज द हार्ड पार्ट।"

"थैंक यू फ़ॉर हैविंग अस ऑन द पॉडकास्ट, एंड फ़ॉर द मेंटरशिप। आय हैव द मेंटरशिप एज़ ऑलवेज।"

"सी यू गाइज़ सून इन द ऑफ़िस।"
