item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] The Genocide That Gave China Its Borders – Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被遗忘的准噶尔：地图上的"负空间"才是理解中国的钥匙

大多数人看中国地图，看到的是"有什么"——汉族聚居区、长城、黄河。但 Paine 让我们看到"没有什么"：准噶尔汗国从人类记忆中被彻底抹除了。这不是失败者写不了历史那么简单，而是连"存在过的证据"都被清算干净。

这里有一个反常识的观察：我们通常把"中华文明五千年绵延不断"视为一种温和的文化韧性，但从地形-气候-民族叠加图看，它其实是一种"生态位垄断"的暴力结果。汉族之所以占据了所有能种粮食的土地，不是因为他们更勤劳或文明更高，而是因为在垂直陡峭的地貌里，可耕地是零和资源——你活下来就意味着别人必须死或者逃。今日新疆的处境，不是"新政策"，而是这套两千年操作系统的又一次运行。

二、"选择性祖先认领"——中国如何用敌人的版图证明自己

Paine 抛出的最尖利的悖论：当代中国主张的"历史疆域"，恰恰来自元、清两个征服王朝——也就是汉人做亡国奴的时代。这在逻辑上等同于印度声称大英帝国的殖民地边界是自己的"神圣领土"，或墨西哥用阿兹特克帝国+西班牙殖民地叠加来划界。

这里藏着一个跨领域的连接：这种"祖先认领"的操作在企业并购史里有个对应物——公司被收购后，被收购方常常反过来把收购方的品牌资产、渠道、专利算作"我们家的传统"。汉文明是历史上最成功的"文化反向收购者"：军事上被征服，然后花两三百年把征服者的行政机器、疆域、乃至身份认同全部吞并消化，最后声称"这本来就是我们的"。蒙古人被赶回草原时，带不走他们征服的成果；满人到民国已经在户口本上消失。这是一种极其罕见的"输了战争，赢了叙事，最后连土地都收回"的三段式。

三、"军队以十万计"——被忽略的战争工业化时间差

Paine 一句轻描淡写的话值得反复咀嚼："中国动辄组织几十万人规模的军队已有数千年，而西方直到拿破仑战争才常规化做到这一点。"

这意味着中国比欧洲早了大约两千年进入"大规模社会动员"状态。我们习惯把工业革命当成现代性的起点，但从"组织能力"这个维度看，中华帝国其实是没有蒸汽机的工业化组织体——它用官僚系统、驿站、粮仓、户籍完成了欧洲需要铁路和电报才能做的事。

跨领域的意外连接：这或许能解释一个当代谜题——为什么中国互联网公司能把"996"、"大厂动员"、"人海战术"做到全球独一档。这不是文化性格，而是大规模人力协同的组织记忆残留。当字节跳动一年招几万人打一场产品仗时，它调用的是同一套两千年老代码。硅谷的"小而美工程师文化"在这套操作系统面前，更像是罗马军团遭遇蒙古骑兵——不是谁更聪明的问题，是组织尺度不在一个数量级。

真正令人不安的洞见：Paine 展示的地图告诉我们，中国的边界不是"谈判出来的"，而是"耕地能长到哪里、军队能杀到哪里"两条曲线的交集。如果我们相信气候变化正在重塑降水线和农业带，那么这张一千年稳定的"汉族核心-游牧边疆"结构图，可能正处于两千年来第一次真正的重绘前夜。而这一次，重绘的方向可能是向北——那意味着俄罗斯远东。

📝 转录文本

一、大陆帝国的地理底色

All right. Uh, whirlwind tour of China on what it looks like to be a continental empire.

So, here's a precipitation map — here's where it doesn't rain very much. Here's temperatures — that's where it's awfully cold. Here's topography — that's where it's flat.

So, if you notice, you want to grow things, you need it where it's warm enough, it rains enough, et cetera. And here's a really good topographical map. And it gives you an understanding of why famine afflicted China for so many centuries of its history, and why it's dependent on food imports today. It's just too much of the real estate's vertical to grow things on.

二、民族地图与"最好的地"的归属

And then, here's an ethnic map. You can see the consolidated pink area — that's where the Han, the preponderant ethnic group of China, live. And then they're surrounded with all these heterogeneous areas around them. You can go, "Hmm, I wonder what's going on there."

And then, here is a simplified ethnic map. It shows China proper. And the curious might ask, "How did the Han wind up with all the prime real estate?" Cuz what's arable is there.

And the answer would be: well, they laid waste to the competing Dzungar and Tibetan empires. I bet you've never heard of the Dzungars. They were wiped out by the Qing Dynasty a long time ago.

And in the continental world, you're faced with a binary choice — you either become Han, or they will kill you. And so, you got to get out of dodge and flee south, or do something else. And genocide is what happens to the losers in continental warfare. And apparently, in our own day, the Uyghurs are slated for genocide.

三、王朝快进：扩张、收缩与征服

All right. I'm going to give you a whirlwind tour, sanitized version of Chinese history.

The Han start up up north in the Yellow River Valley, and they spread, and they spread, and they do fun stuff like they build walls, and they build more walls — not a new idea. And then, they shrink back. And oh, that bad bad time. But then, they're back. And then, I don't know what happened there. But anyway, they're — they're — oh, consolidated.

And then, there's this thing which looks like any other Dynasty except a little bigger. Uh, not so — the Yuan Dynasty are Mongols. They're not Han. This is an occupation Dynasty, and that map's inaccurate. Cuz here's the real story: the Mongols start out east of Lake Baikal, and then they spread in concentric rings more or less over the Eurasian plain in another time of climate change, when their herds — they just had to move south or everyone's going to freeze to death.

The Chinese act like it's like any other Dynasty. No, it's not. It's the Pax Mongolica. It's the Mongol uh world order, when the Han were subjugated people. But they come back with the Ming Dynasty.

But then the Ming succumb to the second largest empire in Chinese history, another conquest Dynasty. These folks aren't Han. They're Manchu.

四、"选择性祖先"的悖论

And what's fascinating is today, when China claims whatever it's historical lands are, they either choose the Mongol Yuan Dynasty or the Manchu Qing Dynasty — when the Han were subjugated people. So try to un— untangle that logic. I'm not even going to go there.

Um, but the point was not to make that snide remark — although I did make that snide remark. Uh, but rather to show you that there's been lots and lots of expansion, lots and lots of shrinkage, and lots and lots of bloodshed while this is taking place.

五、被低估的组织尺度

China has been raising armies denominated in hundreds of thousands of people for thousands of years. The West does not do this — at least not on a regular basis — until the Napoleonic Wars.

Uh, it's a brutal world.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.description:
## 一、被遗忘的准噶尔：地图上的"负空间"才是理解中国的钥匙
大多数人看中国地图，看到的是"有什么"——汉族聚居区、长城、黄河。但 Paine 让我们看到"没有什么"：准噶尔汗国从人类记忆中被彻底抹除了。这不是失败者写不了历史那么简单，而是**连"存在过的证据"都被清算干净**。
这里有一个反常识的观察：**我们通常把"中华文明五千年绵延不断"视为一种温和的文化韧性，但从地形-气候-民族叠加图看，它其实是一种"生态位垄断"的暴力结果**。汉族之所以占据了所有能种粮食的土地，不是因为他们更勤劳或文明更高，而是因为在垂直陡峭的地貌里，可耕地是零和资源——你活下来就意味着别人必须死或者逃。今日新疆的处境，不是"新政策"，而是这套两千年操作系统的又一次运行。
## 二、"选择性祖先认领"——中国如何用敌人的版图证明自己
Paine 抛出的最尖利的悖论：**当代中国主张的"历史疆域"，恰恰来自元、清两个征服王朝——也就是汉人做亡国奴的时代**。这在逻辑上等同于印度声称大英帝国的殖民地边界是自己的"神圣领土"，或墨西哥用阿兹特克帝国+西班牙殖民地叠加来划界。
这里藏着一个跨领域的连接：

item.title: [Latent Space] OpenAI’s Plan to Make ChatGPT the Everything App — Akshay Nathan, OpenAI
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这不是"AGI 产品化"，而是"打工人身份的溶解工程"

表面上大家在讨论 ChatGPT Work 是超级 App、是 Codex 的延伸、是给企业的生产力工具。但如果把 Akshay 反复提到的几句话叠在一起看——"我几个月前和现在做的完全是两件事"、"人们在用 Codex 时那种偷偷摸摸的骄傲"、"work 和 personal 的边界会越来越模糊"、"每个人都会变成 T 型"——你会发现 OpenAI 真正在做的根本不是一个产品，而是在主动解构"职业身份"这个工业时代最坚固的社会契约。

传统 SaaS 是围绕角色建的：Figma 给设计师、Notion 给 PM、GitHub 给工程师。工具定义身份，身份定义工作流。而 ChatGPT Work 反过来——它拒绝按角色分产品（"we shouldn't box them in"），因为一旦按角色分，你就默认了角色是稳定的。OpenAI 押注的是角色本身正在液化。这就是为什么 Codex 和 Work 必须共享 harness：不是技术偷懒，而是意识形态选择。

二、跨领域连接：这是"数据库范式革命"在个人生产力层的重演

Akshay 从 Airtable 出身这件事被访谈者当作花边处理，但其实是理解整场对话的钥匙。

1970 年代，关系型数据库的胜利不是因为它更快，而是因为它把数据的物理存储（怎么存）和数据的逻辑查询（问什么）解耦了。用户不再需要知道底层结构，只需要说 SELECT。

ChatGPT Work 在做同一件事，只是抽象层从"数据"抬到了"意图"： - Excel 是物理存储层——你必须知道单元格、公式、宏 - Site / Artifact 是逻辑视图层——你只需要说"给我一个退休计算器" - Harness + Plugins 是查询优化器——它决定用 sub-agent、Codex 模式还是直接回答

Akshay 说 "sites 正在取代 slide deck 成为 canonical artifact"——这不是"AI 做 PPT"，这是声明式生产力取代过程式生产力的临界点。Codd 花了 20 年让程序员接受"你不需要写循环遍历表"，OpenAI 现在要让所有人接受"你不需要打开应用"。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：Meme Bot 才是最重要的产品信号

访谈里最容易被跳过的一段，是团队里有人做了个"自动扫 Slack 生成 meme"的 scheduled task。Akshay 笑着说"这不是最有生产力的用法"——但这恰恰是他讲的最重要的一句话，只是他自己可能没意识到。

为什么？因为它同时验证了三件此前没有单一产品能同时验证的东西： 1. 模型有了跨语境的意外发现能力（surprising connections） 2. 模型开始拥有"品位"（能判断什么好笑） 3. 人主动放弃了对上下文流的监督（让 agent 后台扫一切）

这三件事的组合，比任何 benchmark 都更能说明"agent 已经越过某个阈值"。幽默是通用智能的最后一块高地——因为它需要理解语境、违反预期、共情听众、并承担社交风险。当一家公司内部开始靠 AI 生成的梗来沟通，说明模型已经嵌入了社交层，而不只是任务层。

更耐人寻味的是：Akshay 反复强调"show don't tell"的产品哲学，而 meme bot 恰恰是AI 在自我 show don't tell——它不是被使用，它在演示自己还能干什么。这是一种诡异的角色反转：产品在给自己做 DevRel。

四、一个尚未被讨论的裂缝：记忆 = 权限，而 OpenAI 还没有权限模型

Sean 敏锐地指出一个几乎所有人都没意识到的问题："我是权限层"——同事问我问题、我去问 ChatGPT、再转发回答，因为我知道哪些不该他看到。

Akshay 承认这是挑战，但没意识到问题多深： - ChatGPT 的记忆是扁平的、个人的 - 但真实工作场景的知识是分层的、有信任边界的 - Chronicle 记录你所有屏幕活动 → 一旦有多人协作，这就是核弹级的合规灾难

企业软件过去 30 年最难的从来不是功能，是权限模型（RBAC、ABAC、审计日志）。OpenAI 目前的架构是"每个人一个超级智能助理"，但协作的本质是"选择性遗忘"——我知道某事，但我在这个语境下假装不知道。目前没有任何 LLM 能真正做到这种"结构化遗忘"。

这就是为什么 ChatGPT Work 会先卡在个人生产力，再卡在小团队，很难吃到真正的大 B 蛋糕——不是能力问题，是记忆架构还没有"社会性"。谁先解决"AI 的礼貌性遗忘"，谁就拿走企业市场。

📝 转录文本

开场：瓶颈已经变成了想法和品位

我觉得瓶颈已经变成想法和品位了。因为任何人现在都可以 build，所以我觉得这真的是一个 bottoms-up ambition 的时代。因为可以被建造的东西太多了，你永远会被同一时间你手上有多少想法、正在做多少事情所限制。

关于 idea 有一个很有趣的点——它们不是凭空出现的。它们通常来自某个地方，在产品开发里，它们来自和用户对话、来自你看到的摩擦或反馈。所以永远会有一类"generalist"是有价值的——就是那些能闭环、能基于反馈和用户对话产出 idea 的人。

主持人开场白

在我们进入今天这期节目之前，我想对听众说一句：谢谢你们。如果不是你们选择点进来收听，我们就没办法把 AI 工程、科学和娱乐内容带给显然想要它的你们。几乎每天都有赞助商找上门，但幸运的是，订阅我们的人足够多，让这一切能够在没有广告的情况下持续下去，我们也希望保持这样。

我只想请大家帮一个忙：你能做的、完全免费、最有力量的一件事，就是点那个订阅按钮。这是我唯一会请求你们的事情，它对我和为 Latent Space 每周努力工作的团队来说意义重大。如果你订阅了，我保证我们不会停止让节目变得更好。

现在，让我们进入正题。

一、嘉宾介绍与 ChatGPT Work 的登场

主持人：好，我们现在在录音棚里，来自 OpenAI 的 Akshay，欢迎。

Akshay：谢谢。

主持人：还有我们信赖的联合主持 Vibhu。你最近发布了 ChatGPT Work，你负责 core product engineering。这一路走过来挺有意思的——你最早是做 no-code / low-code 的，Walrus 和 Airtable。某种意义上 ChatGPT Work 就是"super app 中的 super app"：终极的 no-code——你只需要写一个 prompt。

Akshay：是啊，事情兜兜转转真的挺有意思。我职业生涯很长一段时间在做消费金融，之后有一个假设是：作为工程师我们用代码能做的那些事，如果能以一种更易访问的方式带给更多人，那会非常神奇。

我们做过一个 startup，在 LLM 之前、在 vision LLM 之前研究怎么用 AI 做自动化测试，那时候挺 jank 的，但也在尽力做。后来在 Airtable 工作了一段时间，也是同样的论点：如果能把一个数据库、或者数据库背后的参数带给普通人，那会非常有用。

但 LLM 出现之后，很清楚地看到——这就是缺失的那块技术，是那种能把"代码的魔法"带给所有人、而他们不需要知道底层发生了什么的技术。所以这次的发布、以及我们一直在做的事情，都是那个愿景的实现。

二、加入 OpenAI 之后：什么变了，什么没变

主持人：你 2023 年加入 OpenAI 的时候情况如何？现在东西多了很多——ChatGPT、Codex app、ChatGPT for Work。有哪些变化？

Akshay：我觉得更有意思的其实是"什么没有变"。我加入的时候大概是 500 人，我当时其实有点担心——我在找更 early stage 的东西，会不会不够 startup？结果加入之后发现，天啊，这比我能想象的还要 startup。这一点直到今天都没变。那种自下而上的 ambition、任何人都可以有一个想法然后 ship 出去的能力，真的很酷。

而在 mission 层面，最打动我的是那个愿景——把 frontier intelligence 带给所有人、构建 AGI 然后带给所有人。哪怕在当时也承认这个愿景不会是线性推进的：我们大概率会尝试不同的产品，有些成功、有些不成功。但愿景没变，mission 没变，而现在我们开始看到拼图逐渐拼上，这非常酷。

三、从 Enterprise 学到的：没有 one-size-fits-all

主持人：你做过 enterprise。很多人从来没碰过 ChatGPT Enterprise。你从中学到什么东西被带到了现在的工作里？

Akshay：Enterprise 里没有 one-size-fits-all 的解决方案。我记得 ChatGPT Enterprise 早期的时候，我们和客户聊，那时是 ChatGPT 发布大概一年之后，每个人都非常兴奋要把 AI 引入 enterprise。有各种"AI 部署团队"被组建起来，预算巨大。

但如果你问他们"你们对什么感到兴奋？你们想要 AI 解决什么具体的用例？"——一开始你会得到很基线的答案："我们有很多合同和数据"之类。但你再深挖，答案的方差就会爆炸。

有意思的是：用这些模型和产品，你面对一个盒子，可以对它说任何话——这是魔法。但反过来也意味着，你不知道该拿它做什么。所以 enterprise 的一大块工作，是真正去到用户所在的地方，看他们要解决什么用例，然后教他们如何用 AI 在那里获得杠杆。

主持人：你觉得这和 forward deployed engineering 有本质区别吗？

Akshay：有 go-to-market 那一面，也有产品那一面。我觉得我们更多要在产品那一面。不管 FDE motion 做得多好，最终当用户盯着他们的电脑或手机时，是我们产品的责任去 enable 他们、告诉他们该往哪里走。

四、过去三年的 adoption 变化

主持人：过去三年 adoption 是不是有变化？有 reasoning model 之类的 step function 变化。但企业面对"黑盒不知道怎么用"这个问题依然存在吗？

Akshay：我们看到现在有一个巨大的 uptick，大家都非常兴奋。感觉几百万、几亿人在用 ChatGPT，他们大致理解了怎么和 AI 打交道。

但每当有新能力被解锁——比如现在的 agents——会有一小撮 early adopter 真正"get it"：他们知道任何事情都是可能的，只要 context 到位、连接了对的工具、有监督。但外面有一个 10 倍甚至 100 倍更大的市场还没 get it，还没看到。所以这就是下一个 stage。adoption 在增长，但机会比这大得多。这也是 ChatGPT Work 要去的地方。

五、ChatGPT Work 的缘起：Codex 内部的意外扩散

主持人：ChatGPT Work 大概一个月前发布，决策过程是怎样的？还有把这些合并成 super app——我们现在正式这么叫吗？还废弃了 browser。总结一下最近几个月吧。

Akshay：感觉像过了很久，但其实只是几个月。最鲜明的一个 impetus 是——当我们发布 Codex、甚至更早在内部有 Codex 的时候，OpenAI 内部非开发者的 adoption 有一个真实的 inflection。

我们最近公布了一些数据。在产品开发过程中我们会做 UXR，去和内部人聊。让我印象最深的是：比如你去和 strategic finance 或 marketing 的人聊，他们都在用 Codex 做各种用例——这本身很酷。但更打动我的是他们多么骄傲自己在用 Codex，好像"我不该用它，但我在用"。他们觉得自己拥有了一种超能力。

我们意识到——Codex 和 agents 的力量，我们已经有那么庞大的 ChatGPT 用户基础，那些爱着 ChatGPT 的人——怎么把这个力量带给他们？这是一个很难的产品问题，有很多种走法。我们把这个过程叫做"合并"，叫做 super app，最终在 ChatGPT Work 里落地。它源自那个最初的意识：这份力量不只属于开发者，而是可以扩展到所有人——比我们自己想象得都要早。

六、Codex vs ChatGPT Work：产品定位

主持人：你怎么区分这些产品？Codex 从 CLI 到 app，现在又和 ChatGPT Work 合并——它是给普通用户的？给企业的？给 work 的？怎么定位？

Akshay：如果你在做和 work 相关的事情——用一个更好的词——我们的定位是生产力（productivity）。这就是我团队的名字。之所以叫 productivity 而不是 enterprise 或 work，是因为也有 personal productivity。

我看到有人用 ChatGPT Work 做技术上不能算 work 的事情。比如最近内部 Slack 有人发了个例子：他有一个包裹丢了，只收到了 Amazon 或快递发的照片。他让 ChatGPT Work 去找出这个包裹在哪，agent 极其执着地做了这件事——拿着照片对比周围街区的 listing，最终精确定位到包裹被送到了哪个公寓楼。这类"worky / productivity"相关的事情就是我们想让产品覆盖的。

至于 Codex——我们认为它是一个持久的品牌，但我们有一条原则：不希望用户被卡在某个 tab 或体验里而拿不到产品的力量。所以基本上你能在 Codex 版本里做的事，在 ChatGPT Work 里也能做，反过来也是。但我们做了一些有 opinion 的产品决策：比如你在一个 git repo 里的时候，你想暴露多少 git state 给用户？让 agent 的思考多"diff-forward"？sandbox 该怎么设默认？——这些方面有取舍。但我们不希望用户还得选自己该在哪个体验里。

主持人：这倒是个 AGI 的好目标——用户不想选择要哪个版本的 AGI，他们希望 AGI 帮他们选。

七、Harness 是同一个吗？

主持人：Codex 的 harness 和 ChatGPT Work 的 harness 是同一个吗？只是 UI affordance 不同，还是 prompt 层甚至更深层都有差异？

Akshay：harness 是共享的。两个产品我们都对 harness 做了改进，让它擅长 knowledge work，尤其是 plugin、computer use、artifact 相关的。这份力量不管你在哪个体验里都拿得到。UX 侧我们有 opinionated 的取舍：Codex 模式该长什么样、怎么表现，加上 sandbox 那一块，但底层 harness 能力应该是一致的。

主持人（现场演示）：我试试一个 query 在两种模式下有什么区别。我让它做一个"退休计算器"表格，两种模式都跑。

Akshay：在 Codex 模式下，如果你在一个 repo 里，你会看到它编辑 sheet 的 diff、文件的改动。在 Work 模式下你看不到这些。

八、Productivity 团队之外：OpenAI 还有哪些顶层团队

主持人：你的 productivity 团队之外还有什么？productivity 不是一切吗？

Akshay：有一个团队专注于 ChatGPT 本身——面向 consumer 的 core chat 体验。这不完全等于 productivity：每天有几亿人用 ChatGPT 做搜索、给爱人写消息、学习一个新话题、生成图像等等，这些都值得一个专门的 dedicated effort。还有专注于 enterprise、infrastructure、API 等的团队。

主持人：我把两个模式都跑起来了。这是 Work，这是 Codex 版本。我选了 5.6 Souls，会跑一会儿，我们让它在后台，等它们完成时看差异。

Akshay：马上你能看到 Codex 版本里，因为它检测到你在一个 git repo，会动态处理。有些东西你可能会漏掉，因为它在 chain of thought 里。

九、被否掉的方向：为什么要合并

主持人：有没有你本来想 ship、但反馈之后决定不做的？ChatGPT Work 里？

Akshay：我们本可以走的一个方向是让两个体验完全分开——不同的 app，或同一个 app 里完全不同的体验。为什么要合？Codex 大家明明很爱，为什么把这些合到一起？

直觉是：我们所有人的工作都在被 AI 剧烈改变，几乎每几个月一次。我感觉每天醒来我做的都和几个月前完全不同。我们的假设是——这个技术在给人杠杆。也许是你工作里更琐碎的部分，如果能自动化你就能分享更多想法、做更多事情。因此，"只写代码的人 vs 写 strategy doc 的人 vs 做 marketing 的人 vs 做播客的人"这些边界会越来越模糊。

所以基于"你是谁"来画一条硬边界会越来越难。我们应该 enable 用户去选，但不该把他们锁死。这也是为什么我们把 primitive 统一起来——比如 plugin 在 ChatGPT、Work 和 cloud 上是统一的。事情终将合到一起，我们不想强制规定你什么时候用哪个体验，但也不想 box 住任何人。

十、Harness 简史：从 ChatGPT 到 Codex

主持人：会不会有一些老用户特别习惯以前的 ChatGPT harness，现在事实上被 Codex harness 替代了？

Akshay：ChatGPT 老 harness 今天还在——你在这个 app 里新开一个 chat，不去 Work，就是在和以前的 ChatGPT 对话。

主持人：这是一个 router 决策？

Akshay：是模型做的决定。它看到你要做的事情在 Work 模式里能被更好地服务，就会 push 你去。

主持人：更宽泛地说，我想做一个"harness engineering 的口述历史"。ChatGPT 的 harness 从 o1 时代一直用到现在，现在事实上在被 Codex harness 替代，两者有部分重叠，我很好奇变了什么。

Akshay：我的看法是这里有个持续的 divergence / convergence 循环。Chat 里的很多用例——搜索、学习——我们优化的是延迟和个性。人们爱 ChatGPT，是因为我们长期在优化这些。而 Codex 我们学到的是：如果你给 agent 一个像"电脑"一样无限灵活的环境，它能做非常强大的事。

所以为 knowledge work 选模式的时候，把它放进这个电脑环境更自然——同时把用户不习惯的电脑细节抽象掉，但把同样的力量给他们。当然最终我们希望所有地方都有这份力量，所以后面还会有工作让两种场景能力对齐。

十一、模型选择的建议：先信默认

Vibhu：Harness 之外还有你们发的新模型。有人喜欢 min-max：只用 Tera high reasoning、这时候用 Soul、那时候忽略某个……有 32 个选项。给正在扩展使用 productivity 的人一些建议？

Akshay：说建议之前，首先——没有这些模型什么都不可能。我们看到 Codex 起飞是因为模型变得越来越强，现在又有一次 step function jump。

关于建议：我们希望默认就是最好的。我们有 opinion 地选了默认，认为它对大多数人是最好的。power user 有更多选项——可能现在选项太多了，我们在简化——你可以调 reasoning level、换 model class。但对大多数人建议是坚持默认。如果你发现效率或质量不满足需求，再去改。

Vibhu：我最近在跑 Soul light + Goal，思路是 goal 增加 reasoning effort 但通过更多 termination 和 turn 完成。是好方式吗？和 Soul ultra 或 Soul extra high 相比。

Akshay：很难说，因为这是交互效应，看你个人偏好——怎么和模型协作、你想要多少 termination 让你可以 steer。一般建议：

  • Ultra 或 multi-agent 最适合极其复杂、开放探索、或高度可并行的任务
  • Goal 最适合你能在一段时间内验证性地稳定推进的任务
  • 但大多数任务不在这两个 bucket 里，尤其是开始阶段——所以先试默认，再决定去哪。

十二、Model Slider 的设计哲学

主持人：你们做的那个 slider 很棒，减少了 panic。

Akshay：思路是把多维度投影到一个维度。一边是速度和效率，另一边是质量和 thoroughness。

主持人：我很惊讶它这么多用到 Soul，最低档的青铜级是……

Akshay：Spider 我没记错的话是……

主持人：他们把 Tera 只 preset 成 light 版。我觉得应该有更多人用 Tera——一个原因是 Soul 老是没有容量。（笑）

十三、Artifact 的进化：Excel 都被 agent 了

主持人：看，10 分钟出结果了，退休计算器。

Akshay：这次发布一个大 push 是 artifact。对比 5.5、5.4，artifact 质量有戏剧性提升。产品侧也一样。

主持人：UX 侧也很疯——hosted site，不再需要自己托管网页。

Akshay：这次发布里有很多东西——比如你看到的这个 viewer——直觉是"你在做退休计算器，第一版不会是你要的终态，你想迭代。如果它对最终形态高保真——包括你把它发给同事看到的样子——那会让你更信任产品的迭代能力。"

主持人：说到发给同事，你们会考虑 artifact 的多人协作吗？

Akshay：这是我们正在积极思考的。有一个内部现象：经常有人 ping 我一件事，我去问 ChatGPT Work，然后把答案 ping 回去。你会想——我在这个 loop 里是必要的吗？可能只是复述或加了点上下文，但信息在传递中有损。所以答案会是——预先响应每一个 inbound。

主持人：也就是说我就是"从 AI 到 AI 的消息转发员"。

不过这里有个轻度安全问题：我实际上是权限层。我可以查询你的问题得到自动答案，但那可能不是我该看到的。而且我甚至不知道我不该看什么。

Akshay：尤其是 ChatGPT Work 让你连接 plugin、拉本地文件，agent 拥有的 context 是深度个人化的，这需要被保护。这确实是个挑战。

十四、Sites：知识工作的新 canonical artifact

主持人：有 Excel、有 PowerPoint、有 Docs，你们还想到哪些格式？会不会有 OpenAI Airtable？

Akshay：你没提 Sites——那是这次发布的大重点。人们通常在 X 上把 Sites 说成 prototyping 工具，我们这次发布里那个 model slider 的 affordance 就是几乎完全在一个 site 上做的——设计、工程、产品在 site 上协作、试。

但少被谈论的一面是——Sites 是knowledge work 的 artifact。前几天我和 corporate finance 的同事聊，他们月度报告以前在 slide deck 和 spreadsheet 里，现在直接在 site 里协作。原因是 site 更高带宽：PowerPoint、Excel 无限灵活，但你会撞到边界；而 site 上你可以要什么就有什么。

十五、案例研究：从 Strata 游戏到 auto-research

主持人：让我给你看我的 case study——涵盖了所有热点：ChatGPT Work、5.6、token 亿万富翁、token maxing、sites、auto research。

我喜欢一个叫 Strata 的桌游，物理方块摆在板上。周末我拍了 30 张照片扔进 ChatGPT。17 亿 tokens 之后，出来一个可玩的 site，带 3D 方块摆放。因为需要物理方块、需要朋友训练它才能对战，我也可以训练 AI。

这就进入 auto research。我要训自己的 AI 让它们自我对弈。我在 San Mateo 参会没法监督，所以让它 auto research、创建 benchmark。参数太多我读不完，就让它出一个 site——出了个 lab panel。

它输出的是"研究 artifact"，我后来把它移出 sites，因为想要更多数据库和基础设施，但作为 research output 你可以直接玩。我要 tune 什么超参数、scaling law 是什么、game optimization——全在一个 site 里。

结果就是——我不再读 ChatGPT 输出，我读 site 输出。当然也有 sprawl：这个 site 太长了，无数数字。所以我要开始砍。

Akshay：这就是我们看到的很多团队的 workflow：以前的 canonical artifact 是文档，现在变成 site。因为它就是 HTML，无限灵活。你想 highlight 什么就 highlight，可以让它变 hero image，不像 slide 里会被 braid。

十六、Meta 层的产品设计：做一个"造产品的产品"

主持人：你的工作也变得很 meta——你不是在设计产品，你在设计一个"用来造产品的产品"，怎么管理？

Akshay：我们在 UX 上一直在思考——如何平衡简洁与能力。如果我们设计的产品能做出无数东西，那不能全都摆到你面前，你会崩溃。ChatGPT 上就已经有这个问题，现在能做的更多了。

平衡是：给用户足够的 UI surface，让他们能表达、能验证 agent 用了对的工具和源，然后 UI 退到后面；同时通过系统"show them instead of telling them"能做什么。因为很多事情靠他们自己发现下一个用例。

Vibhu：有趣的是每个人做法都不一样。我做了同样这个游戏的另一版，我没拍照片，直接把规则扔给 goal，18 分 53 秒后得到差不多的版本——虽然没 auto research。而且是用 Codex 不是 Work，也挺有意思。

十七、show don't tell 是最大的产品挑战

主持人：这是 GPT image 生成的头像，非常适合游戏设计。很多游戏设计师非常爱 GPT image。

Vibhu：更广的 takeaway 可能是我们做这些是为了测试工具。这也是 5.6 之前的测试——我之前在 5.5 上做过这个游戏，那时要喂规则给它，它自己找不到这个小众游戏的规则。5.6 就有 auto distribution 能力了。

主持人：你看，work 变成 personal、personal 变成 work 太容易了。因为我个人做的东西直接影响到我合作的人——我给他们看，他们就说"啊 GPT 能这样？"这大概就是增长策略。

Akshay：show not tell 是我们还没完全破解的一块——如何向人展示他们能用产品做什么，而不是通过文章或 onboarding 教他们。

主持人：这是我作为前 DevRel 的职业风险——DevRel 就是要"show"，但产品经理会说"我们不需要你，如果产品足够 intuitive"。（笑）

Akshay：这就是模型的魔法——可以根据用户具体情况、历史、adoption journey 上的位置来定制 tell 或 show 的方式。

十八、路线图：从 developer 到 general knowledge work 到 everyone

Vibhu：Codex、ChatGPT、Work 之外，还有其他分发路径吗？还有更大的市场没被覆盖吗？

Akshay：我把它看作 sequencing——愿景是把有用的 agent 带给所有人。我们从 developer 开始，因为 developer 是 early adopter、愿意忍受更多 friction。下一个机会是我们叫做"general knowledge work"——所有 developer 周边的职能。这里的挑战是 show not tell、让产品更容易理解、加入对这个人群更重要的能力（artifact、computer use 等）。

再下一个阶段是把 general knowledge work 的学习带给所有人，不管他们在生活里做什么。这个游戏例子就在这个边界上。我在家全职用 ChatGPT——前几天让它做个 meal plan、存在 computer 环境里持续回访。是不是每个人都在这样做？还没有，因为我们还有事要做。ChatGPT Life。

十九、给普通用户的 power user 建议

Vibhu：给一些 power user 建议？有些人 24/7 都在用，有些人偶尔用。

Akshay：一是拓宽你对"可能"的想象力。技术推进太快，3 个月前不可能的现在可能。举个例子——我们内部 review 周期，过去大家说"我不想写 review，让 AI 写"，但 6 个月前那基本是 slop、不太有用。现在模型能做得比我好——它有 code、review、Slack 的全部 context，能挖到我可能都没看到的 win。所以哪怕你之前试过某件事没成功，也要再试。

二是你给它越多，它越有价值。在这个 agent 能访问你 ChatGPT Work 或电脑上一切的环境里，你可以随时间创建 artifact、存 library，模型能持续访问。你给它关于你所在领域的信息越多，它就以你可能都没想到的方式帮到你——比如在你不知道的时刻从某个 context 里 proactively 拉出东西。

二十、Review 场景的伦理与礼仪

主持人：Review 这块很敏感。你有下属，我也管理过团队，我很不愿意让下属看到 LLM 生成的东西，因为好像"你不在乎"。OpenAI 里大家似乎更开放于被 GPT 评价？有没有不成文规则？

Akshay：礼仪是——我绝不会用 AI 独自写一段 review 交上去。我说的是收集 context——你可以比以前更精细地 tailor 和 steer 的 agentic search。因为有 Codex、有 ChatGPT，人们能做的事比以前多，所以也很容易漏。所以我们要用同样的工具跟上大家的 impact。

主持人：以 OpenAI 的规模，Slack 里那么多海量消息，你觉得它会漏东西吗？

Akshay：大概率会，但我自己也会漏。所以是相对的。

Vibhu：有时候它找到你不会找到的东西也很好。我 Codex 的 system prompt 是这样设的——每个 project 都有一个 secret 的 notes.md，它会写 learning 进去。全局那个 prompt 可以从所有 project 里拉。所以有时候它说"哦，四个月前你做过这个项目，这里有一条笔记"，把我根本不会想到的东西拉进 context——这就有点 superhuman 了。省下几小时的挖掘，或者发现某件事已经做过了。

Akshay：我有一个好玩的故事：为了这次发布，团队几个月一直在 cook，Slack 和 Docs 里聊天极多。团队里有人设了个 scheduled task，扫所有内容然后生成最好的 meme，post 到一个共享频道。这里有两件酷事：

  1. 模型开始变得有幽默感了——一年前完全不是这样。
  2. 它以出人意料的方式发现联系——这就是 meme 生成的关键，你能看到真正让你惊喜的东西。

这当然不是最"productive"的用法，但它体现了一个正在出现的能力——帮你 define 你原本不会知道的信息。

二十一、发布数据：1000 万用户

主持人：这次发布是我很长时间以来见过最成功的一次，我个人觉得比 5.0 还成功。你宣布了 1000 万用户。感觉不一样吗？你经历过很多 launch。

Akshay：两件事。一是这感觉像一个culmination——我们走了很久的愿景。看到我们达到分发数字非常兴奋。另一面是——要做的事还多得多。ChatGPT 有几亿用户，1000 万是酷，但我们要让所有人感受到这份魔法。这是下一步。

主持人：Codex 会在可预见的未来继续作为品牌存在。

Akshay：比这还强——我们完全打算继续深耕 developer。他们一直是核心市场，Codex 会持续变强，专门服务 software development。这次合并不会消耗那一块，反而会增加 Codex 的效用——因为你可以在写 def、创建 artifact、搜代码之间无缝切换。

二十二、Artifact 这个词内部叫、外部不叫

Vibhu：这些术语普通用户能懂吗？他们要学会说"artifact"吗？

Akshay：我们内部叫 artifact，因为团队这么叫。外部没人这么叫。他们会按自己习惯的方式描述——"ChatGPT Work 很会做 slide"，他们就会说"ChatGPT Work 很会做 slide"——这正是我们想要的。

二十三、OpenClaw 和 ChatGPT Work 的关系

Vibhu：现在是 2026 年 7 月，OpenAI 的另一个大事件是 OpenClaw——很多人第一次真正 max out agent 用于 personal，也从这里跨到 work。据我理解 OpenClaw 依然独立——你有自己的 OpenClaw moment 吗？

Akshay：有很多灵感来源。我和我太太用 OpenClaw 管家里的事——不算多，但挺有用。我们给它一个 calendar，它帮我们创建 event。后来那台笔记本坏了他们就没重新设置。但灵感很多——ChatGPT Work 在 web / mobile 上都给你一个持久 computer 环境：文件在会话之间会保留。目的就是 enable 这类用例。

我们团队有个人以前用 OpenClaw 做 workout planning 和 meal tracking，现在完全转到 ChatGPT Work——它有相同的 primitive：scheduled task、file system、能跨时间引用文件。

主持人：ChatGPT Work 会完全取代 OpenClaw 吗？

Akshay：我不接触 OpenClaw roadmap，说不好。但我认为不会。那个团队做出的开源技术永远有需要，我们从中获取灵感、把 OpenClaw 的魔法带给听过并用过 ChatGPT 的更多人，就算成功。

ChatGPT Work 侧我们有一个强的信念：核心体验是你来到这个产品、开始一段对话，那一刻里你可以做任何事。我们希望做一个可扩展的、带 plugin 的系统——你可以连接你需要的工具。会有一些专注做某件事最好的产品，但我们希望核心体验里有尽可能多的魔法。

二十四、"个人 OS"的架构挑战

主持人：ChatGPT 上能做完 Wolfram 财务能做的所有事吗？

Akshay：我试了。ChatGPT 还不能托管现金和资产，所以那部分不行。但退休规划、财务规划、budgeting 那些配合 finance plugin 都行——我个人来说那部分已经被替代了。

Vibhu：还没插上。有点怕看到答案。（笑）健康和财务一个道理。

Akshay：agentic search 很酷。传统 UX 里你给用户越多力量，就得加越多旋钮和过滤器。现在有对的连接和数据，你想问什么就问什么，得到答案。

主持人：我从数据工程背景出发想说——只靠 JIT 通过 MCP/CLI/API 拉数据还不够，你想要 data warehouse、缓存、semantic layer。你们有吗？

Akshay：具体细节我不能说，但取决于访问模式。如果你要立刻回答，是的，从所有源拉很难。但 ChatGPT Work 想 enable 的很多用例并不需要立即——它是一个 agent 去做的任务。加上 programmatic tool calling、sub agent 并行化，能力的上限被大幅提升。

二十五、Sub-agents 的设计取舍

主持人：你提到 sub agents——Ultra 是新模式，ChatGPT 里有专门的 affordance 显示 agent，但你其实做不了太多，只能看。你有什么设计上的建议给其他 builder？

Akshay：又回到之前那个平衡——展示能力，但保留足够的抽象不 overwhelm。sub agent 我们想传达的是：如果你的任务是可并行的、或者复杂到需要 sub agent 来 handle，这个产品是给你的。当然还有另一种迭代——能看到 sub agent 具体在做什么——但那可能 verge on overwhelming。所以现在的 trade-off 是这样。

主持人：你确实展示了不少 transcript。

Vibhu：有些人会想更多。我基本上会往 goal 里塞很多东西，每一个 goal 我都告诉它用 sub agent。听起来 redundant，但我很多朋友也这样。我理由是：

  1. 净时间效率——扩散到 sub agent
  2. 成本——offload 到小模型

如果你在做重复任务、想每天稳定完成，你可能想去 fine-tune 哪里用 sub agent。默认是 hidden 我觉得 OK，但可以下拉看到更多。5.6 发布时很多人讨论——它太爱用 sub agent，重到 ChatGPT app 崩溃。

Akshay：我们发布产品时对 Ultra 的定位不够 opinionated——后来我们改成要你 turn on、放在 advanced setting 里，因为它就是给理解会发生什么的 power user 的。它也会更快消耗你的 limit。

二十六、Memory 系统的挑战

主持人：最后一块 harness——memory。最近很多人在讨论。ChatGPT 的新 memory system 以前不太行。Samir 和团队在说 memory……

Akshay：Samir 和研究团队做了大量迭代和改进。我和朋友、家人聊，问他们爱 ChatGPT 什么，"它认识我，我的 ChatGPT 就是我的 ChatGPT"排第一。ChatGPT Work 和 cloud 里默认所有对话继承 ChatGPT memory——它们会知道你的 context，也能写回 memory。

主持人：是同一个 V3 memory 系统？

Akshay：是。从 ChatGPT 过来到 ChatGPT Work 感觉像是我已经在做的事情的延伸。

主持人：本质是 retrieval 问题——是取对了还是过度聚焦错了？false positive 多还是 false negative 多？

Akshay：我不直接做 memory 所以不敢说哪个是更大问题。但两面：一是确保它了解你，二是有EQ在合适时刻提出这些事情——proactively，以正面而非负面的方式让你惊喜。非常挑战，但巨大机会。

二十七、跨项目的 memory 与 collaboration

Vibhu：Chat 用户经常做 one-off 事情。Work 场景里可能是一个 project 你做了一个月。有多个 thread 时，memory 怎么处理？

Akshay：我想先挑战一下——chat 和 work 里 memory 的深度并不是根本不同。Chat 上确实短 session 多，但 ChatGPT 这个产品有很多年的 longevity，人们已经在用它做 worky / productivity 相关的事情了。我个人使用中，所有 one-off 加起来，最终是一个相当持久、相当准确的关于我是谁的表征。X 上时不时有人晒 ChatGPT 讲他们所有信息、人们总是惊讶它多深。

二十八、Chronicle：一个被低估的 memory 增强

主持人：memory 里我不常用的一个功能——Chronicle。它是 super memory 吗？

Akshay：它的想法是从你怎么使用电脑里学习，作为 memory 的另一个 input source。目前是实验性、默认关。推荐你试。回到我们之前聊的——ChatGPT 会漏东西吗？你电脑上一切它都能看吗？它能捕捉意图吗？可能不能，但它会找到你不知道的东西，然后在你做任务时 proactively 浮现出来——我发现这可以很有帮助。

Vibhu：还挺被低估的——它能读你的 memory、log，然后加 skill。

Akshay：Chronicle 生成的 memory 深度不一样。

二十九、pre-AI vs post-AI 的建造

Vibhu：整体反思一下，pre-AI 和 post-AI 的建造有什么大不同？

Akshay：变化太大了。从 idea 到"real"的速度快得多。5 - 10 年前如果你很 scrappy 也快，但现在你能建的广度大得多。这也意味着能更快验证、更快闭环，反馈到用户和 doctor。这个 loop 更 closed 了，对产品开发、对消费者都是 win。

Vibhu：那你的团队更小了吗？

Akshay：不。要做的事更多。人可以在更小团队里完成以前需要大团队的事情，但同时野心更大了。

三十、T 型人才与"idea 的瓶颈"

Vibhu：角色范围有变化吗？EM、PM、engineer、designer 之间？

Akshay：我们看到 role 之间的边界在模糊。

主持人：我抛一个 quote——科技行业未来只剩四种工作：AI slop cannon（烧 token 的）、SRE（负责任的成年人）、卖东西的成年人、hot people。（笑）

Akshay：我的看法是每个人都会变T 型。AI 让所有人可以成为 generalist——我以前不会做设计、现在也没有视觉品位，但可以借 AI 迭代。同时每个人有一个专长，那是 T 的竖线，AI 帮你深挖它。有了这个基础，能做的几乎无限。

主持人：你的瓶颈是什么？需要更多设计师？slop cannon？hot people？

Akshay：瓶颈变成想法和品位。任何人都能建，所以是 bottoms-up ambition 的时代。可建的东西太多，你永远被"同一时间有多少 idea"限制。

主持人：模型能帮忙解这个吗？我有一个 skill——给我四个完全不同的方案。烧 token，但我能拧出"我喜欢这、我喜欢那"。但我一直希望的一个自动化——"给我新 idea"——LLM 就是做不好。

Akshay：idea 不是真空里出现的。产品开发里，idea 来自和用户对话、来自你看到的摩擦、反馈，或建立在你已有的规划上。所以那些"能闭环 idea 的 generalist"总有价值。

三十一、生产力如何定义与度量

主持人：你带 productivity team——你怎么定义 productivity？

Akshay：我们的 mission 是让人做以前做不到的事情。现在从 knowledge work 视角想：人们不再被 role silo、不再被背景或 training silo——不管你在哪个职能，你都能突然建东西、访问以前无法理解的数据。这也延伸到 personal——我们希望产品给你杠杆，让你为自己创造时间去做你爱的事。

主持人：那怎么度量生产力？怎么度量杠杆？

Akshay：我们还没想清楚，因为太多元。每个人目标不同，真正的度量是"他们是否达成目标"。你不知道 upfront 那目标是什么，也没为每个人 tailor。

ChatGPT 里的 thumbs up / down 也不给你太多——你不知道他们踩的是内容、氛围还是没帮上目标。这是个我们和整个行业都要解的问题。

Vibhu：过去我们用代理指标——commit 数、代码行数……

主持人：Story point。

Vibhu：都会回来。（笑）

Akshay：那些代理指标开始 fall apart。token 数、PR 数——不再和"团队是否达成目标"高度相关。要新的度量。

三十二、给管理者的建议：at-bats 和 quality

主持人：给听着的管理者一件可以试的事。

Akshay：对我重要的是——at-bats。团队是否在建立肌肉——不只 quantity 更是 quality——能不能从生成 idea、build 出来、拿反馈、响应反馈、验证 / 证伪假设，一路走到下一个 idea？能不能高效地做这件事？这既是写的代码、做的设计、写的 spec，也是团队文化——有没有 humility，能不能反复走完这个流程还保持动力和兴奋。这在技术前沿、可建东西极多的现在最重要。

Vibhu：度量 productivity 里有什么陷阱？很多人加了 LLM、加了 dashboard，但没有真的变化。（笑）

Akshay：陷阱是——混淆 motion 和 progress。因为工具，motion 比以前容易多了。但 progress 要求你对"你要达成什么"非常 prescriptive、deliberate。回到度量：OpenAI 能不能替用户度量生产力？很难，因为多元。但作为一个团队你必须对 progress 是什么有非常 prescriptive、deliberate 的看法。没有这个，就容易混淆二者。

结尾

主持人：这是很棒的一句——motion 和 progress 之间的区别，我们会把这句话放进写稿。非常慷慨的时间，谢谢，恭喜 1000 万。

Akshay：谢谢邀请。

主持人：下一次到 1 亿——两个月后见。（笑）

Akshay：谢谢。

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：这不是"AGI 产品化"，而是"打工人身份的溶解工程"
表面上大家在讨论 ChatGPT Work 是超级 App、是 Codex 的延伸、是给企业的生产力工具。但如果把 Akshay 反复提到的几句话叠在一起看——"我几个月前和现在做的完全是两件事"、"人们在用 Codex 时那种偷偷摸摸的骄傲"、"work 和 personal 的边界会越来越模糊"、"每个人都会变成 T 型"——你会发现 OpenAI 真正在做的**根本不是一个产品**，而是在**主动解构"职业身份"这个工业时代最坚固的社会契约**。
传统 SaaS 是围绕角色建的：Figma 给设计师、Notion 给 PM、GitHub 给工程师。工具定义身份，身份定义工作流。而 ChatGPT Work 反过来——它拒绝按角色分产品（"we shouldn't box them in"），因为一旦按角色分，你就默认了角色是稳定的。**OpenAI 押注的是角色本身正在液化**。这就是为什么 Codex 和 Work 必须共享 harness：不是技术偷懒，而是意识形态选择。
## 二、跨领域

item.title: [a16z] Training Robots in Worlds That Don't Exist | World Labs with a16z
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：机器人公司其实是"反事实推理"公司

表面上，World Labs 收购 Scenix 讲的是"用仿真训练机器人"的故事。但 Fei-Fei 在对话中悄悄埋下了一个哲学炸弹——她把仿真等同于counterfactual reasoning（反事实推理），并类比人类大脑与足球世界杯赛前的战术推演。

这意味着 World Labs 真正在做的不是"3D 引擎的升级版"，而是给机器装上"想象力器官"。真实数据只能告诉机器"发生过什么"，而仿真让机器学习"本可以发生什么"、"如果换一种方式又会怎样"。这一步跨越比它看上去大得多：它把机器人学从归纳学习推向了因果学习——而这恰恰是 LLM 至今没解决的元问题。

一个惊人的推论：World Labs 的世界模型，可能最终会反哺 LLM 的推理能力，而不是相反。语言模型正在渴求的"心智模拟器"，很可能诞生于机器人领域，而非文本领域。

二、跨领域连接：Waymo、好莱坞 VFX、进化生物学 的三角映射

对话中散落着三个看似无关的锚点，其实构成了一个隐藏的三角结构：

  • Waymo：数十亿小时的仿真远超真实路测——证明"高价值领域的 AI 一定是仿真主导"。
  • Weta / 腾讯 VFX（联合创始人 Changyi 的背景）：影视工业早在 20 年前就学会了"如何用不完美的物理换取足够可信的世界"。
  • 进化生物学（Fei-Fei 的类比）：人手不是攀爬树的最优解，而是"未特化换取通用性"的妥协产物。

把这三点连起来，你会看到一个大多数投资人错过的模式："仿真—影视—进化"三者本质上都在解决同一个问题——如何用有限计算/结构来逼近无限复杂的现实。World Labs 招募的团队画像（学术 + VFX + 全栈机器人）不是偶然的人才拼图，而是这三种"世界近似哲学"的战略融合。这也解释了为什么 Fei-Fei 反复强调 "essential structure" 而不是 "physical accuracy"——他们在下一盘更大的棋：建立一门"够用现实学"（good-enough reality science）。

三、被忽视的深层信号：为什么"清洁任务占三分之一"是一个战略信号

Yunzhu 提到一个几乎被一带而过的细节：他们做用户调研收集机器人任务，1/3 是清洁任务。大多数听众会把它当成一个 fun fact，但这其实是整个战略最诚实的自我暴露。

惊人的反常识观察：清洁任务是结构化程度最低、变异性最高、经济价值最低、社会价值最高的任务组合。这个组合意味着——如果你打赌"人形通用机器人 5 年内进家庭"，清洁应该是最不该先做的事；但如果你打赌"世界模型是一切的入口"，清洁反而是最好的实验场，因为它逼迫你解决完全无结构的空间理解。

再叠加 Fei-Fei 说的"从 structured → semi-structured → unstructured"的路径，你会发现 World Labs 的真实商业节奏是： - 短期赚钱：仓库、电子装配等半结构化场景（有人付费、可交付）； - 长期护城河：用清洁这类任务把"世界模型"逼到极限； - 哲学赌注：机器人不是终点，而是验证空间智能是否是通用智能"缺失的第四模态"的最严苛测试床。

换句话说，Scenix 加入 World Labs 的真正含义不是"World Labs 进军机器人"，而是——机器人成了 World Labs 检验自己 AGI 假设的实验容器。这是一种 Fei-Fei 从不明说但一以贯之的科学家式叙事：先假设、后证伪、以硬件为镜。

四、一个让人后背发凉的推论

对话末尾有一句被轻轻带过的话："we can work with robots remotely"（他们会在纽约和旧金山两地远程操控机器人调试系统）。

如果你把这句话和"real-to-sim-to-real"、"embodiment agnostic"、"model agnostic"三个词放在一起看——World Labs 正在无声地构建 "机器人云"的雏形：一个让任何机器人硬件公司都可以像调用 AWS 一样，调用"世界"和"评估"作为服务的基础设施。

这可能才是 a16z 押注的真正东西：不是又一个机器人公司，而是"机器人时代的 AWS S3——但存储的不是文件，而是世界"。

📝 转录文本

引言：什么是空间智能

We are building the next frontier of AI which is what we call spatial intelligence.

As Cynics, we are developing what we call a real to sim to real pipeline. We can replace all the data, all the evaluation we need in the real environment by using the data that can generate at a scalable way in our digital world.

Think about human intelligence. We do a lot of simulation in our head. Why? There's a very important role simulation plays that real world data doesn't play which is counterfactual reasoning.

What we are building is a consistent world — consistent both over space, over time, over different viewpoints, and over different types of interactions.

My north star is: I want the robot to work.

The world we live in can be multiverse that we create technology to allow people, builders, developers to act within different spaces.

Do you believe we'll ever be able to build robots that have the power efficiency of a human being? How far away are we from this? Is this like 5 years or this is like never?

The TL;DR is…

一、World Labs 是什么

All right. Well, it's great to have you both here. So, Fei-Fei, for the listeners that may not have the background, maybe you can give an overview of what World Labs does.

Yeah. Well, World Labs has — I I I think we should just recognize it's a frontier model lab. We are building the next frontier of AI which is what we call spatial intelligence. And spatial intelligence is about creating AI that has the ability to generate, understand, reason with, and interact with spaces — whether it's physical or virtual.

And of course, a means to an end towards spatial intelligence is building large world models. And that's what World Labs is mostly focused on.

二、为什么现在进入机器人

So you've been saying this since the very beginning — the machine's ability to perceive and reason about spaces and act on spaces. But I always had the assumption that the acting on spaces was some longist future thing. But now you're acquiring a robotics company, so maybe talk a little bit about the timeliness of this and the intentions.

Yeah. So first of all, it doesn't just take robotics to act within spaces or to interact, right? I mean, look at the creative field — whether it's VFX or gaming or design. Many use cases: you can create and act within virtual spaces.

World Labs' thesis has always been that the world we live in can be multiverse — that we create technology to allow people, builders, developers to act within different spaces.

Having said that, the ability to act within the physical space is one of the most exciting and most profoundly important capabilities of the future AI world. So robotics is very much that. So World Labs has always believed that robotics is an important application as well as use case of spatial intelligence and world modeling. So by joining forces with — by inviting Scenix's team to World Labs — is part of our long-term vision and mission. We've always committed to that.

三、Scenix 的背景与使命

Amazing. So, Yunzhu, you're the co-founder of Scenix. Maybe provide everyone with a quick overview of your background and what Scenix does.

Yeah. So, I'm Yunzhu. I'm currently co-founder of Scenix and also assistant professor at Columbia University.

Wow.

So, my research started from my PhD at MIT and then postdoc with Fei-Fei at Stanford University.

That's great. The world is small.

The world is small. It is.

Throughout my career, my goal has been very simple: trying to help the robots better perceive and interact with the physical world. I'm a very practical person. I want my robot to work in the real physical environments.

So for Scenix, the unique opportunity we see is that there has been a lot of bottlenecks right now faced by the developments of general-purpose robots — especially around training and also around evaluations.

So we are developing what we call a real-to-sim-to-real pipeline. We want to map the real environments into the digital world that has the best alignment with the real environments. By alignment, we mean that whatever happens in the digital world is also going to happen in the real environments — such that we can replace all the data, all the evaluation we need in the real environment by using the data that can generate at a scalable way in our digital world.

So that is how everything started in Scenix. We put together a very very strong and best teams around robotics, robot learning, and also simulation and rendering — trying to build this real-to-sim-to-real stack to solve some of the key bottlenecks.

四、从客户到合并：一个意外的开始

It's amazing that you two work together.

Yeah. And there is a funny story here. Because you would think — because we worked together, he was my amazing postdoc, we've been talking about this and World Labs integration for a long time. It's actually not true. They came into World Labs as a customer.

Really?

When we released the first version of our generative model called Marble last winter, around November, December, Scenix just signed up.

No kidding. As a customer.

Yes. And I didn't even know what it was. And then I realized this is Yunzhu's company. I called Yunzhu, I'm like, "Wow, this is your company." And then we realized there's so much synergy.

Maybe Fei-Fei could just quickly describe what Marble is.

Yeah, Marble is the code name for the base model that World Labs has been training and iterating on. The fundamental capability right now of Marble that is publicly released is to take a prompt — it can be an image, it can be a few images, or a text — and turn that into a geometrically consistent world that can be represented in 3D geometry, whether it's Gaussian splat or mesh.

Really what Scenix team is doing is trying to solve this extremely difficult problem in robotics: the lack of data. The lack of data in training, the lack of data in evaluation. This is very very different from language models where data is abundant on the internet.

And we know that in order for robotics to work, we have to somehow unlock the power of scaling law. But where does that come from? This is something that is a profound problem that everybody's battling with in robotics.

五、两个团队的互补性

It'd actually be great to talk about this synergy — you have put together a very talented team. To what extent is there overlap, to what extent is this an extension? Maybe talk a little bit about that.

Yeah. The TL;DR is: it's very complementary and with the shared mission.

So Yunzhu is one of the three technical co-founders. The other two are Changyi Zheng, another Columbia professor who has been a world-class technologist in simulation. Changyi has his background also in VFX — he worked at Weta, he worked at Tencent, he's being an entrepreneur.

Then there's Sunny who is a phenomenal engineering leader who was also in a startup that was acquired by Amazon many years ago. So he worked in many different tech stacks in the computer vision field in Amazon.

So when we started talking more seriously, I recognized that a couple of things that Scenix has from a talent point of view is extremely complementary to World Labs.

One is obviously incredible thought leadership and just technical prowess in robotics — from really from hardware full-stack robotics. Even when Yunzhu was my postdoc at Stanford, at that time you already had your faculty offer, so you were there only for one year — I wanted you for more than one year, but he had to go become a — have the real job. So he was a full-stack researcher in robotics, from modeling to hardware.

And of course, Yunzhu and his students at Scenix was that pool of talent World Labs hasn't had yet.

Then on the Changyi side, is just incredible simulation capability. He's such a senior researcher and technologist in simulation. And what World Labs is doing is very much interfacing the world of simulation.

So what they don't have obviously is on the generative model side as well as the computer vision 3D reconstruction side — we're also very strong at World Labs. So that's a technology that Scenix needs.

So together these two sides come together and make it much more complete.

六、Yunzhu 为什么选择加入

Fei-Fei's motivation in this — this is an extension and a compliment to get into robotics. Having been in your situation, which is deciding when to sell a company, it would be great to hear from you: how you think about joining World Labs and kind of the fit there, and why you made the decision to do it.

Yeah. So at the very beginning, we were deciding okay, we want to just keep going. But after chatting with Fei-Fei, after seeing all the synergies that happening in the middle, it just makes perfect sense for the forces to join each other.

So in any sense, as Scenix, what we have been doing is real-to-sim-to-real: to do this reconstruction of the environment. So we capture the appearance of the environment, geometry of the environments, and also the dynamics of the environment — meaning how the environment is going to change when you apply actions.

So this tensor reconstruction right now is still a little bit on the heavier side. And what World Labs right now has been doing involves a lot of profound capabilities around sparse reconstruction and generations.

So we see a lot of opportunities of leveraging Marble and other capabilities at World Labs in order to do very efficient reconstructions and modeling of the environments.

七、能否期待一个机器人基础模型？

So can we expect a foundation model for robotics from World Labs?

World Labs is building a foundation model. As you know, Martin, we're building a base model. And as the technology has been evolving, some of the most exciting base models are omni-models, right? They take multimodal input, they have multimodal outputs.

And what is a foundation model for robotics? It's very likely going to involve actions. It's very likely going to involve the output of actions in addition to the state of the world. And we're definitely not ruling this out.

Yeah. Great.

So for example, for the foundation models, it essentially needs to be a multimodal model. So it has to take into account frame, text, image, depths, and different kinds of modalities — and action is a very very important part of that modalities.

So if you think about frame + actions as inputs, that is essentially a forward simulator that is going to predict how the environment is going to change when you apply a specific action.

When the action is output, this is essentially a policy model that is trying to predict, given a specific goal, what should be the action you take in the real environment to get you closer to that goal.

So this kind of omni-models actually can benefit a lot and actually provide huge amount of values for the robotics communities in trying to understand how to model the environments and at the same time how to act in the environments. And this can also act as a backbone for you to fine-tune into specific robotic applications — to making sure it's really live up to the reliability and efficiency that expected by the clients.

八、为什么不只用视频模型？

You know, Yunzhu, if you don't mind a kind of a lay investor question — I see a lot of robotics companies, and a very popular approach right now for the robotics companies that come in is: we'll use a video model. That's the predominant method. Whereas this is 3D and simulation — it's a very different approach. So maybe you could contrast this popular approach of just using video only versus kind of what the ambition here is.

Yeah. So in order to create worlds where the robot can learn, the worlds — as I mentioned — is to capture the essential structure of the problem. And one of the very important necessary requirements for those worlds will be consistency.

So that is where I actually see there's very very strong synergies with Marble. Because what we are building is a consistent world — consistency both over space, over time, over different viewpoints, and over different types of interactions.

And Marble — the generated worlds from Marble — also provides an infrastructure, a component of that entire worlds that we believe is necessary for the robot to learn.

Imagine if a robot push an object forwards, the object just magically disappear — which has been a problem of many of the existing video prediction models. This won't provides good enough signal for the robot to know what is the right thing to do.

But obviously, right now there has been a lot of investigation on building better and better and stronger and stronger video models. So we actually see a way where some of the infrastructure we build can provide as a initial momentum, and to going through this data flywheel of going from this more simulation-driven models into a robot policy models — which going to do the execution in the real environment, collecting new data, the data will come back in — where the model doesn't necessarily have to be physics only or learning only, but somewhere in the middle, which be able to capture the essential structure of the problem, but at the same times be able to scale and become better and better as you accumulate more data.

九、北极星：让机器人真正工作

You know, I've worked now Fei-Fei very closely for a while, and you've always had this north star which has driven this — you've articulated variously as kind of 3D and a number of other ways. And I'm just wondering, for you, is there also a similar philosophical north star? Or you're more the pragmatic: like I am, build the system, do the thing.

My north star is to make robots work.

Amazing.

Yeah, in the real environment. I'm a very practical person. I want the robot to work.

One interesting thing that's actually coming from my collaborations with Fei-Fei during my postdoc — we are building this kind of benchmark. We actually send out surveys asking the general public what they want their robots to do for them.

Among the thousand tasks we collected, one-third of the tasks are about cleaning. People just don't like to do those dull and dirty tasks. And those are the scenarios we really want to making sure we have robotic solutions to deal with.

One thing I really like about Scenix — Martin, especially continuing your question — there's a lot of robotics companies building models and all that. One thing I truly like about Scenix is Yunzhu and his co-founders have such an incredibly pragmatic approach to robotics. Especially they come from academia — right, Sunny doesn't, but Yunzhu and Changyi come from academia — but their first instinct is work with design partners and customers in real industry, whether it's labs at industry labs, or warehouses, or electronics assembly. That is such a refreshing way of approaching robotics. And that really made me very excited to work with them.

十、创造性用途 vs. 机器人：精确度的鸿沟

Maybe this is for Yunzhu — but this is personal curiosity. It seems to me that for robotics, you have to be pretty exact. I mean, not perfect, but pretty close. But for the creative use cases which World Labs has done a lot of, you kind of don't need to be — sometimes being wrong is stylistic or intentional. And so from a technical perspective, what is the challenge here for reconciling these two things? Or do they never get reconciled? Like, there always be two points in the design space?

So they will be reconciled in the long terms, of course. And modeling of the environments doesn't have to be perfect. The model doesn't have to be perfect in robotics.

And by the way — again this is pure curiosity — is there a bit more formal way to say what that means, not to be perfect? It has to be pretty close.

So let me putting this way. For example, models — over the developments of all different kinds of robotic applications — has been a very important cornerstones. If you look at all the existing robotic applications like planes, drones, Roomba, or even for quadruped robots, bipedal robots — model has been the way for them to actually work and be able to transfer from simulation to the real environment.

But if you look at those locomotion robots like quadruped robots, bipedal robots — they can walking on snows, they can walking on bushes. But you don't need to have a simulator that can simulate all the bushes and snows like very precisely. You needs to have a simulation that capture the essential structure of the problem and do a whole different kinds of randomizations inside the digital environment.

So that is what we're aiming for. So basically with Scenix and together with World Labs, we're trying to investigate: what is the level of fidelity we needs to model the massive worlds, besides the robots, such that we'll be able to transfer the robotic systems training in the simulated environment digital worlds back into the real scenarios.

十一、仿真 vs. 真实数据：不是二元选择

As an investor, I've heard other researchers say — like Sergey Levine say — simulation will always eventually deviate from the physical world, and real world data collection is absolutely critical. And so maybe talk a little bit about the viability of this approach where simulation is a cornerstone, as opposed to some other approach.

So they don't contradict with each other. So if you think about the simulation — simulation is essentially trying to predict how the environment is going to change when you apply the actions. And this is essentially a model of the worlds. It doesn't necessarily have to be pure physics. It can be a combination between both physics and also learning.

We are collecting real-world data. We will be using those real-world data. It just at different stages of this data flywheel.

Maybe at the very beginning, we have stronger emphasize on — we have more physics to making sure we have the right consistency and right structure for us to learn the worlds, for us to train the robot policies. But as we accumulate more and more data, both through data collection and also through the collaboration with our clients, we'll have the data that will be moving towards more towards more learning-based modeling of the environments.

So this kind of transition and also this kind of data flow is really an enabling factor of both getting the best of both physics and geometry and consistency, as well as all the power and magics from the data and compute.

反事实推理：为什么仿真不可替代

I want to add to this and be slightly philosophical here. There isn't a binary choice between simulation or no simulation. All this come together to make robotics work.

Think about human intelligence. We do a lot of simulation in our head. You know why? There's a very important role simulation plays that real-world data doesn't play, which is counterfactual reasoning — that you play out events that hasn't happened, or cannot happen, or you don't have enough data to make it happen in real world. And while you play it out, you learn how to act in it. Humans do this all the time.

We just — I know you were at World Cup.

I was at the World Cup.

Congratulations to Spain winning. I'm sure in the planning of every game there is simulation, whether it's digital or on the whiteboard or whatever. That simulation, the role simulation plays, is counterfactual reasoning. And that's really important in robotics, because we just do not have — cannot possibly have — enough real-world data for that.

Here's a real-life example: the industry of self-driving cars. Waymo has officially said they use billions of hours of simulation. And actually Waymo is more simulation-heavy than just real-world data heavy. So these are real examples. And as you know, Martin — and Andrew too — cars are the simplest kind of robots. So clearly simulation plays a huge role in robotic learning.

仿真提供的两大价值：可靠性与效率

I also want to add to that. If you put things more specific, simulation can provide two levels of benefits: the first one is reliability, and the second one is efficiency.

Reliability. If you're thinking about a robotic system working reliable in the real environments, you need data to provide systematic coverage of all the state space and the variations that robots might encounter. That's how you can learn — how it is robust. So with simulation, you can do systematic randomizations and control the variations of lighting, frictions, geometries, object types, and also all different kind of physical parameters, to making sure you have sufficient coverage of the state space. So this is what can give the robotic systems reliability.

Efficiency. Right now, many people are doing teleoperation. And if you look at many of the teleoperation devices, imagining all the actual skeletons you are using — you're actually collecting the data at a speed that is actually slower than human actually doing the task. But for many of our clients, human speed to them is not good enough. They want faster than human speeds.

So for the robot to move faster, it's not as simple as just drive the robot faster, because the gravity doesn't change. But in simulation, you can do systematic speed-up of the robots' behaviors to train the robots — such that it considers all the dynamics changes of the environments. So this is what can give our clients efficiency.

So both for the reliability and efficiency, there are some kind of very unique values where simulation can provide.

十二、具体用例：训练与评估

You've talked about the technology and the platform, what it does. Maybe talk about the specific use cases people use it for.

There are essentially two specific use cases, especially around both training and also around evaluations.

评估（Evaluation）

Evaluation is something people often overlooked in the robotics. But if you are tuning robotic models, you have to know how well it works, and that is the only source of information for you to iterate.

By the way, every AI person really understands what evals are and uses it all the time. Non-AI people, it often means something a little different. So maybe it's even worth just describing specifically what you mean by evaluation.

Okay. So what I mean by evaluation is: you'll be able to understand — for this specific checkpoint — how well does it perform? Does it perform, for example, 95% of the time, or 99.9% of the time? And the key criteria people use in industry is: how long does it take? How long in walk-clock time does it take for you to distinguish between a checkpoint that is 90% from a checkpoint that is 92 points.

And if you only do that in the real environment, that's just takes so long for you to do the distinguishment. And if you really think about also the robotic evaluations right now people are doing in the real environments — the iteration speeds is multiple orders of magnitude slower than iterations of those language models.

Yeah. So not only is the robotic tasks very varied, very diverse —

Oh yeah, because you actually have to do the thing, right? Atoms have to move through space.

Exactly. Not only there are the laws of physics have to —

Have you watched those robotics videos? Every video has like 10x, 8x — because it moves so slowly.

Exactly. So not only it's slow, it's dangerous, it's costly, but at the same time the speeds is also multiple orders of magnitudes slower.

So some of our clients actually needs this digital environment that can be used to evaluate their robotic systems. And because our digital environment has proven alignments with the real world — so meaning whatever happens in the sim is also likely to happen in the real environment. If a checkpoint is working better in the simulation, it's also highly likely to also work better in the real environments, as we have also been discussed in the blog post.

So that actually give our clients very strong confidence in actually using the data, using the signal from the digital environment to do scalable, safe, and much faster evaluations of their robotic systems.

训练（Training）

Great. So that is on the evaluation. Then on the training.

On the training side — so basically, like I also mentioned — it's about controllability. So you want to control all the different possible variations of states, parameters, lighting, frictions, physical parameters, even object geometry, object types. So you want to making sure you have sufficient coverage of all different kinds of scenarios, such that you'll be able to generate informative data for your robots to be robust.

And this is just going to be so hard to do just in the real environments, like we discussed. If you do teleoperation, the speed at which you're collecting data is slow. You're also limited by how many robots you have, how many teleoperation devices you have. There's a whole different kinds of challenges around all the data operations around it.

But in simulation, everything can be controllable, everything can be systematic, and everything can be understand at a level where you know exactly and making claims about exactly what distribution you have covered — to develop confidence about, within that distribution, we know the robot will work.

So those kind of confidence and efficiency and scalability is something that our clients also value — to use our digital worlds for the training of robotic systems.

来自 Marble 的意外需求信号

Here's the crazy thing: even before Scenix and we are talking, our inbound customers for Marble were already seeing this kind of demand. We just cannot serve these customers. But we are already getting a lot of phone calls from early-stage robotics companies who are developing their models all the way to downstream, very pragmatic use cases. And we're seeing these needs.

十三、World Labs 不造机器人本体

When people hear you're going into robotics, what they're going to envision is you're pulling out a 3D printer and you're going to be making hardware, and then you're going to be programming the brain of a robot, and sticking it in the robot, and then you've got a robot. And I don't think that's what you guys are talking about here. So maybe talk about where this fits in the lifecycle of creating a robot, and where you will end and where the rest of the ecosystem will begin.

So what we have been building, you can imagine, is an infrastructure — with the softwares around this infrastructure — for people to build worlds such that robots can learn and evaluate. And this infrastructure is naturally model-agnostic and embodiment-agnostic.

So I just want to be very clear — just because this is actually a very subtle — for you it's obvious, but it's a very subtle point — which is: from what you said, that's not building a robot. It's building an environment which another company can place their robot brain —

Exactly.

— to navigate and to learn.

Yeah. So for our customers right now, they have all different kinds of robots. Some are using single robot arm, some are using bio-, some are using a fixed arm, some are using mobile manipulators, some using grippers, some are using some more elaborate versions of the end effectors.

So our platform right now is just naturally embodiment-agnostic. We can very easily integrate different kinds of robotic embodiment, be able to put them into the worlds we generated with digitalized, such that we will be able to give those individual robots capabilities of doing the right tasks and at the right levels of reliability and efficiency in the real environments.

And we are also model-agnostic. So we can just using the data generated by our worlds to train different models, either from scratch or doing post-training of existing foundation models like vision-language-action models or world-action models.

So to us, it doesn't matter — we just want to making sure we have the infrastructure, we have all the worlds, such that the robot can work reliably in the real environment.

十四、人形机器人：从结构化环境切入

You have told me that you think a lot of the predictions around humanoids were a little bit aggressive, and we're likely to see more constrained rollouts like warehouses or whatever. Can you talk a little bit about that and how that impacts what you're going to be tackling here at World Labs?

So that's a very good question. If you look at all the progressions of robotic applications in the real environments, it has always followed the trend from going from fully structured environments into semi-structured environments, and then into unstructured environments.

  • Fully structured environments — you have knowledge and control over all the configurations within the environments. Like factories — like factories or for car manufacturing. Those has been automated for decades.
  • Semi-structured environments — you have certain controls over the environments. For example, like the Amazon warehouses, or for example like restaurants, hotels, where you have certain control over the environment to just make the task easier for your robots. But there are obviously many other objects, or for example clothes — those are the objects you don't have control.
  • Unstructured environments — it's like your home. And my house — those is I would say the grand challenge.

Especially my house, trust me. Three dogs, five-year-old.

Yes, dogs. Exactly.

If you're thinking about where does the robustness coming from — robustness coming from a sufficient coverage of the scenarios that robots might encounter. So it's so much easier and more approachable, at least right now, to focus more on the semi-structured environments before we move on to fully unstructured environments. So we will move into that direction. It's just we want to take a more sustainable and more realistic approach towards it.

进化视角：人形是妥协，不是最优

I think your point here is that humanoids mimics human body, and evolution has optimized human body for unstructured environment. And so our fingers, our legs are not the best apparatus to do one thing.

For example, if if our only goal as a species is to climb trees, we will not have this body necessarily, right? So we will have different kinds of fingers. But what humans end up having evolved into is this body shape that can be very general but not necessarily best at everything. And that is for the survival of unstructured environment.

But from a business point of view, from a pragmatic technology point of view, this unstructured environment and a generalized body is actually the hardest problem to solve. It's not necessarily even the right way to solve the problem. We specialize. So we take more specialized body to solve a narrower problem.

But the challenge for Scenix is to be more body-agnostic, so that their infrastructure can serve different bodies and different semi-structured environments.

十五、经济视角：机器人何时能达到人类效率？

You know, a common lens to look at exactly this question is an economic lens, right? You compare it to like generative LLMs where they can create prose or code 10,000 times faster than a human being, a bunch cheaper than a human being. So the economic case makes sense, because our brains aren't very efficient at that. However, our brains and our bodies are very efficient at 3D navigation, right? Like moving through the world or picking things up. And so this is just a prediction question: do you believe we'll ever be able to build robots, at least in the foreseeable future, that have the power efficiency of a human being when it comes to menial tasks? Let's say just basically minimum wage or something like that. How far away are we from this? Is this like 5 years, or this is like never?

I think it's going to take a very long time. So if you really think about robots in the real environment, in the end it will always be a system. So every working robot in the real environment is a system work. You need to be very mindful and thoughtful about how the system are coming together — the hardware, the software, the brain, even to the details of, for example, what's the friction coefficients of your fingers.

So there's a lot of things you have to consider to make these things a reality, and it will take iterations. But what I am excited about is that I have always been at the state of the arts of robot learning, and also trying to push the state of the art forward.

But the state-of-the-arts always moving faster than I expected. So what I'm focusing on and trying to investigate right now is very different from what I when I started my PhD. So this is a speak to how fast the whole ecosystem has been evolving, and all the moving pieces started coming together, or building this robotic systems.

But we also have to be calibrated about our predictions. So we will see a lot of progress, but to achieve, for example, human-level efficiency and capabilities, it will take longer.

Martin, the hardest thing in today's AI is to have the right measured optimism, right?

That's right. It's totally true.

I mean, even LLM does not have human brain efficiency. Human brain operates on 30 watts. So we are far from that.

But performance-to-power, it may be close, right? In narrow tasks like software —

Like generating an image or software engineering — than it is, right. Yeah, I think so. I don't think we're anywhere close when it comes to robotics.

十六、战略野心与整合节奏

Does this change how you think strategically about the level of ambition that your team can go after? Is it changed that, or is it still very much in line with what you expected to do when you started?

It definitely changed the trajectories in a very profound manners. We see a lot of unlock in be able to do this whole process — do the modeling of the environments — much more efficient and much more scalable manners, especially in partner together with World Labs.

And I also want to add to Fei-Fei — if you think about, for example, the current states of the language models — those are models with incredible capabilities. But still, you don't just blind trust it to book your flight tickets or make your hotel reservations. You still, hopefully, there's still a person who reading the output from those language models.

But that is very different from how people will be using robotic models. Because for robotic models, out of the box, the robots has to work reliably in the real environment.

And we don't even have the data, we don't even have all the necessary infrastructures around those for the robots to just out of box work reliable in the real environments.

So for that reasons, be able to create this digital worlds — this scalable digital worlds where the robot can learn in and evaluates within that — is going to unlock so much more potentials for be able to replace all the costly and unsafe data in the real environments with the data generated from the worlds, for the robots to be able to do scalable learning and evaluations.

整合节奏：不急于合并

You know, I've seen many of these kinds of integrations. They actually work very well at this stage when they have this much alignment, which is great. But there's always like this question of: do you integrate now into what's happening now, or do you keep things quite separate and provide kind of like a long-term trajectory that will be realized in the year time frame. How are you thinking about this, Fei-Fei? Is this something that integrates right away, or is this kind of a separate longer term?

This is a great question. I think at this point, you know, Changyi, Sunny, Justin, Ben, and Yunzhu have been talking about this — at this point, we are going to take it thoughtfully. We're not rushing to integrate everything from codebase to teams, because I think Scenix does have a very well-thought and — I wouldn't call it standalone completely — but fairly contained tech stack, as well as their customers, as well as the kind of products they're building.

We're going to take time. We definitely will — we already, on the simulation side, as well as the potential base model, action-conditioned model side — we already are starting to talk. And also they are using Marble as an internal customer. So we will be integrating. But we're not rushing to blend the team as like a full salad bowl.

地理布局：从西海岸到双岸

How are you thinking about geographies with this Scenix move? Is it going to stay in the same place?

We're going to — Yunzhu is going to move.

Oh well, welcome here.

Moving to San Francisco. Yeah, Florence and the Renaissance. Perfect.

I think World Labs is officially becoming a bicoastal company where the headquarter is in San Francisco. I've — you know, I live in Palo Alto, I feel like I'm in a different state — we but I'm actually excited that we're going to have an office in New York that can help us to attract talent on East Coast.

And also we have been talking about making sure that in both offices we set up the robots, so that we get to basically test out and mature our engineering stack, so that we can work with robots remotely — because we have to do that for our customers anyway.

十七、两年后的成功图景

So maybe just to be very concrete, Fei-Fei — maybe let's just pencil out what is the perfect success case in two years? Like what product do you have? Who's engaging with it? How do they use it? Just the crisp: what?

We're very happy that Scenix team and World Labs team will have validated customers in a small number of important vertical use cases, where our system, our infrastructure has proven to be truly beneficial to their automation needs. And these customers became our lighthouse examples to scale our business.

十八、什么时候联系 World Labs？

And how — let's say someone listening to this is running a robotics company — at what stage do they engage with World Labs? Is it really early on? Is it somewhere in the middle?

So right now, for our customers, because we are building this kind of real-to-sim-to-real pipelines — where the simulation is essentially the worlds we're going to provide the training, evaluation grounds — some customers they needs only the real-to-sim part. They want to digitalize the task they care about and be able to do the evaluations of their robotic systems.

Some customers they need this real-to-sim-to-real this entire pipeline, such that they will be able to have policies running on their hardwares. So our platform is also designed in a way that is flexible depending on what our clients needs.

And at the same times, the clients we are working with are actually pretty close to the deployment stage. So basically they are working on very very practical tasks. Those tasks — when replaced, when we have a robotic solutions that are there — can just create value immediately. And they have at least like tons or hundreds of this kind of situations they are thinking about to do the automations for.

So together with World Labs, we'll be able to develop reliable solutions for those scenarios. As we have already showed, we have a number of scenarios already instantiated in our blog post. And we'll be able to further our investigation to see how they can actually solve the key requirements and also constraints faced by the real-world deployments.

Great. I want to be very specific about this. Is it ever too late or too early to call World Labs if you're a robotics company?

No. We want everybody to call us. We want to learn about your use case.

Wonderful. If you're listening to this and you're anywhere close to a robotics project or robotics company, please track World Labs.

Yes. Thank you.

Definitely open for business.

We are open for business.

All right. Not too early. All right. If you're doing robotics, call World Labs. Thank you both very much for coming.

Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：机器人公司其实是"反事实推理"公司
表面上，World Labs 收购 Scenix 讲的是"用仿真训练机器人"的故事。但 Fei-Fei 在对话中悄悄埋下了一个哲学炸弹——她把仿真等同于**counterfactual reasoning（反事实推理）**，并类比人类大脑与足球世界杯赛前的战术推演。
这意味着 World Labs 真正在做的不是"3D 引擎的升级版"，而是**给机器装上"想象力器官"**。真实数据只能告诉机器"发生过什么"，而仿真让机器学习"本可以发生什么"、"如果换一种方式又会怎样"。这一步跨越比它看上去大得多：它把机器人学从**归纳学习**推向了**因果学习**——而这恰恰是 LLM 至今没解决的元问题。
一个惊人的推论：**World Labs 的世界模型，可能最终会反哺 LLM 的推理能力**，而不是相反。语言模型正在渴求的"心智模拟器"，很可能诞生于机器人领域，而非文本领域。
## 二、跨领域连接：Waymo、好莱坞 VFX、进化生物学 的三角映射
对话中散落着三个看似无关的锚点，其实构成了一个隐藏的三角结构：
- *

item.title: [Business of Sport] Frank Smith on Paying Fighters, Conor Benn, & What People Don’t Understand About Boxing Promoters
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三段洞察：拳击推广业的隐藏系统

一、"冷静"才是真正的护城河——一个反直觉的商业发现

Frank 在整场对话中反复使用一个词——"stay calm"。表面上这像是性格特质，但仔细听你会发现：他把"冷静"当作一种可交易的稀缺资源在描述。

这是一个让人意外的观察：在一个由情绪驱动的行业里，反情绪本身就是最大的商业模式。PBC 烧掉 5-6 亿美金、Triller 烧掉 1.5 亿、Boxxer 烧掉 5000 万——这些钱不是被拳手拿走的，是被"兴奋"消耗的。Matchroom 44 年不倒的秘密，本质上是把 Eddie 的"passion"和 Frank 的"spreadsheet"做成一个内部对冲机制——这跟桥水基金 Ray Dalio 的"believability-weighted decision making"是同一套架构。

跨领域连接：这跟精算师主导的保险业惊人相似。Barry Hearn 是特许会计师出身——这不是巧合。拳击业实质上是一个长尾风险管理业务（每周风险 50-100 万，出场费占收入 60-70%，利润率仅 15%），谁能像保险公司一样精算，谁就活得下去。你以为的娱乐业，其实是伪装成秀场的精算业。

二、Conor Benn 事件揭示的"关系资产折旧曲线"

Frank 讲 Conor Benn 那段最耐人寻味的不是他说的话，而是他没说的结构。他反复强调"如果他坐下来跟我们说……"——这暴露了一个所有家族企业都不敢承认的秘密：

基于道德和情谊建立的信任，从来不是资产，而是一种未定价的负债。

Matchroom 用超越合同义务的付出（personal trips、公开支持等）"投资"了 Conor 这段关系，期待的回报是未来的忠诚溢价。但情感投资无法在资产负债表上体现，也无法在合同里对冲——所以当 Zuffa 用 1500 万现金把这层情感一次性兑现时，Matchroom 才发现自己一直在补贴一个不存在的市场。

出人意料的观察：Frank 说"we'll still maintain our values"——但他真正在做的是把关系资本证券化：从今以后，剩两场合同时就要重新谈判续约。这意味着 Matchroom 正在悄悄从"家族企业"进化成"制度化企业"，而 Conor Benn 就是这个转型的定价事件。每个家族企业都会经历一次"Conor Benn 时刻"——那是它必须在灵魂和结构之间做选择的一刻。

三、Zuffa 模式的深层错位：他们买错了行业

所有人都在讨论 Zuffa（TKO 集团）会不会颠覆拳击。Frank 给出了一个几乎所有分析师都错过的判断：Zuffa 不是威胁，是"时间套利者"——他们必须在 2 年内烧钱做增长，但作为上市公司，第 3 年就要面对股东质询"为什么用 20 亿利润的 UFC 业务，去追一个可能只赚/亏 1000 万的拳击业务？"

跨领域最惊人的连接：这个动力学跟 Uber 收购食物配送、Amazon 收购 Whole Foods、Meta 收购 Oculus 完全一样——大平台并购新兴垂直领域时，母公司的资本回报率标准本身就是这个并购的原罪。Matchroom 只需要活过这个"耐心稀释期"（大约 24-36 个月），Zuffa 的高价合约就会自然到期，而市场结构会回归。

真正的核心洞察：拳击 60-70% 的收入进拳手口袋，UFC 只有 17-19%。这不是运营效率差异，这是两个产业的产权结构根本不同——拳击是"艺人经济"（拳手是资产所有者），UFC 是"平台经济"（联盟是资产所有者）。Zuffa 想把拳击"UFC 化"，等于试图把 Spotify 变成 Netflix——不是不行，但需要重构上百年的产权惯例。这不是钱能解决的问题，这是制度经济学问题。

一个额外的彩蛋观察：Frank 说"我讨厌谈钱"、"我不喜欢炫耀"——这在一个以炫富为主流的行业里是极度反常的。而恰恰是这种"反显性信号"，让他成为拳手真正愿意长期合作的对象。在噪音行业里，沉默是最大的品牌——这跟 Berkshire Hathaway、Costco、In-N-Out 这些"沉默巨头"是同一个原理。

📝 转录文本

开场：老朋友回归

We traditionally offer less money than other promoters, but they believe in what we can create with them and where we can get them to. The perception of "you're not on my side." They want to pay me as little as possible. Yes, we want to make money, but we're also the ones investing the money to get you to that point. And we don't have to do that. You know, no one has to do that.

The Connor Benn situation is really unlike anything else we've ever dealt with because of what we did for him. I think there was a feeling that he would always be loyal to us. If Connor would have sat down with us and said, "Guys, I've been offered this crazy deal," you go "fair play." You could not say a thing against it.

Ultimately, Zuffa is a business that coming into boxing—a sport that they say has been terribly mismanaged and run—and they come in, what they're doing is overpaying fighters. So in the short term, they have to overpay fighters. But in the long term, if they want to create a business that is sustainable like they have in the UFC, like they have in WWE, they have to bring those purses down. Business. Fascinating.

寒暄与回顾

Frank, if you can believe it, you were one of our first ever Business of Sport shows.

Since then, we've gotten a lot bigger. You've gotten a lot bigger, too, dude. It looks like some protein gains are working.

Just a little bit. Yeah.

Yeah. I feel like I really sent you on this trajectory. I mean, don't get me wrong, you've had some bigger guests since I was on here—much bigger guests. But, you know, I feel like that starting point, I think they saw me on there, they went, "Actually, we should give that a go."

That's absolutely. We use you as the get for all future guests.

Did a lot of people say that?

Yeah. Yeah. It was the accent.

Yeah. I saw Eddie Hearn's fat assistant on there, so we should get him on.

Like, no hair either this time.

No. So much easier.

It looks good.

Yeah. When you—when I fly so much, I can go into any barbers and tell them what I want and they get it right. Whereas, you know, when I had the curly locks, it was a bit of a mess.

What do you say? They won't let you in that country.

What? Looking like this? Yeah. You know, no—I say I did it 'cause I look a bit tough until I open my mouth, and then people go, "Oh, he's soft."

That's why the glasses help.

Yeah. No, if I take them off—

See, now we're in trouble.

Yeah. So, if I put the glasses on, they know I'm soft.

It's all part of the, you know, reimagined image.

Yeah. No, the biggest thing from that show actually was Harry saying that Darts wasn't very big.

Yeah, you did actually. Do you remember that?

Yeah, I actually remember that. Yeah, you've just schooled him downstairs before we got playing Darts.

Yeah.

But also Darts has actually been all right for the last couple years.

Darts is huge and I just won 500 quid against him.

Yeah. So, you know, what a day.

Also, he hasn't been to an event.

Speaking of which—I haven't. You haven't invited me.

I know. There's not enough tickets to invite people.

Oh, they sell out quickly. Look at him.

关于飞镖与体验经济

I did get invited to that—I went to that, I loved—just before the darts was the pool. Yeah, when the box—uh—

Mosconi Cup.

Mosconi Cup. Yeah. Amazing atmosphere. How do the economics of a fight work? You choose the fighters, you choose the purse. And then it's all built around that.

Yeah. So, we have a couple of different models depending on how big a fighter gets. If a fighter gets huge—you know, like an AJ, those kind of level fights—essentially, you work on a profit. They get the bulk of the profit, you get a percentage, but they're then driven because their earnings are based on the revenue they generate.

On other shows, say you two are fighting, we have a rights fee, we have estimated ticket sales, we have sponsorship, and we say, "Right, we're going to pay U-X, we pay you," and you get those flat fees.

But in boxing traditionally, the boxers are getting 60-70% of the revenue. And you compare that to other sports or even combat sports like UFC, they're paying 19%, 17% of the revenue out to fighters. Tremendous business. I don't sit here slating it as a business, because as someone who likes that world, you go, "Well, fair play." But in boxing, it's just a completely different world. Like I say, 60-70% of revenues get paid out to fighters.

From the cost, don't you?

Yeah. You take risk every week. We do 40 shows a year. And then obviously if you make money on a show, you still got to pay the overheads of the bit.

Like it's not a cash-flow management issue there because the cash flow is very real. That volume of money moving is significant.

Yeah. I mean, and we're lucky because we're such a huge group that's been going for 44 years. And Barry's always found it important—as has shown—like he's a tremendous business person, and he's a chartered accountant by trade. So this is his world. I mean say this—I'm not really interested at all actually in the gossip side of it. So when you've got a relationship with someone that's built—I've known him since he was 18 years old, I've been on trips away with him—I don't get emotional about anything in business. It is what it is. But all he had to do was sit across that table and go, "Guys, look, you've done amazing. But basically, he didn't do that. And it allowed us to say, "Wait a minute." We got no problem with him taking that deal. We'd all be wrong. He was out of contract. We'd all be wrong to say he shouldn't do it. But after everything we've done for him, you'd expect a sit-down.

You didn't go to Taylor Swift's wedding, did you?

No, I got the invite. I couldn't make it. Yeah. Hell of a place to get married. Me and Travis Kelce were going to sign him, but you know.

What's the worst trip for you to go on from a travel perspective?

Australia is a long way away. I love Australia, but it's a long way away. And we go for like four days and it's like, "Oh my goodness."

What do you do in that? Do you adjust?

No. You can't, can you? Because—I don't adjust anyway. I just sleep when I'm tired.

Do you raw dog it?

Yeah.

What have you changed your mind on in the last 12 months?

Your perception of success is not everybody's. Your view of success—like, not everyone—just because someone chooses to do something else doesn't mean they're wrong. I don't know, I guess when we grow up, all success is always—well, for me when I was growing up, it was all about money, this, that, the other. It's like everyone's got different drivers and it doesn't mean they're wrong.

What part of the boxing business is most exciting at the moment?

The competition. Because it's fun having competition.

Which athlete do you not have in the management or talent agency business that you'd most like to have?

Uh, I'd like an F1 driver in the talent business.

Specific one.

I like Charles Leclerc. I think he's cool.

Yeah, he is cool. He's good looking as well.

Does help.

Yeah, does help.

What about—okay, if you could choose an athlete retired who wasn't optimized so we don't feel this conflict. Not optimized, so someone where you look at and you go, "Like me, you were unbelievable, but didn't quite make the most of that, that you could have actually add the value to?"

Thierry Henry. But he did—well, he was optimized at the time. He was optimized often, right?

Paolo Di Canio.

Ah, there you go. That's quality. You could have had him.

Paolo Di Canio or Freddie Ljungberg.

Freddie Ljungberg would have been a good one. He had the KP kind of, you know, mo. But Paolo—'cause he was a bad boy, weren't he?

You were a Spurs fan.

Yeah.

And when he scored that—when he scored that volley—how you feeling at the moment?

Is what it is.

Ah, shut up.

Did you go?

No, I don't go to my—like, I had a season ticket before I started working at Matchroom. And then just that overtook my life. So—

结语

Final one. What's the kindest thing anyone's ever done for you?

Um, kindest thing anyone's ever done for me? My missus is looking after my family. Like, as in being there for my family, making an effort with my family. That means a lot to me because I don't always have the time to do it.

Love that, mate. Thank you so much. Honestly, coming back in has been great, and wow, that has developed a lot over the last few years. So it's awesome to hear it, and well done for everything that you've done.

Appreciate it.

### 一、"冷静"才是真正的护城河——一个反直觉的商业发现
Frank 在整场对话中反复使用一个词——**"stay calm"**。表面上这像是性格特质，但仔细听你会发现：他把"冷静"当作一种可交易的稀缺资源在描述。
这是一个让人意外的观察：**在一个由情绪驱动的行业里，反情绪本身就是最大的商业模式**。PBC 烧掉 5-6 亿美金、Triller 烧掉 1.5 亿、Boxxer 烧掉 5000 万——这些钱不是被拳手拿走的，是被"兴奋"消耗的。Matchroom 44 年不倒的秘密，本质上是把 Eddie 的"passion"和 Frank 的"spreadsheet"做成一个**内部对冲机制**——这跟桥水基金 Ray Dalio 的"believability-weighted decision making"是同一套架构。
