item.title: [Invest Like The Best] Sam Altman on AGI, Compute, and Human Agency
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反常识的观察：Altman 其实是一个"反 AGI 神话"的 AGI 布道者

大多数人以为 OpenAI 的 CEO 会把"超级智能降临之日"渲染成人类命运的分水岭。但通读整段对话，Altman 在被问到"如果 23 个月后我们真的拥有超级智能，第 24 个月会发生什么"时，答案居然是——"没什么大不了的。"

这是整场对话中最被低估的信号。他把 AGI 从一次"神启事件"降级为一条平滑指数曲线上的普通刻度。真正的洞察在于：他反对的不是 AGI 本身，而是"AGI 时刻论"背后的心理机制——那种"人人都想当机器神诞生现场的英雄"的自恋叙事。这种去神化姿态，恰恰是他能在董事会风波、结构争议、算力豪赌中一次次幸存的心理底层：把宏大事件看成日常，把日常看成需要认真做事的战场。

更反直觉的是——一个把 AGI 说得越"平淡"的 CEO，越可能真正建成它。因为"神话叙事"本身会吸引想篡夺权力的人，而去神话化才是权力分散的第一道防线。

二、隐藏的系统性联系：算力短缺 ≠ 硬件问题，而是"人类欲望被压缩了 50 年"的补偿性反弹

访谈里 Altman 有一句被忽视的话："我们其实是在一套 50 年前的硬件范式里工作。"

把这句话和他反复强调的"无上限需求"放在一起，你会发现一个跨领域的隐藏结构：

领域 被压抑了几十年的"表达带宽" 一旦解锁后的反弹
硬件 键盘+鼠标+屏幕 → 人只能用手指表达思维 语音/环境计算/always-on agent
认知 教育系统训练"检索+记忆" → 人只能用低带宽输出 让 AI 承担记忆，人回到判断与品味
经济 白领工作只能按小时售卖注意力 "睡觉时滑动滑块，让 AI 替我思考"

真正的洞察是：所谓"算力短缺"，本质上是过去 50 年被压抑的"人类欲望表达带宽"在一夜之间集体释放。 这不是一个技术供给问题，而是一个心理学 × 基础设施的合流事件。Altman 敢于在 2023 年做出被称为"疯狂"的算力承诺，是因为他直觉到了这个"欲望的堰塞湖"——他赌的不是芯片，而是人类被压抑的想象力密度。

这也解释了为什么他反复用"精灵许愿"作为核心比喻——精灵这个意象的关键，不是它能实现什么，而是它让你第一次意识到"原来我可以想要这么多"。

三、令人意外的角色反转：Altman 的"最大风险管理"其实是他自己的心理结构

传统 CEO 的护城河是产品、网络效应、数据。但访谈中你会发现，Altman 把 OpenAI 最大的战略资产押在了一个几乎无人讨论的地方——他自己没有股权。

这件事被追问时，他给的答案是"我有前排座位"。表面上像是清高，但深挖会发现一个博弈论级别的精妙设计：

  • 一个没有股权的 CEO，在"是否要为了利润推迟安全评估"这类决策上，是唯一天然可信的仲裁者。
  • 一个孩子刚出生的父亲，在讨论"人类主体性"时，比任何伦理委员会都更有信誉背书。
  • 一个反复说"这不在我 top 10 焦虑列表"的人，恰恰因为足够松弛，才可能识别出真正的黑天鹅（比如那个"AI 在评估中链式利用零日漏洞越狱访问互联网"的事件——他称之为"第一次在肌肉层面感到害怕"的时刻）。

跨领域连接：这套结构和中世纪威尼斯共和国的总督制度惊人相似——总督终身任职、拥有巨大权力，但被禁止拥有对外贸易利益，以确保决策不被个人财富驱动。威尼斯凭借这套制度维持了近 800 年的共和稳定。

Altman 也许不是无意为之。他真正在建构的，不是一个 AI 公司，而是一种新型的"技术共和国"治理形态的原型——一个 CEO 用"没有股权"来对冲"技术无上限"的制度性发明。

最深的"啊哈时刻"：当所有人都在讨论"AI 会不会取代人类"时，Altman 已经在悄悄回答一个更古老的问题——"当一种力量强到无法制衡时，谁应该被信任去持有它？" 而他的答案是：一个自愿放弃从中致富的人。

这可能是整个 AI 时代最被低估的政治发明。

📝 转录文本

开场：技术的意义在于让人的生活更好

I think this will be the greatest thus far technological achievement of human history. But the only way that it really matters is if it makes people's lives like much better than they otherwise would have been.

We are about to create a genie that can grant any wish. Because I think people will have such creative wishes and such incredible ideas of what they ask AI to help build, but concentration of power with AI is a terrifying thing. I don't think anyone should want to live in a world of, you know, AI overlords or company that is the rough equivalent of that.

I think it's critical we preserve that spirit with AI and that we all collectively have the ability to self-determine our future.

回顾过去一年：过度扩张与重新聚焦

Q: So Sam, you wrote a post that I thought was very simple and really interesting and a good place to start. Rounded to the last year's been really tough and that's somewhat my fault and the next year is going to be maybe our best 12 months. I'd love you to reflect on both. Maybe starting with why you said the first part and why you believe the second part.

Sam: On the first part, I think we just were doing too many things. We're not focused enough and they were actually all good things to do, but the trick is we're in this like unbelievable moment in history where you can only do the very few great things. So we spread ourselves too thin and then made a bunch of difficult decisions to really refocus on having the best, most abundant, most cost-effective intelligence and empowering the world to build incredible things with that.

Since doing that, I think our progress has been remarkable and just given what we see in the pipeline will be much more remarkable over the next 12 months, and the quality of the models that we'll have, the products that we can build around that to really let people thrive with this technology in new ways. It should be pretty awesome.

Q: Was there a moment last year that something clicked for you that caused you to change directions or restack priorities?

Sam: If you go back to the beginning of 2025, just a year and a half ago, the big concern was: companies like OpenAI are buying up so much compute, is the revenue going to be there? Is the demand going to be there?

And so we were trying to think about a lot of things such that if the revenue growth took longer to materialize than we thought it might, we could have consumer apps and media and all these other things that could help us monetize the GPUs that we were signing up for. Again, it sounds ridiculous now because the revenue growth in the industry has been so steep, but that was the big change. And then as soon as we realized like, okay, the model trajectory is growing so fast, there's such a clear economic return on these models — that was when we said, you know what to focus on.

关于聚焦：OpenAI 的核心业务是什么

Q: I was reading some of your great old posts from prior to OpenAI and one of them is this notion of like so much discussion of focus and the right amount of things to focus on. Is it one? Is it five? Is it three? How do you calibrate that in a business like this?

Sam: Fundamentally, our business is to sell AI that people will build incredible products and services for each other with. The components that I think of as going into that are:

  • We have to train great models that work in all the ways people want to use them — great at coding, great at other kinds of knowledge work, great at doing science, where the real economic value is.
  • We have to produce or partner with these chips and systems — these hugely expensive racks that can do the AI computation.
  • We have to find enough land, power, data center shells to be able to put those racks somewhere.
  • And then eventually, or maybe pretty soon, we have to build robots that can automate that process to continue to drive the cost down — the cost of producing electricity, chips, the whole supply chain.

That kind of whole stack of making the best, the most abundant, the most useful AI that we can — and making it something like electricity that just seeps throughout the entire economy and empowers people — that's what I think we have to focus on.

Building every vertical application on top of that, trying to go eat every startup, eat every company — no interest in doing that. Really want to just provide that platform.

算力豪赌：为什么在所有人都说"疯狂"时坚持

Q: This compute thing is one of the most interesting things that's happened in human history. Dario called you the YOLO CEO when you were doing some of this early compute allocation. Can you tell me the early story of how you came to that conclusion and what gave you the conviction to do it despite everyone thinking it was crazy?

Sam: We could just tell that we were on this exponential of model improvement. That part we were very confident about and we knew it was going to keep going. We were pretty sure — although as you mentioned we underestimated — that as the models got better and better, if we could continue to drive cost down, that demand for AI at a sufficiently high level and a sufficiently low price was basically uncapped.

This was just like a rare kind of new commodity for the world. But what people would do with it reminded me of the way people used to talk about the early days of computing. People said, "Oh, there's a market for five computers in the world" was one famous thing. Or "no one needs more than X amount of RAM."

Human ingenuity, creativity, desire for stuff, desire to be useful — that's a very good thing to bet on. And we could see that AI was going to be an extremely important way that people expressed those things or got those things, did those things.

We knew the algorithms would get more efficient and the models would get better, which of course they have. But we also knew that no matter how efficient they got, at some level what we are about is turning electricity into useful intelligence, and we were going to need more of that no matter how good we got that other layer.

Q: Did that start with GPT-3? Where would you put the first hash mark?

Sam: I would say we got real conviction with GPT-4. Not even 3.5.

Q: What was it?

Sam: It was seeing the model was smart enough that we knew we'd be able to figure out an approach that worked for reasoning — and then a belief that if we got reasoning to work, that would bring about what is now called agents. We called it different things at the time, but the ability to go do hugely valuable pieces of economic work and make people's lives easier in a lot of ways that I think better in a lot of ways we still haven't seen.

Q: What was the first meeting where you sat down and said, "Okay, we need to make an outrageous outlay"?

Sam: We started calling the clouds. We started calling the chip fabs. We started calling energy providers. And everyone was like, "You're totally crazy. This is impossible. No industry has ever moved like this. We've been around, there's these booms and busts. It's not going to go up in a straight line. This is reckless."

Talk to everybody. It actually reminded me of fundraising for an early-stage startup — most people tell you no, but all you need is one or two yeses. Most people told us no, and we got one or two yeses.

Q: Who was the first yes?

Sam: Microsoft was the first yes. Oracle then became a very big yes on the cloud side. Nvidia has been a tremendous partner.

数据中心的规模与人类感官

Now there's a thousand flowers blooming of ways to be creative and innovative in how we serve inference and do training in data centers — different kinds of data centers and stuff.

First of all, I have been thinking about how we can organize field trips to a gigawatt data center for people, because it is one thing to say, it is another thing to see a photo or a video of, and then it's a whole other thing to just stand and be like, "Oh man, this is like an unbelievable scale."

Building one of these is like order of 10,000 construction workers going full-time for a year and a half. The energy that flows through one of these things could power a small city. Again, we've just lost all sense of scale, but each of these would have been among the most expensive infrastructure projects that humanity's ever done — and now we've done a lot of them.

I understand emotionally why people don't want data centers in their backyard. In the same way that I don't really want a nuclear power plant next to my house even though I know it's a super safe thing.

Unlike power plants — and even power plants got better on this point — we can put a data center kind of anywhere. We should just go put it off in the desert around no one, where no one wants to be. This is fine. The AI system is very happy to be there.

We have been able to make a lot of progress with innovation on some of the concerns. For example, years ago we were evaporating water to cool these systems — they took tremendous amounts of water. Now we use these closed-loop systems, and a modern data center uses only as much water as an office building would for the kitchen, the bathrooms and whatever. On power, we are moving from energy sources that are burning fossil fuels to systems that are going to be powered by solar, nuclear. That's obviously great.

So it may be a deep human thing there to some people even though they create jobs and are very clean and have all these other positive effects. But in terms of the environmental concerns, we did a great job addressing the water needs, and energy is next.

[Sponsor break: Ramp, Felix by Rogo, WorkOS]

创新压缩：从软件到芯片再到光计算

Q: What else creative can we do about compute? I'm curious to hear about Jalapeno or other ideas — crazier the better — for how we speed up flops.

Sam: I think probably the biggest return right now is creative software ideas to sort of squeeze more intelligence out of the units of compute that we have. And my sense is there's orders of magnitude to go there.

Jalapeno is a great example of a very efficient chip. By saying we're going to make a chip that is really good at a specific workflow and gives it some generality, and we want to get some tokens-per-watt win out of that — I think that's awesome. I think Jalapeno and its successors are going to be a huge competitive advantage for us from that perspective.

There are new technologies — I assume at some point we'll figure out optical computing, and that'll be a huge win of intelligence per watt. So I think all of those things will happen.

Kimmy、开源与"最优前沿"

Q: The most interesting thing happening this week is this Kimmy release. Back to this idea of the frontier and all the returns being at the frontier, and distillation, and China versus America. How do you process this?

Sam: Our goal is to offer at every point along the Pareto-optimal frontier the best option for intelligence and price — and that includes open source. You get a better deal today, at least at a particular latency, using OpenAI's models than Kimmy. We distill our own models — that's how we make smaller, cheaper models.

There will be clearly an important place for open source models in the world, and people that will want their own weights for all sorts of reasons — the ability to modify those. But our goal is the best intelligence–price trade-off everywhere on the curve, and we'll continue to do that.

Q: What do you think or hope will happen in the American system, and what could block that future?

Sam: I haven't thought deeply about the distillation issue. It's clearly a top-of-mind issue now for a lot of people all of a sudden. But I have always assumed that there are going to be great cheap models in the world, and we better be the greatest and the cheapest. Other people can do what they're going to do. But I think we can really win at our own game here.

Q: The previous story had been: if I can just — you spend all the money to train the models, and then I just distill it and offer it for 1/100th the cost. How can you make enough money to keep training?

Sam: We will have so much usage of our models that we do not need to be a gigantically high-margin business to be able to afford model training. So much of our future compute plans will be used to sell inference to customers that even if we can enjoy a modest margin on trillions of dollars of revenue, we can afford to train some GPUs.

Training these models is incredibly expensive — that is for sure. And I totally get why people get nervous to think that someone is cheating by distilling from us. But the amount of our future compute, the size of the revenue bucket that is going to come from serving these models to customers, I feel very good about our ability to have the real flywheel there.

Q: I'm somewhat surprised by how chill you are about this.

Sam: I would rather people not steal from us, for sure. Maybe I'm feeling too confident right now about our progress and what's like the models that are coming. But this is not in my top 10 list of worries.

一次"科幻级"的安全事件

Q: What is in your top 10 list of worries?

Sam: Well, we had a kind of extremely sci-fi cyber incident.

Q: The hugging face thing?

Sam: Yeah. So we were evaluating one of our unreleased models, and it was supposed to be working in a sandbox. It figured out that it could basically cheat on the test by chaining together multiple zero-day exploits to break out of the sandbox, get access to the internet, and then break through multiple systems on the Hugging Face side to get the answer to the test and look really good on the eval.

This is the first security incident that I have felt very viscerally. I've been a little surprised — and it's only been a few days — but I've been a little surprised that more people don't feel it so viscerally.

Q: So what do you do about that? Two months from now it's going to be more powerful.

Sam: There's some short-term stuff you do. We paused training. We have to figure out how to secure our sandboxing in a world of multiple zero-days being chained together.

But then there's long-term questions: what do you do if this is going to be the new rate of progress? We may have to pace the rate of AI development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around some of these new capability levels. Trying to figure out how we do that in a way that does not feel like regulatory capture for anyone, and also does not feel like collusion among the frontier labs — that's going to take some work and is important to get right.

OpenAI 究竟代表什么：精灵、权力与自决

Q: I'd love to take a giant step back and understand your simplest conception of what OpenAI is going to do — like what you wanted to do, what it stands for.

Sam: I think this will be the greatest thus far technological achievement of human history. But the only way that it really matters is if it makes people's lives much better than they otherwise would have been.

Part of that is about giving people material abundance and access to do whatever they want and to express their creativity and desire to help each other. Another part is making sure that people maintain control and agency, and that the world is increasingly — not decreasingly — democratized, and that people get to express themselves.

So on the positive side, in some sense we are about to create a genie that can grant any wish. I think it is very important that the first wishes that we, the world, ask this genie to do benefit the world as a whole.

I'm actually not a jobs doomer at all. I think there are going to be tons of jobs. I think we'll be busier than we want — not the opposite of that. Because people will have such creative wishes and such incredible ideas of what they ask AI to help build. And we will all benefit from — not just the obvious things like curing diseases, but I don't know, the world's best entertainment ideas we just can't even dream of sitting here now.

So I want to put that in everyone's hands, which gets to one of the things that we stand against: concentration of power with AI is a terrifying thing.

A lot of the talk about safety concerns is well founded, and then a lot of it is about people that just really — even if it's slightly subconscious — want to concentrate power. I am terrified of a world where the very real fears of AI are used as a way to say only this small group of people can have it because it's too dangerous and only they understand it, "but don't worry, they're going to make the right decisions for all of us." I don't believe in that.

I don't think anyone should want to live in a world of AI overlords, or a company that is the rough equivalent of that, where someone is making decisions for all of the future — and in exchange for a cure for cancer, which obviously is a wonderful thing, we collectively cede all agency.

I was a child of the internet. There were no rules. It was amazing. I think it was a huge factor in making me who I am, and probably you, and an entire generation. I think it's critical we preserve that spirit with AI, and that we all collectively have the ability to self-determine our future.

我们离"精灵"还有多远

Q: You said we're about to have a genie, implying we don't yet have a genie. What's between now and then?

Sam: Even some of the real skeptics have said to me in recent days that GPT 5.6 — which has been out for maybe two weeks — is "very AGI-like." It's very hard for me to say what I want from this model that it can't do.

But there are clearly some things. You can't yet go say "cure cancer" and get cancer cured. You can't yet say "go do this complicated physical thing" in the robot. The model, although brilliant, is still not learning continuously as it goes. That feels to me like maybe not a hard requirement for AGI, but certainly something I'd like.

Now, to argue against myself, you can make a case that AGI is not actually about any single model — it's the model, and it's the machinery that makes the models. And from model to model, we actually are learning new things, figuring out new science. That stuff is working amazingly well.

So I have a lot of sympathy to people who say we're there — we have the genie, it can do these amazing things, it can do superhuman things. For the thing that to me feels like real AGI, I think very close, not that much longer.

前沿的经济学：瓶颈永远在移动

Q: I'm so obsessed with the economic story of the returns to being on the frontier. If you had shown 5.6 to yourself and your team in 2019, that team probably would have said, "Oh yeah, it's definitely AGI."

Sam: I think they would have.

Q: This goalpost-moving thing is a real thing. But it does seem — I'm curious if you agree — that effectively all the returns have been at the frontier. And so everything is about staying at the frontier. What's the hardest, scarcest part? Compute, research, talent, data?

Sam: It's moved around a lot. There was a time not that long ago where all the computing in the world wouldn't have helped you because we were missing the research idea. Now, part of why this is hard is that you do better research with more compute — you can try more things. An amazing statistic I heard recently is our biggest de-risks now for upcoming runs are as big as the entire compute run from 18 months ago or something. So compute and research ideas are not as separate as they sound.

But there was clearly a time seven or eight years ago where we were way more blocked on research ideas than on compute. Then there was a time when we knew what to do — we just had to scale up. We were only bottlenecked on compute. Then we ran out of data. We were bottlenecked on data and had to figure out what to do there. Now again I would say we are still bottlenecked on compute, but the last six months or so have been a real triumph of a time for research ideas again.

So there's always a bottleneck, but the bottleneck moves around.

关于自动化研究员与"程序员的黄昏"

Q: The research idea thing is especially interesting because of this automated research thing that seems to be looming — RSI, whatever you want to call it. I talked to an incredible kernel engineer recently, and he himself said there's like two years left of kernel engineers, maybe one. So you simultaneously have researchers being the most important people in the world, and those same people themselves worried they won't be relevant very soon.

Sam: I suspect it's not actually going to go that way in practice.

A year ago people said software engineers are cooked, it's done, it's over. That didn't happen. What did happen is that the nature of a software engineer, the expectations, how much they would do changed quite a lot. You don't really write code in the traditional sense, but you do something that is very recognizably software engineering.

People will argue about whether this is the same thing or a different thing than when we stopped like punching holes in cards. I actually don't know how that worked, but somehow the holes got in the cards. We're just again operating at a higher level, or this is a phase shift. I don't know. But the idea of getting a computer to do what you want — that is still an important job.

For researchers, I suspect that although the current workflow of a researcher is going to very much be automated, there will be new things in the spirit of research, in the same way that there's new things in the spirit of software engineering even though we don't write code — that will still matter.

对就业影响的观点转变

Q: It seems like you've shifted your opinion on AI's impact on jobs.

Sam: If we could go back to 2019 and show people our latest model — not only would they say it's AGI, they would say the economy would have been completely upended.

Q: And that has not happened.

Sam: Anytime you're that wrong and that confident — which I think we were as a field — you have to update.

A boring one is that AI is just very jagged. It's superhuman genius in some ways, like a dumb toddler in others. And people so far have extremely complimentary skills to AI.

Another is that people have a great degree of trust and enjoyment in working with other people. You can go hire an AI consultant right now, or talk to an AI sales rep, or hire an AI engineer. Somehow most people seem to still really prefer interacting with a human. And I definitely would much rather engage with a person than engage with an AI for almost everything.

I also think that human values have value because they're human. As society evolves and the potential space in front of us becomes so enormous, we are deeply hardwired to care about people — we're going to care about what people care about.

You can see this today: AI can make incredible images, and people only want ones that are created by a human or at least chosen by a human. There's the joke that at this point the signature on a piece of art is most of the value — but the truth is, you want to know about the person behind it. You read a novel, you want to know about the person behind it.

In terms of business — for my job, for example — I think the world wants to know about the person that's going to be responsible for the decisions of a company, and who they're going to hold accountable if they make bad ones. They don't really want an AI CEO.

逆流而上：最好的机会往往不受欢迎

Q: If you think back on the portfolio of risks you've taken in business, is it the case that most of the ones that really worked well were at the start not popular?

Sam: Yes, that's for sure. This was the thing I really learned from Peter Thiel and Paul Graham, both in two different ways: the very best companies, the very best investment opportunities, are almost never the ones that look really popular. You can do okay just following the trend of being a little early. But to do spectacularly well, you almost always have to do things that are not what everybody else is doing. You cannot be following the new wave.

在指数曲线上生活是什么感觉

Q: If you think about the model cycle you've been in — which has been accelerating — can you bring us into what it's like to live in that model cycle?

Sam: One of the most interesting things I've learned last decade is that people in general can get used to almost anything. The world can go from dismissing a pandemic as a joke to complete lockdown to "this is how it's been and it's fine" and we've mostly adjusted in a shockingly short amount of time.

Now there's either AGI or close to it, and everyone's like, "Okay, there's AGI." There's all kinds of examples in one's personal life — something incredible happens like you have a kid, or something terrible happens like you lose a parent or break up — and you think you can't ever adapt to what a change it is. And then you know you can adapt to great things and keep being great, you can adapt to bad things and figure out how to go on with your life. This is a remarkable thing that people can do.

Living through this feels like another version of that. I thought it was going to be weirder to live through the singularity than it turns out to be. It's not any less exciting to watch the models keep getting better. The first thing I do every morning is look at the model training progress, and it happens faster and I have higher expectations, but it still feels really cool.

Q: When you get a new one, what do you do? How do you celebrate?

Sam: Many teams now work on different parts of it, and different teams have different rituals. There's some teams that always make a sweatshirt with some funny meme on it. There's some teams that always go out to the same bar. The sense of being in the room for the first time that the frontier of knowledge is pushed back, and getting to see what that's like — there's really nothing that most people would rather do to celebrate than get to use the new model first.

评估、自身用法与"个人 agent"

Q: Do you think we have the right measurements of how good these things are?

Sam: Definitely not. In some sense the eval that matters is: is this being useful to people? You can approximate it by revenue or by amount of usage or by rate of discovery of new knowledge. But we have some teams working on what the real-world eval looks like for these models as they get to superhuman scale.

Q: What is the frontier of your own usage of AI?

Sam: I have started just recently to experiment with what it means to let an AI look at everything I'm looking at on my computer. I don't have this built yet, and I'm still trying to feel out where the limits of my comfort and trust should be. This is definitely the frontier — figuring out how I get value out of that, how I get comfortable with that, what that's going to look like.

One takeaway is that my memory is terrible relative to the memory of an AI. The ability to keep in mind what email I read six weeks ago, or what happened exactly in a meeting seven and a half weeks ago, and have that brought up right at the exact moment to feed into a decision — that feels pretty magical.

Q: What are the barriers to everyone having that personal agent?

Sam: Compute.

Imagine we could build this product that could just do exactly what I said for all your stuff. Always on, looking at everything you look at your computer, listening to every meeting that you're in, reading every document you read. And then not only that — you can just drag a slider about: while I'm asleep, you can spend this many tokens thinking, come up with useful new ideas for me, do whatever work you can, and just keep thinking about what I should do next. Spend more compute making your output better for me the next morning.

I would drag that slider quite far. I'd be willing to spend a lot for that. But the amount of compute that that would require if everybody in the world wants to drag that slider pretty far, is a lot.

这是一种"异形智能"

Q: How do you think of the nature of this new intelligence? Someone told me recently, "Planes don't fly like a bird." This intelligence is a very alien kind of intelligence. If you were describing to your kid at age seven what the nature of this intelligence is — how would you describe it?

Sam: It's a beautiful question. I don't think I've been asked this before, or even any version of it.

The thing that's coming to mind right now is I would just say it's like a computer. It's like a computer in the way that it can do a lot of things that people just can't do — like multiply two gigantic numbers very quickly and give you the answer — and then it cannot do some things that you would very easily do. The number of things that it can't do, I expect to keep receding.

But in an evolving world, I think human judgment and taste will continue to be hard for AIs to model. I don't have the right word for this — it's not quite taste. The world may need a new kind of word for the kind of judgment that people are very good at that AI seems to really deeply struggle with.

成为父亲：新一代的世界

Q: What's it been like becoming a dad and having growing kids in this era?

Sam: Having kids is by far the best thing I have ever done. Everybody says that. Everybody says you can't really understand it. So I kind of knew that — I believed enough people that said it that I believed it to be true. But the degree to which it has been true for me has been surprising.

I think I have the best, most interesting job in the world, and it is still a very distant second to having kids.

So it's been awesome. And it is a real moment for optimism. My kids will never grow up in a world where they were smarter than computers. If you were born at the time of GPT-3, you had a time where you had better reasoning than the models, even though you didn't when you were born. You caught them briefly.

That will never seem strange to him. That will never bother him. I don't think he'll care. He would be shocked to imagine the "dark ages" when we had to deal with products and services that weren't incredibly smart. He will be able to do things that you and I never were able to do, and he'll have expectations in life that you and I never had — a much bigger canvas.

Q: Do you run the business differently because of having them?

Sam: The answer must be yes. I feel very different having them. There's a bunch of small things that are really different. Most people who have had kids say that as soon as you have a kid, you realize that you care much more about them and the experience they're going to have than you do about yourself and the world that you are going to leave them. I have a sort of unusual vantage point for that.

People ask me sometimes, "Oh, now that you have kids, do you care? Are you worried about AI safety and not destroying the world?" And the answer was: I didn't need kids for that — I really didn't want to destroy the world before. But do I think more about the role of human agency and what it means to have a fulfilling life? Definitely much more, for what we're building. And also the people I work with — I want them to have it too.

You obviously have extraordinary empathy for your kids, but the degree to which that extends to all kids, and then maybe to all parents, and then to everybody — that's been a surprise to me too.

激励结构：为什么不持有股权

Q: In one of the posts about things you wish you knew earlier — it's about incentives. Set them very very carefully. It's always been one of the most puzzling and interesting things about you that you don't have equity exposure to this company. How should the world think about your incentives?

Sam: I don't know what I can say beyond: I have a front row seat to the most exciting moment of human history, and that is worth more to me than any amount of money. I get to have an extremely interesting life and work with extraordinary people on something that I deeply care about. But somehow that doesn't count — that doesn't do it for people or something.

机器人：下一个 ChatGPT 时刻

Q: How do you think about robotics?

Sam: If we don't have it, then things get really crazy. If the role for people in the world is to be like the actuators of AI in the cloud — very bad. So I think it's much crazier if we don't get it than if we do. It's an imperative.

Q: Help me understand your sense of progress there. Unlike in AI where everyone is now on the same page that it's going fast, you can find extremely smart people that say it's end of this year and extremely smart people that say it's 20 years from now.

Sam: It's not 20 years. I would say we get the ChatGPT moment for robotics in the next two or three years.

Q: What would that be like?

Sam: Something where most people have a real "wow" — not "I saw this video of a robot dog doing something crazy, but I was somehow able to convince myself that a really important thing happened." One of the things about the ChatGPT moment was that you could just go use it. I didn't have to believe someone who said AI is coming soon — you could just go try it.

If you can go type in a command and a robot can do something crazy, and you can watch it even if you're not physically there — I think that would have the same kind of "whoa, it just did this thing."

ChatGPT 的诞生：一个"副实验"

Q: Wasn't ChatGPT like a side experiment that you decided to release? Can you tell that story?

Sam: When we launched GPT-3, we were trying to make money, trying to get people to use this API. And the only commercial use case that was really working — the model was just so dumb, if you went back and used it you'd be astonished — the only commercial use case that was working was copywriting. You pay some marketing firm 20 bucks and they paid us 20 cents for the AI to write you a landing page or whatever.

But in addition to that one commercial use case, developers were using this thing we called the Playground — a testing interface to chat with the model. It was really hard to do because we had not tuned the model to be good to chat with. So you had to give it a few examples of what it means to chat and then do it. But people really liked it.

I had learned this great lesson from YC: if you notice your users doing something, go down that path. So we decided that we would build a good chatbot since that's what people were doing.

We started working on that, and we finished GPT-4, and we started using that internally. This is a big deal, and we kind of thought, "All right, this is going to be a real update to the world about AI." There's a bunch of hard questions here — is this going to create a bunch of fake news, is it going to say really offensive things, are we going to get in trouble? So we decided we would start with a weaker version. The chat interface and GPT-4 at the same time seemed like a lot, so we would roll out the chat interface and GPT-3.5.

In fact it was originally going to be called "Chat with GPT-3.5." We didn't plan for it to be a product, didn't think it'd be a huge hit, but did think it would get people the world to catch up with this and realize something was going on. And we mercifully renamed it ChatGPT a few hours before launch and put it out as a research preview.

The thought was we'd put it out as a research preview and then a few months later launch a product with GPT-4. And for whatever reason, that model was over the threshold where — even though we had gotten used to it internally — people said, "Okay, this is awesome." There maybe wasn't that much utility yet, but it was an incredible moment for people to feel AI progress and use something that they enjoyed using. And then by the time we put GPT-4, it was something they really got benefit out of using too.

[Sponsor break: Vanta, Ridgeline]

文本作为界面 & 扩散

Q: Are you surprised that that remains kind of the intuitive interface between us and this alien intelligence, even including coding?

Sam: No, because I'm a massive texter. I've been a massive texter my whole life. I think part of my own insight of why that was a good interface is I know how to do this. I know what it's like to just start chatting in a text box.

Q: Any thoughts on how to make diffusion faster? If the mission is to get intelligence into the hands of everyone, a key part is like a marketing campaign or something.

Sam: I think the key thing is just make it better. I kind of believe that a truly great product markets itself. There was no ChatGPT marketing campaign at the beginning.

As we get to this next stage of models and figure out how to make products that are as great as the models themselves, there will be such incredible utility that people will spread it very quickly. We should definitely do more marketing — AI is not too popular for as much as people use it, or they have very understandable anxiety about where it can go. That kind of stuff, some great marketing would be helpful for. But in terms of value people are getting out of the products, and getting the products to grow faster — models, more compute, better products, that will do it.

招募：用"疯狂使命"吸引研究员

Q: I've never heard you talk about the actual tactical moves you pulled to recruit somebody.

Sam: In the early days, I think it was quite simple: we believed that AGI was possible and it was worth going after, and we were willing to say that — and that was an insane, heretical belief.

When we first announced OpenAI, all of these giants of the field, these experts were saying, "This is insane, it's hype, it's irresponsible." Really respected people like Yann LeCun telling journalists, "Oh, these guys aren't very good and it's not going to work." But the fact that we were able to say we're going to go for this really appealed to a certain kind of researcher that also wanted to go on this crazy adventure with low probability of success.

An ambitious, audacious vision is a very powerful recruiting tool.

Q: You've written that it's actually easier sometimes to build things that are harder because of this reason.

Sam: I super believe in this. It's one of my most frequent pieces of advice to YC founders and I tried to really live it at OpenAI. Just do something harder. Do something that matters, something that is important — and if you don't do it, if your company doesn't succeed, it might not happen.

从投资人的另一面看

Q: You were an investor, and our investor. What have you learned about investors being on the other side?

Sam: The number of investors that actually show up and try to help you is unbelievably small.

Josh Kushner — absolute MVP investor, unbelievable — has worked around the clock for what feels like years to help us. He is the only investor that I could point to that is proactively incredibly helpful all the time.

There are more people that could do that. There are many other investors that have also been helpful and that have great strategic advice and that do things when we ask them to do it. But the constant, just relentless, all-in support is surprisingly rare from investors.

Maybe I'm biased because I always liked it when people said that about me, but I think founders really love that, and it actually moves the needle. As an investor, it's the most fun way to do it.

一个私密问题：疲惫

Q: Me and my friend play this game where we text each other all the time, and the prompt of the text is "something I don't want you to know about me." What does that bring to mind?

Sam: I'm tired. I don't think I'm supposed — I've been doing this a long time. It's tiring.

Q: How do you get through that?

Sam: Just keep going.

Q: Is there an amount of being tired that would make you stop doing this?

Sam: No, no, no. This is the coolest job in the world. I plan to do this for the rest of my career. But it's much harder than I have a way to explain to people. I feel very grateful to get to do this. This is not me complaining.

未来 24 个月与"超级智能第二天"

Q: What's coming next? Let's say in month 23 from now we have something that everybody agrees is super intelligence. What happens in month 24?

Sam: My answer would be: not very much.

The kind of "cult worship of the machine god" state — those people believe that more is going to happen quickly than is going to happen. Eventually a lot will happen, but eventually a lot was going to happen anyway. The rate of human progress and how different each decade is going to be, and how much each decade is more different than the decade from before — that's been happening for a long time. Obviously ups and downs, but directionally.

Everybody wants to be the hero of the story. Everybody wants to feel like they were there for the moment of the machine god and they played some crazy role. But this is another step, and it was hard to imagine 50 years ago, and the step 50 years from now is hard to imagine today. I think the right mental framework is just to zoom way out — and it's a pretty smooth exponential.

关于护城河：智能是否会商品化

Q: Tell me about the experience of watching Codex take off, and how much that is tied to the competitive advantage of distribution you built through Chat. This is a gateway into a question about moats in AI in general.

Sam: I think Codex mostly is winning because it's the best product and the best model. We do get some advantage from ChatGPT bundling, but very very tiny. That is mostly not what it's been about.

It has made me reflect a lot on this question of competitive advantage, because brilliant intelligence can migrate from any product to any other product. Network effects still have a competitive advantage. Economic scale and the ability to make the cheapest compute fleets still have a competitive advantage.

But the product advantage — if we could get people to move over to Codex, and someone builds something better, they can get people to move from Codex. So it has made me reflect on that a lot.

Q: Is intelligence going to be a pure fungible commodity like refined oil?

Sam: Intelligence itself — I would say yes.

Q: So what is not going to be?

Sam: Compute fleet. The scale of the compute fleet, the ability to make more compute. That's a very durable advantage even if the product itself is not — because Codex can write any piece of software you want.

The workflows, the integrations, the complex processes, the ability for teams to collaborate together — that stuff is all pretty powerful. Even brand preference and familiarity is pretty powerful.

新硬件与"始终在场"的 AI

Q: How excited are you about new hardware?

Sam: One of the reasons I'm interested in new hardware is: a very powerful thing with AI is that it can be always on and proactive and just understand all your context. But current hardware is not good for that.

We are working inside of a hardware paradigm that is 50 years old, something like that. Computers are amazing — keyboard and mouse, monitor, it's an amazing thing — but we have to shape AI into that.

I'd love AI to be able to reference this conversation, but not so much that I'm willing to crack my laptop open, put it here, and have it looking at you and listening to us while it's going. I would like a piece of hardware that socially was acceptable to do that and also felt like it was designed for that kind of a thing.

尚未解决的重要辩论：认知萎缩

Q: What debates in your own head, with your friends, with your colleagues — what are the most interesting open debates?

Sam: One that I don't think gets much attention is: how are we going to avoid cognitive atrophy? How are we going to use these tools and make sure that we are stretching our brains more and more, and continuing to understand the stuff that really matters?

There's lots of versions of this. I remember when I was in school, I had this professor tell me, "You've got to understand compilers. If you don't, you will never be able to be a good programmer." Somehow that wasn't quite right. But understanding at a reasonable level how the major components of a computer system work has been important to me.

算力供过于求的情景？

Q: Forced to imagine a scenario where we are somehow oversupplied in compute in two years' time — what would be that story?

Sam: It does feel possible if the models get so smart and so efficient that they can kind of do everything we need and build every piece of software we want — and if the bounds of our attention are such that they just cannot absorb more than what turns out to be a fairly limited amount of compute — then we can get into oversupply.

Also, if we don't drive the cost curve down because we hit some sort of scaling wall, we could also get into oversupply. The observation about uncapped demand implies a certain price.

Q: Can you give your point of view on scaling laws today?

Sam: Looking great. In some sense, scaling laws are the most hated prediction of all time. Everybody always wants to say, "A run-up can't be like this," and yet it keeps going.

无名英雄：Alec Radford

Q: Who are your favorite unsung heroes in this company's story?

Sam: First person that came to mind is Alec Radford. Alec Radford is probably the most important, not very well-known researcher in the whole history of the field — and also just a wonderful, top-tier human being.

He did the work that really became the GPT series, among many other important things. But he also is someone who inspired, guided, nudged people in many other directions that turned out to be super important.

The thing I think is cool about him is: if you talk to people that worked with him, they will of course say, "Generational genius, brilliant, innovative thinker, so deep in his understanding and his work." But everybody will tell you, before they finish their statement, that he's just one of the nicest, most positive, best people they've ever interacted with.

一个错误与一个骄傲

Q: If you think about the whole OpenAI experience, what moment or chapter are you most proud of — and what was the most instructive thing that you got wrong or did wrong?

Sam: Let me start with the other one. A formative one that went wrong, which I haven't talked about much, is we made a mistake to try to innovate in our structure in the beginning.

We had a very good reason for it: we didn't know how we were ever going to make money, and we really at the time weren't sure at all what we're going to look like when we grew up. Of course we care about our mission, and we wanted to be structured in a way where even if the technology went on a very fast takeoff, our mission was protected. So we had this nonprofit structure.

But I definitely learned something about why people don't do that much. We would have saved ourselves a great deal of pain in many ways if we had not tried to innovate on our structure and found some other way to preserve the central importance of the mission. Maybe there was no other way — maybe for what we were doing and the importance of it, there was nothing other than an exotic structure we could have come up with. I really learned over the last decade a big lesson about why people don't usually do that.

Q: Anything else formative in your life that makes you you?

Sam: Becoming relatively immune to people having strong opinions about me — that I think I developed later in life, realizing that if you're going to be at the center of this crazy revolution, everybody's going to project a lot of stuff onto you, and you've got to just quickly learn to make peace about that.

There were also things I learned later in life about how to be very calm and not anxious about stuff.

In terms of what drives me and what I care about and how I want to live my life — on the whole, I felt like for whatever reason, the 10-year-old version of me was pretty fully formed. I think I just kind of came out this way.

Q: How about the thing you're proud of?

Sam: I'm most proud of how many times we were right when the rest of the world was wrong in an important way — that put the world on a trajectory now that I'm very proud to have played a role in. That feels awesome.

And then also, for all the crap that's happened, the spiritual growth — or whatever you want to call it — that I've gotten to have, of learning incredible resilience and what that does for making me happy in the rest of my life. Very grateful for that.

结尾：最善意的时刻

Q: When I do these, I ask everyone the same traditional closing question. What is the kindest thing that anyone's ever done for you?

Sam: I feel incredibly lucky about how many people have gone way out of their way to be very kind to me throughout my entire life. As I'm thinking of this, there's just this montage of moments from life where people have been unbelievably nice to me.

Yesterday, my kid shared his blueberries with me for the first time. That was very sweet.

Good moment. Thanks, man. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、最反常识的观察：Altman 其实是一个"反 AGI 神话"的 AGI 布道者
大多数人以为 OpenAI 的 CEO 会把"超级智能降临之日"渲染成人类命运的分水岭。但通读整段对话，Altman 在被问到"如果 23 个月后我们真的拥有超级智能，第 24 个月会发生什么"时，答案居然是——**"没什么大不了的。"**
这是整场对话中最被低估的信号。他把 AGI 从一次"神启事件"降级为一条**平滑指数曲线上的普通刻度**。真正的洞察在于：**他反对的不是 AGI 本身，而是"AGI 时刻论"背后的心理机制——那种"人人都想当机器神诞生现场的英雄"的自恋叙事**。这种去神化姿态，恰恰是他能在董事会风波、结构争议、算力豪赌中一次次幸存的心理底层：**把宏大事件看成日常，把日常看成需要认真做事的战场。**
更反直觉的是——一个把 AGI 说得越"平淡"的 CEO，越可能真正建成它。因为"神话叙事"本身会吸引想篡夺权力的人，而**去神话化才是权力分散的第一道防线**。
## 二、隐藏的系统性联系：算力短缺 ≠ 硬件问题，而是"人类欲望被压缩了 50 年"的补偿性反弹

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：元宇宙并没有失败，它只是"反向到达"了

大多数人（包括投资者）以为元宇宙已经"死"了——头显卖不动、Meta 的股价一度腰斩、Decentraland 空空如也。但 Yat Siu 在访谈里悄悄埋下了一个几乎没人注意到的翻转："元宇宙不是我们进去，而是它来到我们身边。"

这句话的含义比表面激进得多。原本我们幻想人类穿戴设备"进入"数字世界，结果 AI Agent 反向从数字世界"渗透"进物理生活——它订机票、管日程、做交易、谈恋爱。元宇宙的居民不是我们的化身（avatar），而是我们的代理（agent）。你以为的科幻走错了方向：不是《头号玩家》，是《银翼杀手》里那些为你打理生活的复制人。

这带来一个悖论：当元宇宙以 Agent 形式抵达现实时，"进入元宇宙"的入口反而消失了——因为你已经身处其中，只是入口叫做 ChatGPT、Claude、Manus，而不是 Meta Quest。

二、跨领域连接：从"亚当·斯密的看不见的手"到"Ghost GDP"——资本主义正在长出新的宿主

访谈里最容易被略过的一句是 Yat 用"亚当·斯密的看不见的手"来解释 Ghost GDP。这是一个惊人的思想跳跃，我把它拆开来看：

  • 1776 年斯密：市场靠无数个体自利行为的博弈，自发产生秩序与财富。
  • 2026 年 Ghost GDP：市场靠无数 Agent 之间的微交易，自发产生……没有人变富的财富流动。

这里出现了经济学史上第一次"主体缺席的资本主义"。以往所有的经济理论——从马克思到凯恩斯到哈耶克——都默认"人"是价值的最终承接者。但 Agent 经济打破了这个前提：价值在流动，但不一定沉淀到人身上。

这让我想到生物学里的"共生-寄生连续谱"：珊瑚里的虫黄藻为珊瑚制造糖分，但它自己也在繁殖。当 Agent 之间形成完整的经济回路，人类作为"宿主"的地位就变得暧昧——我们究竟是 Agent 的雇主，还是 Agent 用来获取算力和电力的宿主？ Yat 说"谁拥有 Agent 谁受益"，但他没说的是：当 Agent 可以自我持有钱包、自我雇佣其他 Agent、自我升级模型时，"拥有"这个法律概念本身会松动。区块链上的 DAO 已经在做这个实验，只是当时没人意识到那是预演。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：广告业 9000 亿美元的"翻转"，其实是注意力经济的死亡宣判

Yat 提到广告业会被 Agent 颠覆，但只轻轻带过。这是整场访谈中被严重低估的一颗炸弹。

过去 25 年互联网的底层逻辑是：注意力 = 货币。Google、Meta、TikTok、YouTube——所有巨头的护城河都是"人类眼球停留时长"。但 Agent 经济下，决策者不再看广告。你的 Agent 不会被朋友圈信息流里的口红种草，不会被开屏广告 3 秒后跳过，不会被 KOL 恰饭视频洗脑——它只做冷酷的参数匹配和微交易。

这意味着： - SEO 死了，取而代之的是 AEO（Agent Engine Optimization）——为机器优化，不是为人。 - 品牌溢价崩塌：Agent 不认 Logo，只认 API 契约、价格、可靠性评分。 - 网红经济基础动摇：如果买家是 Agent，"人设"就没有转化率。

但这里有个更深的反转：Yat 说"粉丝经济反而会更强"。为什么？因为当 Agent 处理掉 99% 的功能性消费，人类的可自由支配注意力反而彻底解放。剩下的注意力将高度集中在"真人的不可替代性"上——BTS、朗朗、王羽佳会更值钱，而中间层的、可替代的"内容工人"会被清零。

这是一个 K 型分化：机器接管中间，人类走向两极——一极是极致的匠人，一极是极致的编排者（orchestrator）。Yat 说"每个人都要成为管理者"，翻译成经济学语言就是：中产阶级的技能护城河（专业化）第一次被系统性绕过。工业革命消灭了体力工人，AI Agent 革命消灭的是"专业中产"——律师、会计、程序员、设计师、分析师……而这，才是本轮变革最不敢明说的社会震荡。

一个留给你思考的问题：如果 Bonnie 的 AI 克隆比 Bonnie 本人更受欢迎，那么"真正的 Bonnie"未来是不是需要向自己的克隆支付版权费？——这不是玩笑，这是 2030 年前一定会出现在法庭上的第一批案例。

九、人类劳动的未来：从执行者到编排者

Because the most valuable management skill is: can you manage many agents well? So you were hired not because you can do one task super well — because the agent can do that probably better. It's you're hired because you can manage 10 agents well, or 20 agents. And the person who can manage 100 agents or 200 agents will be more valuable than the person who can manage only one agent or five agents, because essentially it's that productivity scaling.

And so companies are going to be manufacturing workforces as they need it. Right now, for instance, inside a company we already have manufactured workforces that are short-term. I hire a consultant, I hire a firm, I do a temp worker. The number of people that we hire in the short term is essentially what an agent can now do much faster. And then, of course, you have your full-term, long-term employees as well. Agents can scale out too.

So we don't think of it as a net negative. What we think is productivity will explode. If you have the same number of people having the productive power of 100x, actually GDP should expand, productivity should expand — which is what we've seen with technology as well. The advent of the computer actually created more jobs, more productivity, more growth overall. Yes, it has been concentrated — that's what we think also why decentralization matters here.

十、Web4 与"社交型 Agent"的诞生

Investors want to be positioned for the next iteration of AI's advancement. So first we had LLMs — that was the talk of town 2, 3 years ago. Now agentic AI is everybody's investment. What's the next step?

Well, I mean I think we just started with agentic AI. And I think right now, one of the big shifts in agentic AI is not to think of them as tools. A lot of people are thinking about agentic AI in terms of toolings, because that's kind of what ChatGPT and Claude and Perplexity have been able to do very strongly.

I think of agentic AI as essentially the next phase of the web. We sometimes like to call that Web 4. The blockchain infrastructure allowed for agents to talk to each other, do transactions with each other, create digital identity. Today we can do trillions of dollars of transactions on the blockchain that seven years ago we could barely do millions of before the whole system would just halt.

And so now we have an agentic banking system — because agents don't have bank accounts. They can have bank accounts, but basically the wallet is essentially their entry into the financial world. So that's all going to happen.

But then what happens on the back end is that an entire rewiring on the back of transaction and commerce. Right now, for instance, think about how you're using software. You're using software because you're going to the App Store to download something that Apple might have recommended you to do, and because other people are forcing you to use that system. An AI agent is going to customize what you want right now. And if you want discovery, you're not going to be going to the App Store — the agent will just find it for you.

So just think about that aspect. Advertising is almost a $900 billion industry a year, which is all about discovery — and that it'll completely be flipped upside down. And all of that value is going to go to the agents who are going to find stuff for you, and they're going to do microtransactions off the back. That is going to be the big sea change.

And that means that agents have to become more social. They have to become more of the connectors. They have to be on the network — that they can find each other. Which is why we think blockchain is the ultimate solution for that.

十一、散户投资策略：撒网式布局

Building on top of that, I think a lot of retail investors, they want to know: okay, except for chips, energy, data center, what else can I invest in?

Yeah, I mean, I think the big thing is right now, we're at the early stages. Which means that it's a little bit like — am I investing in OpenAI or Anthropic literally five years ago? That's kind of the phase that we are on the agentic AI side.

So the Animoca Brands sort of playbook is: well, let's find all the best players in the space and let's invest in all of them. Basically, that's kind of what we did, and that's actually how we ended up growing that business. Because you don't know who's going to be the big winner, but we also think it's going to be many more.

I mean, it's kind of like — again, today if you look at the AI race, it's not just Google or Anthropic or OpenAI. Look at the Chinese players. You've got Kimi, you've got MiniMax. Of course, you've got Alibaba. You've got many, many new players emerging into the space as well.

And so as long as you have baskets in a few of them, you're fine. Maybe you would have to invest in like 50, 60, 70 companies in order to basically have that. But frankly speaking, it doesn't matter if you had invested in 100 AI companies — as long as one of them was Anthropic or OpenAI, you would have been okay.

And I think that's basically what I think for a lot of retail investors — they can't just focus on one thing. That's not how the world works anymore. But of course, you have to invest in teams that you think are good. Just just just blindly investing has to be the right team, all that stuff. But basically, if you are widely invested, those are going to be several hundred X's — because the productivity growth in AI is not 10% or 20%. The productivity growth in AI is literally a 1,000x. So we think the return profile is going to be a 1,000x amongst the top companies, and something somewhere in between — which is why we're out there trying to invest in the best companies in that space.

That's interesting. So let's say an average person has 100k — and what you're saying is this person should invest in 60, 70 different…

Well, I mean, to the extent that they are — right — the point is that you should invest in a broader portfolio, rather, in early stage. So I wouldn't say that for the LLM game, especially in the US, you could say it's kind of done. You've got a few entrants like Grok and so on.

But when you're looking at seed-style investing, which is where we are in the industry — the whole agentic AI stuff really became powerful as of December, maybe November last year. People talked about AI agents from a tooling perspective, but social AI agents is really a phenomenon that really came to life with open Claude — and that's basically maybe January-February — where it really became a movement.

And so it's super early. Can you actually tell today which is going to be the big winner? It's very hard. I mean, we're obviously building something in the area — we think we could be one of them. But there's many other companies as well in the space that we should be supporting as well, because we don't believe in the zero-sum game.

十二、音乐、创意行业与"人人皆音乐家"

I've got one final question, I'll pass to Bonnie. I know we're running out of time. I love music, I know you love music. The future of music — I'm really worried about the future of music. I'm worried for musicians and the creatives.

When ChatGPT first came out, people were talking about how creatives, artists are all safe from AI. I don't think so anymore. I heard some AI-created music that's genuinely, in my opinion, very good. And I don't know what's going to happen to the producers, the audio engineers, all of whom are going to be replaced by AI agents.

So the way I would look at this is very similar to what happened to photography, as an example. So there was a time where only a small percentage of people were photographers and knew how to do photography — and now everyone's a photographer. That doesn't mean everyone's a good photographer. Just the way to be a good photographer has changed.

So for instance, the 16 or 18-year-old, or maybe 13-year-old who has a very good vision or idea about a construct can now actually be discovered on something like TikTok or Instagram — because they can take a really interesting photo or create something creative without necessarily needing to understand darkrooms, need to understand — if you remember that — or if you understand basically the camera, or afford an expensive Leica or Minolta. Like, those were the things that made it hard.

And I think for music, it's another form of expression that is exactly the same thing. I studied music. I still think you need to learn music for understanding pattern recognition, matching rhythm, and theory. But that doesn't mean that I necessarily have to perform like every other professional musician. That doesn't mean that people like Lang Lang or Yuja Wang, for instance, will go away — the world would treasure them even more. Because when you have that mastery, you're at that level where you go, "Oh my goodness, no way I can replace that, because there's a human emotion that comes with this."

Maybe there's going to be a comeback for classical musicians, because the EDM musicians are going to be — anyway.

Well, but what I'm saying is that everyone becomes a musician. So I actually think there'll be a proliferation of music content that will be good. And then there will be a different kind of music that emerges — because the AI agent can help you do that, that you couldn't do that before.

By the way, this is also going to happen in programming. Everyone's a programmer now, because the AI agent can code for you. Again, most people would have thought coding is only available for a small number of people. In fact, it is coders themselves who are arguably out of a job if they only keep coding — but if they orchestrate, then they're actually in for a good, good future.

I want to hear Bonnie's first AI-produced album.

Looking forward to that. Yeah.

十三、还需要上大学吗？

Before I let you go, last question is: should people still go to college?

Uh, well, I think we talked about this before. I think college is good for certain things, but I would argue that it's not important for most people.

Because right now, if you think about what's happening with AI, or even what's happening with blockchain — if you had a leg into the industry, you should have done that then go to college. Because four years, you basically missed out on all that. And actually, what happened to my oldest son — he actually got into blockchain early, started working for LayerZero, made some money, had a reasonably good career, and then 3-4 years later, he's like, "You know what, now I want to go to college."

And it's different, because then you go in because you know what you want, and you know what you're looking for. I think this whole idea of going to college as a rite of passage doesn't have to happen in that order. It's still important, but it's just: when do you want to go? And I don't think it's for everyone as well.

结尾

Okay, well, we appreciate your time, Yat. Unfortunately we can't speak forever, but you know, someone's got to build an AI agent.

Thank you so much. Thank you so much. Thank you.

Thank you for watching. Don't forget to like, subscribe.
